aarons-rod-and-the-bronze-serpent-nehush.context_blurb:
The book of Numbers follows the Israelites through their wilderness years after the escape from Egypt, led by Moses and his older brother Aaron, who became Israel's first high priest. Two strange signs from those years gather around a staff and a bronze snake, and the second sign comes back to trouble a king of Judah centuries later.

The first story begins with jealousy. Tribe after tribe muttered that Aaron had no special claim to the priesthood, so God set Moses a test. Each tribal chief handed over his staff, one for every tribe of Israel, and Moses left all twelve overnight in the Tabernacle, the tent where Israel worshipped.

At dawn eleven staffs were still dead wood. Aaron's had come alive: in a single night it had sprouted buds, opened into blossom and set ripe almonds. The almond is the first tree to flower in that land each year, so the staff carried a sign of first fruits. Aaron's staff stood for the house of Levi, and the sign ended the quarrel: Israel's priests would come from the tribe of Levi and from no other.

The flowering staff became a treasure. The New Testament letter to the Hebrews places it inside the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-covered chest Israel carried through the desert, beside the golden pot of manna and the stone tablets of the covenant. Later Jewish tradition argued over whether those things sat inside the chest or next to it, but Hebrews puts all three within.

The second story comes further along the march. The people turned on God and Moses again, crying that they had been led out of Egypt only to perish in the desert. Numbers says God answered with fiery serpents, snakes whose bite probably burned like fire with venom, and many people died. When the people repented, Moses made a serpent of bronze and raised it on a pole, and anyone bitten who looked up at it lived.

Centuries passed, and the bronze serpent was still kept in Jerusalem, where worshippers had started burning incense to it as if it were a god. King Hezekiah of Judah smashed it and mocked the pieces with a name, Nehushtan, a pun on nehoshet, the Hebrew word for brass, as if to say the relic was nothing more than a lump of metal.

abraham-called-from-ur-to-canaan-and-the.context_blurb:
Genesis, the first book of the Bible, opens the story of Israel's founding family with Abram, an old man, together with Sarai his wife and Lot, his brother's son. Some four thousand years ago, the story says, God called Abram away from home to walk hundreds of miles toward a country no one in his family had seen, and a chain of promises, new names and strange visitors followed.

The family set out from Ur of the Chaldees, a mighty walled city beside a southern river in Mesopotamia, and paused at Haran on the road north before turning toward Canaan. When Abram reached Shechem in Canaan's hill country, God appeared to him under a great oak and promised the land to his children's children, and Abram marked the place by building an altar there to God.

Years went by. Abram grew rich, but he had no son, and a servant stood to inherit everything. One night God took him outside and pointed him at the sky: he was to count the stars of heaven if he could, because his descendants would be as many.

The promise became a covenant, and the covenant brought new names. God renamed Abram as Abraham, meaning father of a multitude, and on that same day renamed his wife too: Sarai became Sarah.

Then came the visitors. Abraham was resting at his tent door in the noon heat, among the oaks of Mamre, when three strangers arrived, and he hurried to feed them with a calf and fresh cakes. One of them said that within a year Sarah would have a son. Sarah, overhearing from inside the tent, laughed to herself at the thought of a baby at her age, so when the boy came he was named Isaac, which means "he laughs".

Abraham's story holds an even stranger meeting. Years earlier Abram had rescued Lot from four raiding kings, and on his way home he was met by Melchizedek, both king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brought out bread and wine and blessed him. His name means "king of righteousness", and Jewish and Christian writers have argued about him ever since.

The three visitors went on toward Sodom, and the cities of the plain burned under fire and brimstone. The angels told Lot and his family to run and not look back. Lot's wife turned for one last look at the home she was leaving and became a pillar of salt. Travellers later pointed to salt formations near the Dead Sea as what remained of her.

the-binding-of-isaac-on-mount-moriah.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, God tests the old patriarch Abraham by commanding him to take his son — the long-awaited child of promise he had waited decades for — up a mountain in the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt sacrifice. Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey, cuts the wood for the fire, and walks three days with the boy and two young servants. The moment the angel calls down from heaven at the last second echoes through the New Testament and the Quran. Source: Genesis 22 KJV.

jacobs-ladder-at-bethel-and-the-wrestlin.context_blurb:
Jacob, the younger twin son of Isaac, is the great schemer of the book of Genesis. He tricks his brother and deceives his blind father, then runs for his life and meets God twice in the wilderness: once in a dream of a ladder, and once in a wrestling match that leaves him limping, with a new name his descendants will carry.

Jacob's twin, Esau, was a hunter. One day Esau came in from the fields half-starved and begged for some of the red lentil stew Jacob was cooking, and for that single bowl he handed over his birthright, the elder son's right to lead the family and take the double share. From the red stew he got the nickname Edom, "Red."

Later their father Isaac, old and blind, prepared to give Esau his blessing. Their mother Rebekah helped Jacob steal it: she covered his smooth hands and neck with goatskins so that he would feel as hairy as his brother. Isaac said the voice was Jacob's but the hands were Esau's, and he blessed him anyway.

Esau swore to kill him, and Jacob fled. When night caught him far from any town, he lay down on the bare ground with one of the stones of that place under his head for a pillow. He dreamed of a ladder standing on the earth with its top in heaven, and on it angels ascending and descending. When he woke he was shaken, saying God was in this place and he had not known it. He set up his stone pillow as a pillar, poured oil on it, and named the place Bethel, "house of God"; it had been called Luz before.

Twenty years later Jacob came home, rich, with wives and children, and Esau was coming to meet him. On the last night he sent his two wives, his two maids and his eleven sons across the ford of the Jabbok and stayed behind alone. The river's name sounds like the Hebrew word for wrestling.

That night a stranger seized him, and the two wrestled until the sky grew light. When he could not throw Jacob, he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh and wrenched the hip out of its socket, and Jacob limped ever after. Still Jacob held on and would not let go without a blessing. So the stranger gave him a new name: no more Jacob, but Israel, because he had striven with God and with men and won. Jacob called the place Peniel, saying he had seen God face to face and lived.

josephs-coat-of-many-colors-and-the-pit-.context_blurb:
Joseph was the favourite son of the patriarch Jacob, and Genesis tells how that favour nearly killed him. A splendid coat, a pair of boastful dreams, a dry pit, a caravan of spice traders and a slave market carried him from his father's tents to an Egyptian prison, and from there, in time, to power.

Jacob loved Joseph best of all his sons, because he was the child of Jacob's old age, born to his beloved wife Rachel, and to show it Jacob gave him his famous coat of many colours; his older brothers hated him for it. The Hebrew words are hard to translate, and some read them as a long coat with sleeves, but the King James phrase is the one that stuck.

Joseph made things worse by telling his dreams. In one, the brothers' sheaves of grain bowed down to his; in another, the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowed to him. When the brothers saw him coming across the fields, they sneered to one another, "Behold, this dreamer cometh," and began to plot his death.

At Dothan they tore off his coat and threw him into a dry pit. As they sat down to eat, they saw a caravan of Ishmeelites out of Gilead coming down the road, camels loaded with spices, balm and myrrh for Egypt. Judah spoke up: what good would it do to kill their own brother? So they sold Joseph to the traders for twenty pieces of silver.

They killed a young goat, dipped the coat in its blood and sent it to their father with a cold message, not even using Joseph's name: Jacob should look and judge whether this was his son's coat or not. Jacob knew it at once, tore his clothes and mourned his son for many days.

In Egypt, Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh's guard, bought Joseph and soon put him in charge of his whole household. But Potiphar's wife grabbed at him, and when he ran from her she kept his garment in her hand and used it to accuse him falsely. For the second time a piece of Joseph's clothing was turned into lying evidence, and he was thrown into prison.

In prison two royal servants who had angered the king told him their dreams: Pharaoh's chief butler and his chief baker. In three days, Joseph said, the butler would be given back his post and the baker would be hanged, and both things happened. The butler forgot all about him for two years.

joseph-reveals-himself-i-am-joseph-your-.context_blurb:
Joseph, the favourite son whom his brothers sold into slavery, had risen to become the second most powerful man in Egypt. Then famine drove his brothers to his door, and Genesis tells one of the great reunion stories of the world, full of tests, tears and secrets.

When famine reached Canaan, Jacob packed off ten of his sons to Egypt for grain, and they bowed with their faces to the ground before the governor of the land. The governor was Joseph; he knew them at once, but after more than twenty years they did not know him.

Joseph hid who he was and spoke harshly to them through an interpreter. He accused them of being spies, come to see where the land was weak. He would keep one brother in prison while the rest went home to fetch their youngest, Benjamin, and he chose Simeon, binding him before their eyes; Jewish commentators say he passed over Reuben because Reuben had once tried to save him.

The brothers did not know the governor understood their Hebrew. Talking among themselves, they confessed that this trouble was God's punishment for what they had done to their brother, whose pleading they had refused to hear when they sold him. Joseph turned away and wept.

When they came back with Benjamin, Joseph gave them a feast at his house. To their amazement they were seated in order of birth, from the firstborn down to the youngest, something no Egyptian steward could have known. Then Joseph sent them food from his own table, and Benjamin, his only full brother, got five times as much as any of the others, a test of whether the old jealousy would flare up again.

At last Judah offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, for their old father's sake. Joseph could hold back no longer. He sent every Egyptian out of the room and wept so loudly that the whole house heard; then he told his brothers that he was Joseph and asked whether his father was still alive. They were too terrified to answer. Years later he would tell them that what they had meant for evil, God had meant for good.

moses-in-the-basket-of-bulrushes.context_blurb: A new Pharaoh has arisen in Egypt who did not know Joseph. He enslaves the Hebrews and orders a horror against every newborn Hebrew boy. A Levite woman gives birth to a healthy son and hides him for as long as she can — then floats him down the Nile in a waterproofed basket of reeds, with the baby's older sister watching from the bank. The scene opens the whole Exodus story. Source: Exodus 1–2 KJV.

the-burning-bush-and-the-name-i-am.context_blurb: Years after fleeing Egypt as a young man, Moses has become a shepherd in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law. He leads the sheep to the backside of the desert and comes to the mountain of God, where he sees a bush that is on fire but is not being burned up. The voice that speaks from the bush gives him both his life's work and the great mysterious name of God that the Hebrew Bible treats as holiest of all. Source: Exodus 3–4 KJV.

the-ten-plagues-of-egypt.context_blurb: The book of Exodus tells how Moses and his brother Aaron go before Pharaoh and demand that the Hebrews be let out of Egypt. Each refusal brings a plague — ten in all, each worse than the last — that batter the land, the water, the livestock, and finally the firstborn of Egypt. Pharaoh breaks and lets them go, and the Hebrews march out carrying unleavened bread and bitter herbs for a Passover meal that would be kept once a year ever after. Source: Exodus 5–12 KJV.

the-parting-of-the-red-sea.context_blurb: The Hebrews have marched out of Egypt and are camped at the edge of the Red Sea when Pharaoh changes his mind one last time and sends his chariots after them. Moses stretches out his hand with his staff; God sends a wind that blows all night; the waters stand up on both sides and the Hebrews walk through on dry ground. When the Egyptian chariots follow in after them, the walls of water come back down. Source: Exodus 14 KJV.

sinai-the-tablets-and-the-golden-calf.context_blurb: Three months out of Egypt, the Hebrews reach the foot of a mountain in the Sinai wilderness. Thunder, cloud, and the long blast of a trumpet come down on it. Moses climbs up alone and stays forty days and forty nights. He comes down carrying two stone tablets inscribed by the finger of God — and finds that in his absence, Aaron and the people have made themselves a different god of molten gold. Source: Exodus 19–32 KJV.

noah-and-the-ark-the-raven-the-dove-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, God sees that the whole human race has grown wicked and resolves to wipe it from the earth with a great flood. He chooses one man — Noah — and tells him to build a wooden ark, and to bring his family and pairs of every kind of animal onto it. Rain falls, the fountains of the deep break open, the ark floats, and when the waters finally begin to go down Noah sends out two different birds in turn to see whether dry land has come back. Source: Genesis 6–9 KJV.

hagar-and-ishmael-sent-into-the-wilderne.context_blurb:
Genesis tells the story of Abraham's family as a tale of promises and bitter rivalries. One of its most moving stories belongs to Hagar, an Egyptian servant woman, and her son, who were driven out into the desert and saved there by a well.

Abraham's wife Sarah could not have children, so she gave Hagar, her Egyptian maid, to her husband to bear a child for him, and Hagar gave Abraham his first son, Ishmael.

Years later Sarah bore Isaac in her old age, and she demanded that the servant and her boy be driven out. Early one morning Abraham set some bread and a skin bottle of water on Hagar's shoulder and sent her away with the child, and gave her nothing else. She wandered lost in the wilderness of Beersheba, in the dry south, until the water was gone.

Hagar could not bear to watch her son die of thirst. She laid him under a bush and went and sat down about a bowshot away, so that she would not have to see him die, and she wept. Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water close by; she filled the bottle and gave the boy a drink, and he lived. Genesis says Ishmael grew up in the desert and became an archer.

It was not the first time Hagar had met God in the wilderness. Years before, fleeing Sarah's harshness while she was pregnant, she had met an angel at a spring on the road to Shur, and there she did what no one else in Genesis does: she gave God a name, El-Roi, "the God who sees me." The well was afterwards called Beer-lahai-roi, "the well of the Living One who sees me."

deborah-barak-sisera-and-jaels-tent-peg.context_blurb:
In the age of the Judges, before Israel had kings, a prophetess named Deborah led the people. The book of Judges tells her story twice, once in prose and once in an ancient victory song, and it ends with a general killed not by a warrior but by a woman with a tent peg.

Deborah judged Israel sitting under a palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim, between Ramah and Bethel, and people called it the palm of Deborah.

Israel was groaning under Jabin, the Canaanite king who ruled from Hazor, and his general Sisera, so Deborah called the war-captain Barak and gave him God's command to raise ten thousand men and go to war. Barak would go only if Deborah went with him. She agreed, but warned him that the glory of the day would go to a woman.

Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots, and for twenty years he had used them to grind Israel down; iron was still rare and costly then, and Israel's foot soldiers had nothing that could face them on open ground. Barak mustered on Mount Tabor, and Sisera's chariots rolled down into the valley of the river Kishon. A sudden storm turned the riverbed to mud, the heavy wheels stuck fast, and Sisera's army broke and ran.

Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. She welcomed him in, hid him under a mantle, and when he asked for water she gave him milk instead, butter in a lordly dish as the song remembers it. Warm and full, he fell into an exhausted sleep. Then Jael took up a hammer and a tent peg, crept to him and drove the peg through his temple. Deborah's warning to Barak had come true.

Deborah's victory song in Judges 5 refuses to give all the credit to spears or to a tent peg. It says heaven itself fought: the stars fought from their courses against Sisera, and the river Kishon swept his army away.

Its last verses leave the battle behind for a Canaanite palace, with Sisera's mother at a latticed window, peering down the road and asking why his chariot was so slow to come home, while her ladies assured her the men must be sharing out the spoils. The listener knows that her son lies dead in Jael's tent.

gideon-the-fleece-the-three-hundred-and-.context_blurb:
The book of Judges tells of Israel's wild early days, before it had kings, when one hero after another rose to save the tribes. For seven years Midianite raiders on camels had swept in at every harvest and stripped the land bare, until the Israelites hid in caves. Then a frightened farmer named Gideon was called to fight them.

The call found Gideon hiding. He was beating out his wheat in a winepress, a sunken pit meant for treading grapes, because threshing on an open floor would have shown the raiders where the grain was. An angel appeared and greeted the trembling man as a mighty man of valour, a promise about what he would become rather than a picture of what he was.

Gideon wanted proof. He laid a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asked that by morning the fleece be wet with dew while all the ground around it stayed dry, and at dawn he wrung a bowlful of water out of it. Then, in case wool simply held the damp, he asked for the reverse, and the next morning the fleece was dry and the ground was wet with dew. People still speak of "putting out a fleece" when they ask for a sign.

Gideon mustered thirty-two thousand men. God told him the army was too big: if they won, Israel would boast that it had saved itself. So Gideon told everyone who was afraid to go home, and twenty-two thousand left, leaving ten thousand.

That was still too many. God had Gideon take them to the stream and sort them by the way they drank. Most knelt down to drink, but three hundred lapped the water with their tongues, the way a dog laps, and those three hundred were the men Gideon kept.

With his three hundred, Gideon surrounded the great Midianite camp at night. Each man carried a trumpet, and a blazing torch concealed in an earthen jar. At his signal they blew the trumpets, smashed the jars so the torches flared up all round the camp, and roared their war-cry: "The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon!" In the sudden light and noise the Midianites panicked and turned their swords on one another, and the three hundred hardly had to fight.

He grows up to be the strongest and strangest of Israel's judges, a one-man wrecking crew against the Philistines who makes riddles, tears a lion apart with his bare hands, and finally brings down a pagan temple on his own head. Source: Judges 13–16 KJV.

ruth-gleaning-in-the-field-of-boaz.context_blurb: The book of Ruth opens in the days of the Judges, when a famine drives a Bethlehemite named Elimelech to leave Israel with his wife Naomi and their two sons. The family settles in a neighboring country east of the Dead Sea, where the sons both marry local women. When all three men die, Naomi walks home empty-handed; one of her foreign daughters-in-law refuses to be sent away and walks beside her. The rest of the book is about how that foreign widow is gathered into Israel in a barley-field at Bethlehem. Source: Ruth KJV.

joshua-at-jericho-the-trumpets-and-the-w.context_blurb:
The book of Joshua tells how the Israelites entered Canaan after forty years in the wilderness. Their first great obstacle was Jericho, a walled city on the plain beyond the Jordan, and the story of its fall is one of the strangest battles in the Hebrew Bible: two spies, a woman on a rooftop, a mysterious swordsman and a week of marching.

Moses died on Mount Nebo within sight of the promised land, and his lieutenant Joshua son of Nun took his place, led the people across the Jordan on dry ground and turned toward Jericho.

Joshua first sent two spies into the city. Rahab, a woman whose house was built into the city wall, hid them on her flat roof under stalks of flax she had laid out in rows to dry. She let them down from her window on a rope, and they made her a promise: if she tied a scarlet cord in that same window, her house alone would be spared when the city fell.

Near Jericho, Joshua met a man standing with a drawn sword and asked whether he was for Israel or for its enemies. The stranger said neither; he had come as captain of God's own army. Joshua fell on his face and was told to take off his sandal, for the ground was holy.

The plan for taking the city was like no other. For six days the army marched once around the walls in silence, led by seven priests who walked ahead of the sacred ark sounding trumpets made of rams' horns. When the seventh day dawned they circled the city seven times; then the priests blew, the people gave a great shout, and the walls fell down flat.

God had commanded that all the plunder of Jericho be destroyed or given to the sanctuary. But at the next battle the little town of Ai routed Israel, and Joshua cast lots to find the guilty man. A soldier named Achan confessed that he had stolen a fine robe from Babylon, along with silver and a bar of gold, and hidden them under the floor of his tent.

choose-you-this-day-whom-ye-shall-serve-.context_blurb:
Joshua succeeded Moses as the leader of Israel, took the people across the Jordan and led the conquest of Canaan in the book that bears his name. In its last chapter he is an old man, and he gathers the tribes for a farewell that gave the world a line still quoted everywhere.

Joshua told the assembled tribes to choose that very day whom they would serve, and he ended with the words that have travelled around the world: whatever the rest of them chose, he and his house would serve the God of Israel.

He held the farewell at Shechem, in the hills of Ephraim, the old covenant town where long before Abraham had pitched his tent and built his first altar in Canaan, and where Jacob had paid a hundred silver pieces for a field.

The old warrior had seen wonders. Years earlier he had led the march around Jericho, with seven priests carrying trumpets of rams' horn before the Ark. For six days the people circled the city once a day, and on the seventh day they went around it seven times; then the trumpets sounded, the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat.

The book ends with two burials. Joshua was laid in his grave, and so at last were the bones of Joseph, brought up from Egypt by his people and carried all through the wilderness years; they buried them at Shechem, in the field Jacob had bought.

david-and-goliath.context_blurb:
The duel of David and Goliath in 1 Samuel 17 is the most famous underdog story in the Western world. A shepherd boy with a sling faces a giant champion in bronze armour, and the story is full of small, exact details that make it come alive.

The Philistines and King Saul's Israelites were camped on two hills, with the Valley of Elah lying between them. Twice a day, at dawn and at dusk, the Philistine giant Goliath came striding down in his bronze armour and challenged the Israelites to send out one man to fight him, and for forty days not one of them went down to meet him.

David was not with the army. His father Jesse sent him from the sheepfold with food for his three eldest brothers, an ephah of parched grain and ten loaves of bread, and ten cheeses for their captain.

When David offered to fight, Saul dressed him in the king's own armour, but David took it off. Instead he went to the brook, picked five smooth stones out of the water, and dropped them into his shepherd's bag.

Goliath cursed him, and David answered that the giant came with sword and spear and shield, but that he himself came in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel's armies, so that all the earth would know there was a God in Israel. David ran at him, slung one stone, and it sank into Goliath's forehead, and the giant fell on his face to the earth. Scholars still puzzle over how a helmeted giant left his brow exposed.

The story has a dark sequel. Years later, fleeing King Saul, David came unarmed to the priest Ahimelech at the sanctuary town of Nob, and the priest fed him with the holy bread and gave him Goliath's own sword. For that kindness Saul ordered Doeg the Edomite to cut down Ahimelech along with eighty-five priests of the town.

A puzzle hides in the text as well. At 2 Samuel 21:19 the credit for killing Goliath of Gath goes to another man of Bethlehem, Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim. The parallel verse in 1 Chronicles smooths it over by saying that Elhanan killed Lahmi, Goliath's brother.

david-and-jonathan-the-sworn-brotherhood.context_blurb:
Jonathan was the eldest son of King Saul of Israel and heir to the throne. From the day the young David killed Goliath, the books of Samuel say, Jonathan loved him as his own soul, and their sworn brotherhood held even when Saul tried to kill David, and even though David was marked to take the crown Jonathan should have worn.

Jonathan sealed the friendship by stripping off his own royal robe and his garments and giving them to David, together with his sword, his bow and his belt: the outward signs of a prince handed to the man who would one day take his place.

Saul grew jealous of David's fame. Twice, while David played the harp to soothe the king's black moods, Saul seized his javelin and flung it at him, meaning to pin him to the wall, and twice David slipped aside.

David fled and hid in a field, and Jonathan arranged a signal. He would come out as if for archery practice and shoot three arrows past a servant boy: if he shouted that the arrows lay on this side, David was safe, and if he shouted that they lay beyond, David must run. The arrows went beyond. The two friends met in secret one last time, wept on each other's necks, and swore an oath that God would stand between them, and between my seed and thy seed forever: their children, and their children's children. Years later that oath saved Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth.

Then the Philistines broke Israel's army on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan and his brothers were cut down around their father, and Saul, wounded by archers, fell on his own sword when his armour-bearer would not kill him. The Philistines hung the bodies on the wall of Beth-shan, but the men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had once saved from the Ammonites, marched through the night, took the bodies down, burned them beneath a tamarisk tree at home and fasted seven days.

When the news reached David, he sang a lament over Saul and Jonathan whose refrain still echoes: How are the mighty fallen. Turning to Jonathan alone, he called him my brother and said that Jonathan's love for him had been wonderful, passing the love of women.

david-and-bathsheba-and-nathan-the-proph.context_blurb:
King David is the great hero-king of the Hebrew Bible, the shepherd boy who killed Goliath. But the Second Book of Samuel does not hide his darkest hour: the story of Bathsheba, a husband sent to his death, and a prophet brave enough to tell the king to his face what he had done.

It begins in spring, the season when kings rode out to war. David's general Joab was besieging Rabbah, the Ammonite capital across the Jordan, but David had stayed at home in Jerusalem, in his own palace. One evening he rose from his bed and strolled across the palace rooftop, and from there he saw a very beautiful woman bathing in a courtyard below.

Her name was Bathsheba, and she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner who fought for Israel and was later named among David's thirty mighty men. David took her for himself, and when she was expecting his child he arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle and married the widow.

Then the prophet Nathan came to the king with a story. A rich man with great flocks and herds had a poor neighbour who owned only one little ewe lamb, which he had brought up indoors, sharing his food and his cup with it and holding it like a daughter. When a traveller came to visit, the rich man spared his own flock and took the poor man's lamb for the meal.

David burned with anger and swore that such a man deserved to die. Nathan answered him in four words: Thou art the man. The lamb was Bathsheba, and the rich man was the king.

Bathsheba's baby fell sick. For seven days David fasted and lay on the ground, refusing food. When the child died, his servants were afraid to tell him, but David got up, washed, put on fresh clothes and asked for a meal. He told them that while the child lived there had been hope; now he would one day go to the child, but the child would never come back to him.

elijahs-mantle-and-the-harp-of-david-the.context_blurb:
The Hebrew Bible is full of remembered objects that carry a person's whole story: a shepherd's harp, a prophet's cloak, a pair of bronze pillars, a staff that flowers. Each one marks a calling, a succession or a choice.

When an evil spirit tormented King Saul and drove him to rage, the young shepherd David of Bethlehem was brought to play for him, and whenever David played the harp the king was refreshed and the spirit left him. The Hebrew word, kinnor, really means a small lyre, but harp is the word the story is remembered by.

When Elijah's time was nearly over, he found his successor, Elisha son of Shaphat, ploughing behind twelve pairs of oxen, and without a word he threw his mantle across Elisha's shoulders. Elisha would take up that same mantle again at the Jordan when Elijah was gone.

Only one verse describes Elijah's own look: a hairy man with a girdle of leather about his waist, so distinctive that a king knew him from the description alone. Centuries later John the Baptist came out of the wilderness wearing camel's hair and the same leather belt, and people wondered whether Elijah had come back.

When Solomon built the Temple in Jerusalem, he set two huge bronze pillars before its porch and gave each a name: on the right Jachin, meaning he shall establish, and on the left Boaz, meaning in him is strength.

Some of these objects seem alive. When the tribes of Israel quarrelled over the priesthood, a rod for each tribe was laid overnight before the Ark, and by morning Aaron's rod had budded, blossomed and borne ripe almonds, marking his tribe of Levi as Israel's priests.

elijah-at-cherith-and-zarephath-the-rave.context_blurb:
Elijah the Tishbite is the fiercest prophet of the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Kings 17 he confronts King Ahab of Israel with an oath: no dew and no rain until he says so. Then he has to vanish, because the king and his queen want him dead.

The queen hunting him was Jezebel, Ahab's foreign-born wife, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, who was killing the prophets of Israel's God wherever she found them. God sent Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan, and there ravens brought him bread and meat every morning and every evening, unclean birds keeping the prophet alive, while he drank from the brook.

When the brook dried up, God sent him to a widow in Zarephath, a town on the coast of Sidon, deep in the very land Jezebel came from, where no hunter of hers would search.

At the town gate he found the widow gathering firewood and asked her for water and a little bread. She told him she had nothing baked, only a handful of flour and the last of her oil, and that she was gathering two sticks to bake a last small cake so that she and her boy could eat one last time and then die. Elijah told her to bake for him first, and promised that her barrel of meal would not run out, nor her cruse of oil fail, until the rain returned; and so it was.

Later the widow's son fell sick and stopped breathing. Elijah carried the boy up to his own room, laid him on his bed, lay down full length upon the child three times, calling on God, and the child's breath came back. He carried the boy down to his mother with four words: See, thy son liveth.

Not everyone at Ahab's court served Jezebel. The king's own steward, Obadiah, who secretly feared God, hid a hundred prophets in caves, fifty to a cave, and fed them on bread and water.

The New Testament remembers the drought twice, in Luke, where Jesus recalls Israel's many widows, and in the letter of James, which praises Elijah's prayer, and both give it the same length: three and a half years.

horeb-the-still-small-voice-the-fiery-ch.context_blurb:
Elijah was the fiercest prophet in the Hebrew Bible. On Mount Carmel he called down fire on his altar and humiliated the priests of Baal, and within hours his life was in danger. The books of Kings follow him from despair in the desert to a mountain where God spoke to him in an unexpected way, and finally to a whirlwind.

When Queen Jezebel swore she would have Elijah dead by the next day, the prophet of the Carmel fire fled alone into the desert, sat down under a lone tree and begged to die. In the King James Bible it is a juniper tree, a tough little desert bush. He fell asleep, and an angel touched him and showed him food by his head: a cake baked on hot coals and a jar of water. He ate and slept, and the angel woke him to eat again.

On the strength of that food Elijah walked forty days and nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, also called Sinai, and took shelter in a cave there.

God told him to stand on the mountain. A great wind tore at the mountains and broke the rocks, but God was not in the wind. An earthquake followed, and God was not in that, and then came a fire. God was not in the fire either. After the fire Elijah heard what the King James Bible calls "a still small voice," and he wrapped his face in his cloak and went to the mouth of the cave.

The voice gave him work. He was to anoint Hazael as king of Syria and Jehu as king of Israel, and to anoint Elisha to be prophet after him, in his own place. Seven thousand in Israel, God added, had never bowed to Baal.

Years later Elijah walked to the Jordan with Elisha, knowing it was his last day. He took off his mantle, rolled it up and struck the river, and the Jordan split apart so the two of them crossed on dry ground. As they walked on, a chariot of fire with horses of fire swept between them, and the King James text says Elijah went up into heaven by a whirlwind. Like Enoch, he never died.

elisha-the-double-portion-the-bears-and-.context_blurb:
Elisha was a farmer's son who became the heir of Elijah, the fiercest prophet of ancient Israel. The books of Kings follow him from a ploughed field to his grave, through some of the strangest wonders in the Hebrew Bible: savage bears, an axe head that would not sink, and a dead boy who sneezed his way back to life.

The calling came without a speech. Elisha was ploughing behind his father's oxen when Elijah walked up and tossed his own hairy cloak over the young man's shoulders. That cloak, Elijah's mantle, was the prophet's sign of office, and laying it on Elisha marked him as the one who would take Elijah's place. Elisha answered with a bonfire. He killed his oxen, broke up their wooden yokes and the frame of his plough for fuel, and boiled the meat to feed his neighbours. With his tools burned to ash, there was no farm to go home to.

Years later the river Jordan opened to let the two prophets walk across, and Elijah asked what his follower wanted before he was taken away. Elisha asked for a double portion of the old prophet's spirit. Under Israel's inheritance law a firstborn son received a double share of his father's goods, so Elisha was asking to be Elijah's firstborn heir. Then a whirlwind carried Elijah up, and the fallen mantle parted the Jordan for Elisha on his way back.

On the road up to Bethel a crowd of small boys poured out of the town and jeered at his shiny scalp. Twice over they shouted at him to go up, calling him a bald head, perhaps sneering that he should vanish into the sky the way his master had. Elisha turned and cursed them in God's name, and two she-bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the children.

One of the young prophets lost a borrowed axe head while cutting timber by the river; it flew off the handle, sank, and he could not afford to repay it. Elisha cut a stick and threw it where the iron had gone down, and the heavy head rose and floated; the King James Bible says simply that "the iron did swim."

A rich woman of Shunem always fed Elisha when he passed through. She and her husband built him a small upstairs room and furnished it with a bed and a table, a stool and a candlestick, four plain gifts that turned "the Shunammite's chamber" into a byword for welcoming holy men. Elisha promised the childless woman a son, and the boy was born. Years later he cried out in the harvest field that his head hurt, and by noon he lay dead in his mother's arms. She rode to fetch Elisha, who shut himself in with the body and stretched himself over the boy. The child sneezed seven times and then opened his eyes, a homely detail no reader forgets in a story about raising the dead.

Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, came next, sick with leprosy. Elisha sent a messenger to tell him to wash seven times in the Jordan, and the proud general stormed off: were not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than any water in Israel? His servants talked him round, and after the seventh dip his skin came back as clean as a little child's.

Elisha refused every gift Naaman offered, but his servant Gehazi ran after the general. Gehazi claimed that two young prophets had just arrived and that his master wanted silver and fine robes for them, then hid the silver for himself. Elisha knew at once and told Gehazi that Naaman's leprosy would cling to him and to his descendants for ever, and Gehazi walked out a leper, white as snow.

Even death did not end Elisha's story. Years after he was buried, some Israelites were carrying a dead man to his grave when they spotted a band of Moabite raiders. In their panic they shoved the body into the nearest tomb, which was Elisha's, and as soon as the dead man touched the prophet's bones he came back to life and stood up.

jonah-the-great-fish-nineveh-and-the-gou.context_blurb:
The book of Jonah is four short chapters about a prophet who would rather do anything than his job. God sends him east to warn Nineveh, the great and cruel capital of Assyria, and Jonah runs the other way, into a storm, into the belly of a fish, and finally into an argument with God about mercy.

The runaway was Jonah, son of Amittai. Ordered to cry out against Nineveh, he hurried to the harbour at Joppa, bought a passage and set sail westward for Tarshish, as far from Nineveh as he could get.

God sent a great storm after the ship. The crew heaved their freight into the sea and every sailor begged his own god for help, while Jonah lay sound asleep below decks, deep in the inner part of the ship, until the captain shook him awake. To learn whose fault the storm was, the sailors cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. He told them to throw him into the sea. They tried to row for shore first, but at last they flung him over, and the sea went calm.

A great fish swallowed him; the book says a great fish, and the whale came later in the retelling. Jonah stayed in its belly for three days and nights. He prayed from inside it, and when God spoke to the fish, it spewed Jonah out onto dry ground, an undignified landing right where his journey should have begun.

This time he went. Nineveh was so vast it took three days to cross, and Jonah walked a day into it with one blunt warning: in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown. To his dismay, the city repented, and God spared it.

Jonah sat sulking outside the city in a little shelter, and God made a leafy gourd vine grow up over him for shade. But at dawn the next day God sent a worm that gnawed the plant until it withered, and a hot east wind and the sun beat on Jonah's head until he begged to die. God's last word turned the lesson on him: Jonah pitied a plant he had not even planted, so should God not pity Nineveh, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who could not tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle too?

daniel-in-the-lions-den.context_blurb:
The Book of Daniel follows a young Jewish captive who rises to power in the courts of foreign kings. Its most famous story comes in chapter 6, when the old statesman's rivals turn the law against him and he spends a night shut in with hungry beasts.

When King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took Jerusalem, he carried off the brightest young Hebrew captives to train at his court, and Daniel was among them. The Babylonians renamed the boys after their own gods, and Daniel became Belteshazzar.

Decades later, under King Darius the Mede, Daniel was a great official, and jealous rivals persuaded Darius to sign a law forbidding prayer to any god or man except Darius for the next thirty days, on pain of death. Daniel did not hide. He climbed to the upper room of his house and, as he always did, knelt three times a day by windows open toward Jerusalem, the city of the Temple, toward which the exiles turned to pray. So Darius, trapped by his own law, had him thrown into a den of lions.

The den's mouth was blocked with a great stone, and Darius sealed it with his own signet ring and the rings of his lords, so that no one, not even the king, could change what had been done to Daniel.

Darius spent a sleepless night without food, and at first light he ran to the den and called down to Daniel. Daniel answered from the dark that his God had sent an angel who shut the lions' mouths, so that they had not harmed him. Daniel was drawn up without a scratch, and Darius turned his fury on the men who had tricked him: he had them thrown into the den along with their wives and children, and the lions overpowered them before they reached the bottom.

belshazzars-feast-and-the-writing-on-the.context_blurb:
The Book of Daniel, in the Hebrew Bible, tells of the last night of Babylon's power. Around 539 BC the Persian armies of Cyrus were closing in on the great city, yet inside the palace the king was throwing a banquet. Chapter 5 tells what happened when a hand came out of the air and began to write on his wall.

The king was Belshazzar, and his feast was a wild one, with a thousand of his lords drinking in the hall. Halfway through, he sent for the gold and silver cups that Nebuchadnezzar, the king Daniel calls his father, had carried off long before from the Temple in Jerusalem when his army sacked the city. The guests drank from the holy vessels and praised their own gods, and the writer of Daniel does not even name those gods. He simply lists what the idols were made of: gold and silver, brass and iron, wood and stone.

In that same hour, close to the great lampstand, fingers appeared, a man's hand with no arm or body, and began writing across the plastered wall of the palace.

None of the king's astrologers could read the words. Then the queen-mother remembered Daniel, a captive from Judah who had served in Nebuchadnezzar's day. Belshazzar promised him three things if he could read the writing: a robe of scarlet, a chain of gold for his neck, and the rank of third ruler in the kingdom. Third, because Belshazzar himself ruled as second, under his father Nabonidus, a detail archaeologists later confirmed.

Daniel turned down the gifts and read out the four Aramaic words on the wall: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. Then he explained them to the king's face, and the middle word, tekel, carried the line still quoted at any moment of reckoning: Belshazzar had been weighed in the balances and found wanting.

Daniel had told the king his kingdom was finished, and the very next verse is brutally short: that same night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed. Darius the Mede, a man of about sixty-two, took the kingdom after him.

nebuchadnezzars-dream-and-the-fiery-furn.context_blurb: King Nebuchadnezzar, the mightiest ruler of the ancient world, has torn Daniel and his three Jewish friends out of Judah and marched them east into captivity. The king first dreams a great statue made of several different metals in layers, and only Daniel can tell him both the dream and its meaning. esther-mordecai-haman-and-the-feast-of-p.context_blurb:
The book of Esther in the Hebrew Bible is a palace thriller set at Susa, also called Shushan, the winter capital of the Persian king Ahasuerus, whom the Greeks called Xerxes. It has a beauty contest, a plot to murder a whole people, a sleepless king, a gallows and a queen who risks death to speak. Jews still retell it every spring at the festival of Purim.

The story opens with a party. To show off his riches, the king feasted his princes and nobles from Persia and Media for 180 days, half a year, and then gave the people of the city a further week of feasting. When that week ended, Queen Vashti refused his summons to appear before the drunken lords, and he threw her out.

A search for a new queen swept the empire. The girl chosen was Hadassah, a Jewish orphan, and once crowned she took the Persian name Esther. Her older cousin Mordecai had brought her up as his own daughter, and he spent his days at the palace gate; he warned her to keep her Jewish birth a secret, and the festival of Purim remembers the two of them together.

The king's proud chief minister, Haman the Agagite, expected everyone to bow to him, and Mordecai would not. In his rage Haman cast lots, called pur, to choose a day for killing every Jew in the empire, and he offered the king a fortune in silver to seal the decree. Purim takes its name from those lots.

Mordecai put on sackcloth and begged Esther to plead with the king. But anyone who walked into the king's inner court unsummoned could be put to death. Mordecai warned her that silence would not save her, and asked who knew whether she had come to the throne for just such a time as the one they now faced. Esther asked the Jews of Susa to fast for her for three days and nights, then promised to enter the king's presence against the law, ending her message with the grim resolve that if she perished, she perished. That fast is still kept as the Fast of Esther, the day before Purim.

On the third day she put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court. The king held out the golden sceptre, the sign that her life was spared, and Esther touched its tip.

She invited the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second one. Haman went home proud but still seething at Mordecai, and his wife Zeresh urged him to build a gallows at once. He made it fifty cubits high, some seventy-five feet, a monstrous height meant to shame Mordecai before the whole city.

Sleep would not come to the king that night, so he had the royal chronicles read to him. They told how Mordecai had once saved his life by exposing two doorkeepers, Bigthan and Teresh, who had plotted to kill him, and how no reward had followed.

At dawn Haman came to ask for Mordecai's death, but the king spoke first, asking how he ought to reward a man he wished to honour. Haman, sure the king meant him, proposed the king's own horse, a royal robe, and a herald proclaiming through the streets that thus it shall be done for the man the king delights to honour. Then the king ordered Haman to do every bit of it for Mordecai.

Over wine at the second feast, Esther pointed at Haman as the enemy who meant to destroy her people. The king stormed out into the garden, and Haman threw himself on Esther's couch to beg for his life; the king came back, found him there and took it for an assault on the queen. A chamberlain, Harbonah, mentioned the tall gallows standing in Haman's courtyard, and the king gave a three-word order: "Hang him thereon." Haman died on the frame he had built for Mordecai, and the festival of Purim was founded to remember the rescue.

One more strange thing marks the book: in the whole of Esther, God is never named, by any title at all. Jewish tradition reads that silence as the point, with providence at work in what looks like chance: a sleepless night and a chronicle read aloud.

isaiah-coals-to-the-lips-and-the-seraphi.context_blurb:
Isaiah was one of the great prophets of the Hebrew Bible, a man of Jerusalem in the 700s BC. The sixth chapter of his book tells how he was called to be a prophet in a vision of overwhelming holiness, and the books of Kings remember him at the bedside of a dying king.

In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah stood in the Temple in Jerusalem and saw God enthroned, high and lifted up, and the train of the royal robe flowed out until it filled the Temple. Above the throne hovered seraphim, the "burning ones," calling to one another "Holy, holy, holy." Each seraph had six wings: one pair covered its face, one its feet, and with the last it flew.

Isaiah cried out that he was lost, a man of unclean lips. Then one of the seraphim took a live coal from the altar with a pair of tongs, flew to him and touched his lips with it, and his sin was taken away. A voice asked whom it should send, and who would go. Isaiah answered at once, offering himself: here he was, ready to be sent.

Years later King Hezekiah of Judah lay dying, and Isaiah told him he would live fifteen more years. As proof, Isaiah offered him a sign on the sundial built by Hezekiah's father Ahaz. Hezekiah said a shadow moving forward was an easy thing, so he asked for the harder sign, and the shadow went back ten steps on the dial.

jeremiah-the-potters-wheel-and-the-linen.context_blurb:
Jeremiah was the prophet who watched his own kingdom fall. He preached in Jerusalem through the decades before its fall in 586 BC, warning Judah that Babylon would destroy it, and his book is full of strange acted-out signs: a potter's wheel, a buried belt, a field bought in wartime and a scroll fed to the flames. He lived to see Jerusalem burn.

His call came while Josiah was king of Judah, when he was a young man, the son of a priest. Jeremiah protested that he could not speak, for he was only a child, but God reached out and touched his mouth and made him a prophet to the nations.

God told him to go down to a potter's house and watch the man at his wheel. The clay pot on the wheel came out spoiled in the potter's hands, so the potter squeezed it down and shaped it again into another vessel, whatever form seemed good to him; as clay is in the potter's hand, the lesson ran, so Israel was in God's hand, to be remade.

Jeremiah could be bitter. Judah was so used to doing evil, he said, that it had as much hope of doing good as an Ethiopian had of changing his skin, or a leopard of losing its spots. Another sign was stranger still. He bought a linen girdle, a loincloth worn close against the skin, wore it unwashed, then carried it far to the Euphrates and hid it in a crack in a rock; when he dug it up long afterwards it was rotten and good for nothing, like Judah's pride.

His warnings made him hated. As the Babylonians closed in, his enemies lowered him into the cistern of Malchiah, which held no water, only deep mud, and left him to sink and die. A court official, Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian eunuch of the king's household, went to the king, won permission and pulled the prophet out. He took thirty men and let down worn-out rags and old cast-off clothes on ropes, telling Jeremiah to tuck them under his armpits so the cords would not cut him as they hauled.

With the Babylonian army camped around the city, Jeremiah did something that looked mad: he paid his cousin Hanameel seventeen shekels of silver, weighed on the scales, for the family's field at Anathoth, as a sign that the land would one day have buyers and sellers again. He had his scribe Baruch put the sealed deed and the open copy in an earthen vessel so they would last for many years.

Years earlier Jeremiah had dictated a scroll of warnings, and it was read aloud to King Jehoiakim as he sat by a fire in his winter house. Each time the reader, Jehudi, finished three or four columns, the king sliced them off with a penknife and fed them to the flames, column by column, till nothing of the scroll remained. Jeremiah simply dictated it again, with more added.

ezekiel-the-wheel-and-the-valley-of-dry-.context_blurb:
Ezekiel was a priest of Jerusalem who was carried off to Babylon with the first wave of Jewish exiles, around 597 BC. Beside the river Chebar, far from the Temple he had served, he began to see visions so strange that his book is still the wildest in the Hebrew Bible: winged creatures, wheels covered in eyes, and a valley of bones that stood up.

In his thirtieth year, the book says, the heavens opened over the exiled priest Ezekiel. A whirlwind blew out of the north, a great cloud wrapped in fire and glowing at its heart like hot metal. Out of the fire came four living creatures with wings and calves' feet, and each creature had four faces: a man's in front, a lion's on the right, an ox's on the left, and an eagle's. Christian tradition later borrowed those faces, by way of the book of Revelation, as the emblems of the four gospel writers: the man for Matthew, the lion for Mark, the ox for Luke and the eagle for John.

Beside each creature stood a wheel built like a wheel inside another wheel. Their rims were so high they were frightening, and the rings were full of eyes all the way around, as if the whole chariot-throne could see in every direction at once.

Above the creatures spread a sky like crystal, and above that sky stood a throne that looked like sapphire, with the shape of a man seated on it and a rainbow's glow all around. Long before, Exodus says, Moses and the elders had seen a pavement of sapphire beneath the feet of Israel's God. Next a hand reached toward him with a scroll written front and back with laments, mourning and woe, and a voice told Ezekiel to eat it. He obeyed, and in his mouth the bitter message was as sweet as honey. A prophet, the story suggests, has to swallow his message before he can speak it.

Ezekiel acted out his prophecies as well as speaking them. Commanded to bear the guilt of Israel and Judah, he lay on his left side for 390 days, one day for each year of the northern kingdom's sin, and then on his right side for forty days, one for each year of Judah's.

His hardest sign cost him his wife. God warned him that the woman he called the desire of his eyes would die suddenly, and that he must not mourn her: no tears, no torn robe, no going barefoot. She died that evening, and he kept the command. When the exiles asked why, Ezekiel told them his silence was a sign that the Temple in Jerusalem, the desire of their own eyes, was about to fall. They too would lose what they loved and be unable to mourn it.

Then God set Ezekiel down in a valley of bones bleached dry and asked whether they could live. Ezekiel prophesied over them, and with a rattling and a shaking the bones came together, in the King James phrase, "bone to his bone." Sinews and flesh and skin covered them, the wind breathed into them, and they stood up on their feet, an exceeding great army.

samuel-anointing-saul-and-later-david.context_blurb: Before he was ever born, the prophet Samuel was promised to God by a barren mother who had wept and prayed at the shrine of Shiloh until the priest Eli mistook her silent moving lips for drunkenness. Samuel grew up to be the last of the judges of Israel and the kingmaker who anointed its first two kings — first a tall Benjaminite who hid among the baggage out of embarrassment, and then, long after the first king had been rejected, a young shepherd summoned in from the pasture by Samuel at Jesse's house in Bethlehem. Sources: 1 Samuel 1, 10, 16 KJV.

solomon-wisdom-the-two-mothers-the-templ.context_blurb: In 1 Kings of the Hebrew Bible, the young king Solomon — son of David by Bathsheba — goes up to the high place at Gibeon to offer sacrifice. That night God appears to him in a dream with a startling offer: 'Ask what I shall give thee.' Instead of long life or riches, Solomon asks for one thing, and his wisdom becomes famous across the ancient world. The two mothers before his throne, the building of the Temple in Jerusalem, and the visit of the Queen of Sheba all follow from that early choice. Source: 1 Kings 3–10 KJV.

solomons-temple-menorah-showbread-and-th.context_blurb: In 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, King Solomon builds in Jerusalem the first great Temple of God in Israel. For seven years and more he gathers cedar from Lebanon, hammered gold, olivewood for the giant inner cherubim, and twelve brazen oxen to carry the molten sea. The Holy Place has a seven-lamped golden lampstand, a table of showbread, and ten lavers for washing; and the inmost chamber shelters the Ark of the Covenant with the tablets from Mount Horeb. Sources: 1 Kings 6–8; 2 Chronicles 3–7 KJV.

bethlehem-the-manger-and-the-shepherds.context_blurb:
The Gospel of Luke tells the best-known birth story in the Western world. Joseph and Mary journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judea, and there Mary's son Jesus is born in the humblest possible place, while out in the fields the first visitors hear the news.

They travel because the emperor Caesar Augustus has ordered a census of the whole empire, and each man must be counted in his family's home town; Joseph's is Bethlehem. There Mary wraps her newborn son in swaddling clothes and lays him in a manger, a trough that animals eat from; the word itself comes from a Latin root meaning to eat. Luke gives the reason in a blunt half-line: the inn had no room for them. Luke never mentions an ox or a donkey; later artists borrowed those from the prophet Isaiah.

On the hillside outside town, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks by night when an angel appeared, and Luke says the glory of the Lord shone round about them, and they were terrified.

Then the sky filled with angels. Their song opens with glory to God in the highest, and its second half promises peace on earth and good will toward men. The shepherds ran into Bethlehem, found the couple and the child in his manger, and told everyone what the angel had said. Then Luke turns to Mary by herself: she kept all these things, turning them over quietly and pondering them in her heart.

Twelve centuries later, at Christmas 1223, Francis of Assisi brought Luke's scene to life. In a hillside cave at Greccio, a small hill town north of Rome, his friend Giovanni Velita set up a real manger full of hay, with an ox and a donkey standing by, villagers came with torches and candles, and Mass was said over the crib: the first live nativity scene.

gabriel-to-mary-and-the-leap-in-elizabet.context_blurb:
The first chapter of Luke's gospel tells how two births were announced: the birth of John the Baptist to an old couple, and the birth of Jesus to a young girl. One angel brings both messages, and the two mothers, who are kinswomen, meet in the Judean hills in one of the most painted scenes in Western art.

In the Galilean village of Nazareth, Luke says, the angel Gabriel came to Mary, a young woman of the town, greeted her as highly favoured, and told her she would bear a son and name him Jesus.

Mary did not faint or argue. She asked one plain, honest question: how could this be, seeing that she had never known a man, the Bible's old way of saying she was a virgin? Gabriel added proof that God could do the impossible: her cousin Elizabeth, old and long called barren, was already six months pregnant.

Mary hurried south to the hills of Judea to see her. When Mary's greeting reached Elizabeth at the door, the child inside Elizabeth leaped, and Elizabeth said afterwards that her baby had leaped for joy. That unborn child was the future John the Baptist.

Elizabeth blessed her, and Mary answered with a long song of praise. It is known by its first Latin word, Magnificat, because Mary begins by saying that her soul magnifies God, and monasteries have sung it at Vespers, their evening service, night after night for over ten centuries. Its sharpest line is a great reversal: God, Mary sings, has pulled the mighty down from their thrones and raised up those of low degree. Reformers and poets have quoted that line for centuries, and it echoes the old song of Hannah in the book of Samuel.

The same angel had already visited Elizabeth's husband months before. Zacharias, an old priest, was taking his turn in the Temple at Jerusalem and had gone in to burn incense when Gabriel appeared to him, standing on the right side of the altar of incense in the Holy Place. Zacharias doubted the promise that his old wife would bear a son, so Gabriel struck him mute, unable to say a word until the baby was born.

the-magi-the-star-herod-and-the-flight-t.context_blurb: Matthew's Gospel opens its Nativity story with strangers walking into Jerusalem from a long way east. They go straight to the palace of King Herod the Great and ask the question that terrifies him — where is the newborn king of the Jews? They explain how they knew to come at all. Herod sends them on to Bethlehem with orders to come back and tell him what they find; instead they go home another way, and the holy family flees south to escape what Herod does next. Source: Matthew 2 KJV.

the-boy-jesus-in-the-temple-at-twelve.context_blurb: Only one of the four Gospels gives any scene from Jesus's childhood after the Nativity itself. Luke tells how his parents went every year to a great feast in Jerusalem, and the one year they lost him on the trip home. They turn back and look for a day and a half, and finally find him in the Temple — sitting among the teachers of the Law. The scene closes with the first words of Jesus the gospels record. Source: Luke 2:41–52 KJV.

john-the-baptist-locusts-honey-and-the-d.context_blurb:
John the Baptist was the wild prophet of the wilderness who prepared the way for Jesus. The gospels tell of his miraculous birth, his strange way of life, the day he baptized Jesus, and his death at the order of a king, and he is one of the great figures of Christian art.

His parents were the old priest Zacharias and his wife Elizabeth, Mary's kinswoman, who had long been thought too old to have a child. Luke says an angel announced the birth to Zacharias while he served in the Temple, and that Elizabeth's unborn child leaped when Mary came to visit.

He grew up to preach in the desert east of Jerusalem, wearing a coarse cloak woven of camel hair, belted with leather, the outfit Elijah had worn long before. Camel-hair cloth was rough and cheap, the opposite of a rich man's fine wool. He lived on locusts and wild honey; the Greek word means the insects, which the law of Leviticus counted as clean food. People in Arabia still eat them roasted or dried.

People streamed out of the city to confess their wrongdoing, and John dipped them in the river Jordan, which is why he is called the Baptist, from the Greek word for dipping. It was the river Joshua had crossed into the promised land, a fitting place for a fresh start. When Pharisees and Sadducees came for baptism, he greeted them as a generation of vipers and asked who had warned them to run from the coming wrath. Jesus would later throw the same insult at the same men. He told them that a mightier one would follow him, a man whose sandal strap he was unfit even to bend down and unloose. Untying a master's sandals was a slave's job.

One day Jesus came down from Galilee and stepped into the river to be baptized. John was appalled, and he protested that it was he who needed to be baptized by Jesus, not the other way round. Jesus insisted, and John gave way. When Jesus rose from the river, the sky split open, and God's Spirit descended in the form of a dove and alighted on him. Then a voice from heaven declared that this was his beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased. The same voice speaks again, almost word for word, when Jesus shines on the mountain of the Transfiguration.

Later, as Jesus drew bigger crowds than John, John's disciples grumbled. John answered them that Jesus "must increase," while he himself "must decrease."

His end came at a royal party. He had condemned King Herod Antipas for marrying Herodias, his brother's wife, and Herod threw him in prison. When the daughter of Herodias danced at the king's birthday banquet, Herod promised her whatever she wished, and at her mother's urging she demanded John's head on a charger, a large serving platter. The historian Josephus places John's prison and death at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.

forty-days-in-the-wilderness-the-three-t.context_blurb:
Before Jesus began to preach, the gospels of Matthew and Luke say, he went into the Judean desert alone. Fresh from his baptism by John in the Jordan, he fasted until he was starving, and then he met his enemy face to face. The tests he faced there are among the best-known scenes in the gospels, and they still shape the Christian calendar.

The fast lasted forty days and nights, a number that echoes Moses's forty days on Mount Sinai and Elijah's forty-day walk to Mount Horeb. At the end of it, weak with hunger, Jesus met the devil, who put him to the test three times over. Matthew calls him the tempter, and Jesus later names him Satan.

Christians still mark that fast every year. Lent, the season of prayer and penance before Easter, runs forty days if its Sundays are left out, and its length and readings both recall the forty days Jesus spent alone in the wilderness before his ministry began.

The first test was hunger. The devil pointed at the stones on the desert floor and dared Jesus, if he really was the Son of God, to command them to become bread. The pale limestone of that wilderness is scattered with rocks the size and shape of small loaves. Jesus answered with a line from Deuteronomy, that people do not live by bread alone.

In Matthew's order the second test came in Jerusalem. The devil set Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, the highest point of its walls, and urged him to leap, citing a psalm's promise that angels would bear him up before his foot struck a stone. Again Jesus answered from Deuteronomy.

For the last test the devil took him up an exceedingly high mountain and showed him, in one sweep, every kingdom of the world and all its glory; all of it would be his if he would bow down and worship the devil. Jesus did not argue. In the King James wording of Matthew he answered with a curt command, "Get thee hence, Satan," and quoted Deuteronomy a third time: worship God, and serve him alone.

The devil left him then, and Matthew says that angels came and cared for him.

water-into-wine-at-the-wedding-in-cana.context_blurb: At a village wedding in Galilee, Jesus, his mother Mary, and his new disciples are all guests. Partway through the feast the wine runs out, which in that honor-conscious culture would be an acute humiliation for the host family. Mary goes to her son. The six large stone jars standing nearby at the door were meant for ceremonial washings; Jesus has them filled with water, and sends a sample to the master of the feast. The sign — the first of seven 'signs' in John — opens Jesus's public ministry. Source: John 2 KJV.

the-sermon-on-the-mount-and-the-beatitud.context_blurb: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus climbs a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, and before he begins his longest single teaching he takes the posture a rabbi always used when teaching students. The sermon that follows runs three chapters and contains some of the most famous lines of Western literature — the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, the lily of the field, the Golden Rule, and the house built on sand. Source: Matthew 5–7 KJV.

the-sower-and-the-mustard-seed.context_blurb: Jesus pushes a small fishing boat a little way out from the shore of the Sea of Galilee, sits down in it while the crowd stands on the beach, and opens a parable with a farmer image. Later in the same chapter he gives another parable about the smallest of all garden seeds growing into a tree where the birds come and lodge. The 'kingdom of heaven' chain in Matthew 13 and Mark 4 is one of Jesus's great teaching sequences. Source: Matthew 13; Mark 4 KJV.

the-good-samaritan-on-the-jericho-road.context_blurb: A lawyer tries to test Jesus by asking who exactly counts as his 'neighbor.' Jesus answers with a story. He sets it on a specific road — a man traveling downhill from Jerusalem — a road that dropped more than three thousand feet in just over fifteen miles, perfect ambush country. Three different people pass the half-dead victim before the one who finally stops. Source: Luke 10:25–37 KJV.

the-prodigal-son-the-ring-the-sandals-an.context_blurb: In Luke 15 Jesus tells a parable that opens with a plain one-line setup: 'A certain man had two sons.' The younger boy walks up to his father one morning with a demand that would have shocked every listener at the time. He goes off to a far country, spends what his father gave him, ends up feeding animals Jews considered unclean — and finally comes to himself, rehearsing a short speech on the long walk home. The father's answer and the complaint of the older brother who stayed are the heart of the parable. Source: Luke 15:11–32 KJV.

the-lost-sheep-and-the-lost-coin.context_blurb: In Luke 15 Jesus tells three parables that are all about finding what was lost. The first is a shepherd who has a hundred sheep and finds that one has strayed. The second is a woman with ten silver coins who sweeps the whole house for the one that fell out of her head-dress. Each parable ends the same way — joy, calling in the neighbors, the simple triumphant line that heaven rejoices in the same way. Source: Luke 15:1–10 KJV.

lazarus-and-dives-and-the-sheep-and-the-.context_blurb: Jesus tells a parable in Luke 16 about two men who die on the same day. One is a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen who feasts every day at his own table; the other is a poor beggar covered in sores who lies outside the rich man's gate hoping for the scraps that fall. The parable turns everything upside down after death. In Matthew 25 Jesus gives another vision of the final judgment — a shepherd separating two kinds of animal — that has worked on Christian imagination ever since. Sources: Luke 16; Matthew 25 KJV.

the-talents-and-the-ten-virgins.context_blurb: In a pair of parables in Matthew 25, Jesus tells of a rich man who entrusts different sums of money to three of his servants before a long journey, and of ten young women waiting at night with lamps for a bridegroom's wedding procession. Both are parables about being ready. Source: Matthew 25:1–30 KJV.

come-forth-raising-jairuss-daughter-and-.context_blurb:
The gospels tell several stories of Jesus raising the dead, and two of the best known come from Mark and from John. In Mark a twelve-year-old girl dies while her father is still pleading for help; in John a grown man has already lain for days in his tomb when Jesus arrives.

In Mark's gospel a synagogue ruler named Jairus pushed through the crowd, threw himself down before Jesus and begged him to come and lay hands on his little daughter, who was dying at home.

Before they reached the house the girl had died, and hired mourners were wailing. When Jesus told them she was not dead but sleeping, they laughed him to scorn, so he put them all outside and went in with only the parents and three of his disciples.

He took the dead girl by the hand and spoke to her in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee: Talitha cumi. Mark, writing in Greek, explains that the words mean little girl, get up. She rose and walked about the room while her parents stared. Jesus's last instruction was strikingly ordinary: he told them that she should be given something to eat.

John's gospel tells a slower and larger story. In Bethany, a village two miles from Jerusalem, lived Lazarus and his two sisters, Martha and Mary, and when Lazarus fell ill the sisters sent word to Jesus, their friend. This Mary is Mary of Bethany, not Mary Magdalene and not the mother of Jesus. Jesus deliberately waited, and by the time he came Lazarus had lain in the tomb four days; when Jesus ordered the stone taken away, Martha warned him that by now the body would stink. Then Jesus called into the tomb for Lazarus to come forth, and the dead man walked out in his grave clothes.

five-loaves-and-two-fishes-feeding-the-f.context_blurb:
Of all the wonders the gospels tell of Jesus, only one appears in all four of them. Late in the day, beside the Sea of Galilee, a vast crowd that had followed him out of the towns found itself far from any food, and a boy's packed lunch became a feast. Each gospel writer adds his own sharp detail.

The disciples wanted to send the people off to buy supper in the villages. The food came instead from a boy in the crowd, carrying five small loaves and two fish of his own.

Jesus would not send anyone away. He told the disciples that the crowd need not leave, and that they themselves should give the people something to eat. The task, in other words, was theirs. Matthew counts about five thousand men who ate that day, and that was without counting the women and children.

John adds the people around Jesus. Jesus tested Philip by asking where bread enough for this crowd could be bought, though he already knew what he would do, and Philip answered that two hundred pennyworth of bread, some two hundred days' wages, would not give everyone even a little. Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, brought forward the boy with the loaves and fish, wondering aloud what so little could do among so many.

Mark adds the order. Jesus had the disciples seat everyone in companies on the green grass, and the people sat down in ranks of hundreds and of fifties, as neat as an army and easy to count.

John notes the grain as well: the boy's loaves were made of barley, the cheap bread of the poor in Galilee, humbler than wheat, so his lunch was about as plain and small as a meal could be.

Jesus blessed and broke the bread, and everyone ate until full. Then he told his followers to gather up the leftovers so that nothing would be wasted, and they filled twelve baskets with fragments, far more than the boy had brought. All four gospels give the same count of twelve.

Mark tells of a second feeding too, when seven loaves fed four thousand people. Later, when the disciples fretted in a boat because they had forgotten to bring bread, Jesus made them count the leftovers: twelve baskets after the five thousand, and after the four thousand, they answered, seven.
