the-storm-on-the-sea-and-walking-on-the-.context_blurb: The disciples Peter, Andrew, James, and John worked as commercial fishermen on the same lake Jesus later crossed many times with them. On one crossing Jesus slept through a violent storm in the stern of their boat; the terrified disciples woke him. On another night the disciples were in the boat alone when a figure walked out across the waves toward them, and Peter asked to walk out and meet him. Sources: Mark 4:35–41; Matthew 14:22–33 KJV.

the-paralytic-through-the-roof-and-blind.context_blurb: Jesus is teaching inside a packed house in Capernaum, and four men arrive carrying a paralysed friend on his sleeping mat. The crowd at the door is too tight to push through — so they find another way in. Later in Mark's gospel, Jesus is leaving the city of Jericho surrounded by a huge following when a blind beggar sitting by the road hears who is passing and shouts out his own name over and over, refusing to be hushed. Sources: Mark 2; Mark 10 KJV.

the-transfiguration-on-the-mountain.context_blurb: The gospels say Jesus led a small group of his closest disciples up a high mountain, apart from the rest. There his clothes began to shine, and two long-dead figures from the Hebrew Bible appeared with him on the mountainside. A cloud came and covered them, and a voice spoke out of the cloud. The three disciples came down the mountain in silence. Sources: Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9 KJV.

palm-sunday-and-the-whip-of-cords.context_blurb: On the Sunday before his death, Jesus sends two disciples ahead of him into a village just outside Jerusalem to find and bring back a particular animal tied up near a door. He rides down the Mount of Olives into the city on it as the crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road. Days later, in the Temple itself, he drives out the money-changers and the sellers of sacrificial animals with a scourge of small cords. Sources: Matthew 21; John 2 KJV.

the-last-supper-the-kiss-and-let-this-cu.context_blurb: In an upper room in Jerusalem on the night before Passover, Jesus eats the Passover meal with the Twelve. Partway through the meal he tells them that one of the men eating with him will betray him, and as they go around the table they each begin to ask the same short, worried question. Later that same night in a garden across the Kidron Valley, Jesus prays three times under the olive trees while his closest three disciples cannot stay awake, and the betrayer finally arrives at the head of an arresting party with a single pre-arranged signal. Sources: Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18 KJV.

peters-denial-and-the-cock-crowing.context_blurb: On the night Jesus is arrested and taken to the high priest's house for questioning, one of his closest disciples follows the arresting party at a distance and slips into the courtyard. The servants and guards there have kindled a fire against the cold, and the disciple stands among them warming his hands. Three different people recognise him through the course of the night, and each time he insists he does not know Jesus — until a bird crows just before dawn. The last scene of John's gospel reconciles the same disciple to Jesus by a very similar charcoal fire. Sources: Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18, 21 KJV.

pilate-the-crown-of-thorns-and-what-is-t.context_blurb: Dragged by the Jewish authorities at dawn to the Roman governor's residence in Jerusalem, Jesus is questioned by the Roman prefect of Judea. The governor's opening question cuts straight to the political charge: 'Art thou the King of the Jews?' Jesus does not deny it. The soldiers plait a crown out of thorn-branches, dress him in a scarlet robe, and the governor finally offers the crowd a choice between Jesus and a prisoner named Barabbas. Sources: Matthew 27; John 18–19 KJV.

simon-of-cyrene-the-seven-last-words-and.context_blurb: On the walk out of Jerusalem toward the execution ground, Jesus is too exhausted to carry the crossbeam alone. Roman soldiers grab a random bystander from the crowd and force him to shoulder it. Mark's gospel names him in one phrase. At the hill called Golgotha a sign in three languages is hung above the cross, and across the three hours of darkness the four gospels together record a handful of famous last sayings — including a Hebrew cry from Psalm 22 and a single Greek word meaning 'it is finished.' Sources: Mark 15; John 19 KJV.

joseph-of-arimathea-and-the-empty-tomb.context_blurb:
The gospels say that on the day Jesus was crucified, one rich and powerful man took the risk of burying him, and that two days later women coming to that tomb found it open. These are some of the most closely told scenes in the gospels, full of small, human details.

That afternoon a rich man dared to go before Pilate, the Roman governor, and request the dead man's body. He was Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the ruling council who had been waiting for the kingdom of God; Luke says he had not agreed with the council's verdict.

Pilate was surprised that Jesus had died so soon, since crucifixion usually took days to kill, and he called the centurion to make sure before he handed over the body. Joseph bought fine linen, took the body down from the cross and wrapped it. He laid it in a tomb newly cut for himself in the rock, and rolled a great stone across the doorway.

The burial was rushed to finish before the sabbath began at sundown. Very early on the first day of the week, Mark says, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome set out with spices to anoint the body properly. All the way there they kept asking each other one worried question: who was going to roll the heavy stone back from the door for them? When they looked up, the stone had already been moved.

Matthew tells how. An angel came down from heaven, rolled the stone aside and sat on it; his face shone like lightning, and his clothes were as white as snow.

emmaus-doubting-thomas-and-the-153-fish.context_blurb:
The gospels of Luke and John close with a string of strange meetings. After the crucifixion in Jerusalem, they tell, Jesus came back to his followers alive, yet again and again they failed to know him at first. A stranger on a country road, a figure in a locked room and a man cooking fish on a beach at dawn: each scene turns on a moment of recognition.

Luke's story begins on the third day, as two disciples walked home from Jerusalem to Emmaus, a village about seven miles away. A stranger joined them and asked what they were talking about, and Luke explains why they did not know him: their eyes "were holden," held back from recognising him.

The stranger walked on with them, opening the scriptures as he went, and at evening they begged him to stay. At the table he took the bread, blessed it and broke it. Luke says that as the bread broke, their eyes were opened and they recognised him, and in the same instant he vanished. The two turned to each other and asked whether their hearts had not been burning inside them while he talked with them on the road.

John tells what happened that same evening. The disciples had locked themselves in a room, afraid that the authorities who had crucified their master would come for them next. Though the doors stayed shut, Jesus stood among them, and his first words were "Peace be unto you." One disciple was missing that night: Thomas, whom John calls Didymus, a Greek nickname meaning "twin." No one knows who his twin was.

Thomas refused to believe the others. He would not believe, he said, until he had seen the nail marks in Jesus's hands and put his finger into them, and until he had thrust his hand into the wound in Jesus's side, where a Roman soldier's spear had pierced him on the cross. Eight days later, in the same shut room, Jesus turned to Thomas and offered him his hands and his side. Thomas answered in five words, hailing Jesus as his Lord and his God.

John's last chapter moves to the Sea of Tiberias in Galilee. Peter and six others had worked through the night without landing a single fish when a figure on the beach at dawn told them where to throw the net, and suddenly it was full. The disciple whom Jesus loved, whom tradition identifies with John, knew him first and said to Peter, "It is the Lord." Peter wrapped his fisher's coat around himself, jumped into the sea and swam for the shore.

When Peter dragged the net to land it held a hundred and fifty-three big fish, and yet the net did not tear. Jesus had a charcoal fire burning on the beach, with fish and bread on it, and he gave them breakfast.

After the meal he spoke to Peter alone. Calling him Simon son of Jonas, Jesus asked Peter whether he loved him, then asked the same thing a second time and a third, until Peter was hurt by the asking. Each time Peter said yes, Jesus gave him the same short charge with one word changed: "Feed my lambs," then "Feed my sheep," and "Feed my sheep" again. John's word for that charcoal fire appears in only one other place in the New Testament, the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter had sworn three times that he did not know Jesus. The man who failed beside one fire was given his work back beside another.

andrew-and-the-x-shaped-cross-of-patras.context_blurb:
Andrew, brother of Simon Peter, was a fisherman from Galilee. The Gospel of John makes him one of the earliest men to follow Jesus, and later Christian tradition follows him to a cross in Greece and his bones to a cold northern shore, where the shape of his cross still flies on a nation's flag.

Andrew began as a disciple of John the Baptist. One day beside the Jordan he and another of John's followers went after Jesus and stayed with him until evening, and the first thing Andrew did afterwards was hurry off to find his brother Simon, the man Jesus would rename Peter, and bring him to Jesus.

What Andrew told Simon is one of the first announcements in the gospel story: he and his friend had found the Messias, the Greek form of the word Messiah. In John's gospel it is Andrew, not Peter, who speaks that word first. Because he answered before any of the others, the Greek Orthodox churches give Andrew a title no other apostle shares: Protokletos, the First-Called.

John's gospel gives Andrew one more quiet, practical moment. A crowd of some five thousand had trailed Jesus out to a deserted spot by the Sea of Galilee and found itself without food. It was Andrew who noticed a boy carrying five barley loaves and two small fish and brought him forward, wondering aloud what so little could do among so many, and from that small offering came the feeding of the whole crowd.

Later tradition sends Andrew preaching through Greece until he was condemned to crucifixion at Patras. He was not nailed to an upright cross like the one Jesus died on but bound to one shaped like an X, the shape heralds call a saltire, and ever since it has carried his name as Saint Andrew's Cross. The story that Andrew asked not to die on the same shape as his master is a later Western legend, but the X is the shape that stuck.

A medieval legend says a monk named Regulus carried some of Andrew's bones by sea, was shipwrecked on the coast of Fife, and founded the town later called Saint Andrews. Scotland chose Andrew as its patron, put his white cross on a blue ground as its flag, and marks Saint Andrew's Day, the thirtieth of November, as its national holiday.

bartholomew-flayed-alive-in-armenia.context_blurb:
Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles Jesus chose, a man the gospels barely describe. Later Christian legend made up for that silence: it sent him east to preach, gave him one of the most horrifying martyrdoms in the saints' stories, and turned his flayed skin into one of the strangest images in Western art.

Matthew, Mark and Luke each give a list of the twelve, and in all three Bartholomew's name follows Philip's, as though the two were partners. His feast falls on 24 August, one of the oldest apostle days in the Christian calendar.

The name Bartholomew is really a family label, not a given name. In Aramaic, the language Jesus and his followers spoke, it means son of Tolmai. John's gospel never mentions a Bartholomew, but it pairs Philip with a disciple called Nathanael, and since the two names never appear in the same gospel, Christian scholars often take Nathanael and Bartholomew to be one man.

An early tradition sent Bartholomew east as far as India. The later and stronger tradition, standard from the medieval Golden Legend onward, sent him to Greater Armenia, high in the mountains beyond Persia, where he won over its king, Polymius, and baptised him at Albanopolis. No Armenian king list knows a Polymius, so the tale is legend, but Armenia became the traditional place of his death. It was not the king who killed him. The king's brother, Prince Astyages, furious at the conversion, had the apostle seized and put to death.

The Golden Legend and centuries of painters tell how: Astyages had him skinned alive and then beheaded, and in old paintings Bartholomew carries the knife that did it. Other traditions say he was crucified or simply beheaded, but the flaying is the version the West remembered. Because of that death, butchers, tanners and leather-workers, whose trades all deal in skin and hide, took Bartholomew as their patron saint.

Michelangelo gave the legend its strangest image. In the 1530s he painted the Last Judgment across the altar wall of Rome's Sistine Chapel, with Bartholomew among the saints around Christ, holding up his own empty skin. The face on that sagging skin is Michelangelo's own: the artist painted himself as a hollow pelt in a flayed saint's hand. Scholars read it as anything from a prayer for mercy to a bitter protest at being made to paint the wall.

matthew-the-tax-collector-at-the-receipt.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve apostles had a job before he was called that made his neighbours despise him: he sat at a customs booth on the trade road by the Sea of Galilee, collecting taxes for Rome. Jesus walked past, said two words, and the man got up and left his table. The scene has been painted many times — most famously by Caravaggio, in a huge canvas for a chapel in the French church in Rome. By tradition the same man wrote the first of the four gospels in the New Testament. Sources: Matthew 9:9; Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27 KJV.

philip-and-nathanael-under-the-fig-tree.context_blurb: The day after John the Baptist first pointed Jesus out at the Jordan, Jesus met a young man from Bethsaida — the same fishing town as Peter and Andrew — and called him with two words: 'Follow me.' This young apostle immediately went to find his skeptical friend sitting under a tree and brought him to Jesus. Jesus greeted the friend as an Israelite in whom there was no guile, and said he had seen him under that tree before the two of them ever met. Source: John 1:43–51 KJV.

thomas-the-twin-put-your-finger-here-and.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve apostles is introduced in the Gospel of John by a Greek nickname that means 'the twin.' He is the disciple who was not with the others on the first Easter evening when the risen Jesus appeared in the locked room, and who refuses to believe them. A week later Jesus comes back through the door with him there, and offers him the physical sign he had demanded. Later Christian tradition carries this apostle farther east than any of the others, as far as the Malabar Coast of India. Sources: John 20:24–29 KJV; Acts of Thomas.

simon-the-zealot-and-thaddaeus-the-two-l.context_blurb: Every Gospel list of the Twelve Apostles ends the same way: two names paired together just before Judas Iscariot. The second-to-last is a Simon — not Peter, a different one — carrying a one-word tag that would eventually become his standard name. The one just ahead of him is a figure called Thaddaeus (and in some lists Lebbaeus or Judas not Iscariot). Later tradition pairs them together on missionary journeys; one of them becomes the great Western patron of lost or impossible causes. Sources: Matthew 10; Mark 3; Luke 6 KJV.

james-son-of-zebedee-the-first-apostle-k.context_blurb:
James, son of Zebedee, was one of the first men Jesus called to follow him, and one of the three closest to him. The gospels show him fiery and ambitious; the book of Acts records his death in a single line; and medieval Europe built one of its great pilgrimage roads around his bones.

James and his brother John were fishermen who worked with their father Zebedee on the Sea of Galilee, mending their nets in the boat when Jesus called them. Because of their fiery tempers Jesus gave the pair an Aramaic nickname, Boanerges, which Mark translates as "sons of thunder."

With Peter, James and John formed the inner circle. Jesus took the three of them alone up a high mountain, where his face and clothes shone like the sun and two figures from long ago stood talking with him: Moses and Elijah.

Once the brothers asked Jesus for the places of honour on either side of him in his coming kingdom. He answered with a question of his own: could they drink the cup of suffering he was going to drink? They said they could.

James was the first of the apostles to drink it. Around the year 44, King Herod Agrippa I began to persecute the church in Jerusalem, and Acts says Herod had James, John's brother, put to death with the sword; it is the only death of one of the Twelve that the New Testament describes. Seeing that the killing pleased the crowd, Herod arrested Peter next, but in the night an angel struck off his chains and led him out of the prison past the guards.

That one line in Acts grew into a road. Medieval Spanish tradition said James's body was carried by ship to Galicia, in the far northwest of Spain, and for centuries pilgrims walked the Camino to his shrine at Santiago de Compostela; "Santiago" means Saint James. Along with Rome and Jerusalem it became one of the three great pilgrimages of Europe, and pilgrims still bring home his emblem, a scallop shell.

james-the-just-the-fullers-club-at-the-t.context_blurb:
James the Just, also called James the Righteous, led the first Christian church in Jerusalem. He is a different man from the two apostles named James. Early writers remembered him for his strict holiness and for a violent death at the Temple, and both the Jewish historian Josephus and the Christian historian Hegesippus recorded how he died.

The gospel of Mark names James among the brothers of Jesus of Nazareth, when the people of his home town ask whether this is not the carpenter, the brother of James.

After Jesus's death James became the head of the church in Jerusalem, and he stayed there, leading it for some thirty years. When the apostles argued over whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the Jewish law, James gave the deciding word at a council in Jerusalem, and Peter and Paul accepted it.

Hegesippus, writing in the 100s, described his way of life. James never drank wine and never ate meat, and he wore linen rather than wool. He spent so many hours on his knees in the Temple that their skin grew hard and thick, like a camel's.

Around the year 62, at Passover, the leaders at the Temple resolved to stop his preaching. They set the old man up on the pinnacle of the Temple, above the crowds of pilgrims, and told him to turn the people away from Jesus; instead he declared that Jesus was the Messiah. They threw him down. He survived the fall, and he rose to his knees and prayed for the men who had thrown him, which only made them pick up stones.

As the stones fell, a fuller, a cloth-worker who beat wet cloth clean with a heavy wooden club, ran in and brought that club down on James's head, and so he died.

judas-iscariot-the-thirty-pieces-the-kis.context_blurb:
Judas Iscariot is the disciple who betrayed Jesus, and his name has become a word for traitor. The gospels and the book of Acts tell his story: the money he kept, the price he took, the signal he gave in a dark garden, and two different accounts of his death that both end in a field of blood.

He had a trusted job among the Twelve: he carried the shared money bag for the little band of travellers. At supper in Bethany, Mary anointed Jesus's feet with expensive perfume and dried them with her hair. Judas Iscariot complained aloud that it was a waste, since the ointment could have been sold to help the poor. John's gospel adds sharply that he said it because he was a thief who helped himself from the bag.

Soon afterwards Judas went secretly to the chief priests and offered to hand Jesus over when no crowd was near, and Matthew says they weighed out thirty pieces of silver for him. The sum carried a sting. In the law of Exodus, thirty shekels of silver was what an ox's owner had to pay when his ox gored a slave to death.

Late that night, among the olive trees of Gethsemane, Judas came with an armed crowd carrying torches. He had told them that the man he kissed was the one to seize, and he walked up to Jesus, greeted him as master and kissed him.

The gospels disagree about how Judas died. Matthew says that when Judas saw Jesus condemned, he was struck with remorse, flung the silver down in the Temple, and went and hanged himself. The chief priests would not put blood money back in the treasury, so they purchased a potter's field with it, to serve as a cemetery for strangers. The book of Acts tells it another way: Judas himself bought a field with his reward, fell headlong there, and his body burst open.

In both versions the field got a grim name in the local Aramaic, Akeldama, "the field of blood." Afterwards the eleven remaining apostles chose a replacement by casting lots between two men, and the lot fell on Matthias.

Matthew says the purchase of the potter's field matched the words of a prophet about thirty silver pieces thrown to the potter. He names Jeremiah, but the passage about the potter and the thirty coins comes from the book of Zechariah, a puzzle scholars still discuss.

peters-chains-the-angel-in-the-cell-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Acts, King Herod Agrippa I has just put the apostle James the son of Zebedee to death with a sword, and seeing that this pleased the people he also arrests Peter and locks him up in prison chained between two soldiers, with four squads of soldiers assigned to guard him in turn. During the night an angel appears in the cell, taps Peter awake, and leads him out. Meanwhile the Jerusalem church is praying for him at the house of Mary the mother of John Mark — and a young servant-girl named Rhoda is the first to hear his knock at the gate. Source: Acts 12 KJV.

pentecost-the-wind-the-fire-and-the-thre.context_blurb: Fifty days after Passover, in the opening chapters of the book of Acts, about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus are shut in a single upper room in Jerusalem. A sudden sound as of a rushing mighty wind fills the house, and a flame as of a small tongue of fire comes to rest over the head of each of them. They go out into the street and begin to speak, and every one of the pilgrim visitors in Jerusalem for the feast hears his own home-language. One of the Twelve stands up with the Eleven to preach to the whole crowd. Source: Acts 1–2 KJV.

stephen-the-first-martyr-and-the-young-m.context_blurb: In the early Jerusalem church, the apostles are overwhelmed and pick seven men to handle the daily food-distribution to the widows so that they themselves can keep preaching. Acts 6 names the very first of these seven — a man 'full of faith and of the Holy Ghost' — and the long speech he gives before the Sanhedrin in Acts 7 is the longest in the book. His execution follows at once, and a young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus is standing nearby holding the coats of the men who throw the stones. Source: Acts 6–7 KJV.

peter-and-john-at-the-beautiful-gate-sil.context_blurb: In the book of Acts chapter 3, two of Jesus's apostles walk up together to the Temple in Jerusalem for the afternoon prayer, as they did every day. A man who has been lame since birth is laid daily at the gate called Beautiful to ask alms of the people going in. The two apostles stop, Peter speaks a famous line about silver and gold, and the man rises and goes into the Temple leaping and praising God. The Sanhedrin then arrests them for the night. Source: Acts 3 KJV.

the-damascus-road-the-light-the-voice-an.context_blurb: Before he was the apostle Paul, Saul of Tarsus was on the road hunting Christians. He carried official letters from the high priest in Jerusalem authorising him to arrest any followers of Jesus he could find in the synagogues of a particular city and drag them back in chains. On the way a sudden light from heaven knocked him to the ground and a voice spoke. The scene is told three times in Acts and remembered forever as the pattern of a sudden conversion. Sources: Acts 9, 22, 26 KJV.

the-jerusalem-council-and-the-split-of-p.context_blurb: At Antioch some men who had come down from Judea began teaching the Gentile converts that they could not be saved unless they also kept the full Law of Moses. The dispute was so sharp that Paul and Barnabas were sent down to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders. Acts 15 tells of the great council that followed and the letter the Jerusalem leaders sent back out to the Gentile churches. The same chapter ends with a sharp quarrel between Paul and Barnabas over whether to take John Mark along on a second journey. Source: Acts 15 KJV.

paul-at-the-areopagus-the-altar-to-the-u.context_blurb: Paul reaches Athens alone, waiting for Silas and Timothy to catch up. He walks the streets of the city, and one sight above all others stirs him up — the countless altars and statues on every corner. He is invited to speak at the Areopagus, the open-air court on a rocky hill below the Acropolis, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers are curious about his teaching. He opens from an altar he had seen in the city and quotes a line from the Cretan poet Epimenides. Source: Acts 17:16–34 KJV.

paul-and-silas-midnight-singing-the-phil.context_blurb: In the Macedonian city of Philippi, a slave girl follows the apostle Paul and his companion Silas through the streets for days, shouting after them. She is possessed by a particular kind of spirit, and when Paul finally commands it out of her, her owners drag the two missionaries into the market-square. By nightfall Paul and Silas are stripped, beaten with rods, locked in the inner prison with their feet in the stocks — and singing hymns at midnight. An earthquake opens every door. Source: Acts 16 KJV.

paul-before-agrippa-and-festus-almost-th.context_blurb: After his arrest in the Temple at Jerusalem, Paul is held for two years in Roman custody at the Mediterranean port that served as the governor's headquarters in Judea. His case passes from one Roman governor to another and finally comes before the local Jewish king Herod Agrippa II and his sister Berenice. Paul tells his conversion-story for the third time in Acts, and Agrippa gives the famous half-answer that has become a proverb. Source: Acts 24–26 KJV.

shipwreck-on-malta-the-alexandrian-grain.context_blurb: In the autumn of about 60 CE Paul, still a prisoner, is being shipped from Caesarea to Rome under a Roman centurion named Julius. While the ship is at Fair Havens on the south coast of Crete, Paul warns against sailing on so late in the season. The centurion overrules him, a storm catches the ship, and the fourteen-day drift ends in shipwreck on a small Mediterranean island. The whole party reaches shore alive. The island's chief Publius takes them in. Source: Acts 27–28 KJV.

paul-beheaded-on-the-ostian-way.context_blurb: The book of Acts ends with Paul in Rome under a light form of house arrest, in his own rented house, receiving all who came and preaching freely. Acts does not describe his death. Later Christian tradition — Tertullian, Eusebius, and the Liber Pontificalis — places it under the emperor Nero and executes him by the sword rather than by the cross because of his Roman citizenship. His tomb is now covered by the great Roman basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls on the Ostian Way, and his feast is kept the same day as Peter's. Source: Acts 28; Tertullian, De Praescriptione.

john-on-patmos-the-four-horsemen-and-the.context_blurb:
Revelation, the book that closes the Christian Bible, is a blaze of visions: horsemen, a dragon, a war in heaven and a city of gold. By Christian tradition the aged apostle John wrote it in exile, banished by the emperor Domitian late in the first century.

John says he was on the island called Patmos, a speck of volcanic rock in the Aegean, off Asia Minor, when the visions began. A voice like a trumpet told him to write letters to seven churches on the mainland of Asia Minor: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. Smyrna is told to be faithful unto death; Laodicea is scolded for being neither cold nor hot.

Turning, he beheld a radiant figure in a long robe, one like a son of man, with hair as white as wool and eyes of fire, and out of his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword.

Then John was shown a scroll sealed with seven seals. As each of the first seals broke, a horseman rode out. The first rode a white horse, wore a crown that had been given to him, and carried a bow, and he went out conquering. Later tellers labelled the other riders, but the text gives a name only to the last, who rides a pale horse: his name is Death.

A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman wrapped in the sun, standing on the moon, wearing a crown of twelve stars, and crying out in labour. A huge red dragon, seven-headed and ten-horned, crouched before her, ready to swallow her baby as soon as it arrived. The child was caught up to God, and the woman fled into the wilderness.

Then war broke out in heaven. The archangel Michael and his angels fought the dragon, the old serpent, and threw him and his angels down to the earth.

At the end of the visions, John saw a New Jerusalem coming down out of heaven, adorned like a bride. Its walls were jasper, and each of its twelve gates was made from a single pearl, while its street was pure gold, as clear as glass.

peter-crucified-upside-down-at-rome.context_blurb: By the end of his life, Christian tradition places the fisherman apostle Peter far from Galilee, leading the small Christian community in Rome itself. His first epistle sends greetings from 'Babylon,' which early Christians read as a code-name for Rome. In the summer of 64 CE the emperor Nero burned Christians to clear his own blame for the great fire of Rome; by tradition Peter was martyred in that persecution on the Vatican hill in a particular posture he had asked for because he counted himself unworthy to die the same way as Jesus. In 1968 Pope Paul VI announced that the bones under the high altar of St Peter's were almost certainly his. Source: 1 Peter 5; Eusebius 2.

the-silversmiths-of-ephesus-and-the-riot.context_blurb: In the city of Ephesus the apostle Paul rents out a lecture hall and teaches in it daily for two full years. The whole province hears him. The silversmiths of Ephesus, who make a living casting silver souvenirs of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — see their business falling off and start a riot. For two hours the mob in the theater of Ephesus shouts the same line in Greek over and over, until the town clerk finally calms them. Source: Acts 19 KJV.

aphrodite-born-from-the-sea-foam.context_blurb:
Love and beauty belong to Aphrodite among the Greek gods, and her birth is the strangest of any Olympian. The poet Hesiod, in his Theogony, has her rise full-grown out of the sea, while Homer gives her an ordinary divine family. Rome took over her stories, and a Renaissance painter made her arrival from the waves one of the most famous pictures in the world.

The Romans, who retold the Greek myths under Latin names, called her Venus, and the planet Venus still carries that name. Her bird is the dove: doves perch on her statues, draw her chariot in later art and nestle in pairs at her feet.

Hesiod's story begins in violence. The Titan Cronus attacked his father, the sky god Ouranos, with a sickle and flung what he cut away far out to sea. White foam spread where it fell, and from the foam rose Aphrodite, already grown; Hesiod even draws her name from aphros, the Greek word for foam. The west wind, Zephyr, carried her across the water to the little island of Cythera and then on to Cyprus, and from that landing she took her titles Cypris, the Lady of Cyprus, and Cytherea. Her temple at Paphos on Cyprus became one of the great shrines of the ancient world.

Artists from ancient times onward pictured her coming ashore standing on a scallop shell, and the shell became her emblem. Centuries later the same scallop became the badge of Christian pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela, a curious echo between traditions. Where she stepped onto the beach, Hesiod says, fresh grass sprang up from the soil under her bare feet, and painters ever since have added roses and myrtle around her.

The goddess of love made a stormy wife. In Homer's Odyssey, a bard sings how her husband Hephaestus, the lame smith of the gods, caught her with her lover Ares, the god of war, under a net of golden threads finer than a spider's web, then called all the gods in to laugh at the pair. She also owned a girdle, an embroidered sash whose magic left anyone who looked at the wearer helpless with love. In Book 14 of the Iliad, Hera borrowed it to beguile Zeus on Mount Ida, so that he would look away from the war while the Greeks won back ground.

Not every poet agreed on how she was born. In Homer's Iliad, when the mortal hero Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in battle, she flees to Olympus weeping and is comforted by her mother, Dione, for Homer makes her simply the daughter of Zeus and Dione. Plato later treated the two, the heavenly foam-born goddess and Homer's daughter of Zeus, as two different Aphrodites.

Around 1485 the Florentine painter Sandro Botticelli painted her arrival from the sea. His Birth of Venus, which hangs in Florence's Uffizi, still shapes how the West imagines her.

apollo-at-delphi-the-python-and-the-pyth.context_blurb:
Apollo is the shining Greek god of music, prophecy and the bow. His shrine at Delphi, high on the mountainside of Parnassus, was the greatest oracle of the ancient world, where kings and cities came for answers. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo and later poets tell how he was born, how he won Delphi, and what that victory cost him.

Apollo and his twin sister Artemis, the huntress of the forests, were children of Zeus and the Titaness Leto. Hera, jealous, ordered every land to refuse Leto a place to give birth, and Leto wandered without shelter. In the end Delos, a little floating island that Hera's ban on land could not bind, took her in and fastened itself to the seabed, and there, clutching a palm tree, Leto bore her twins.

Hera had also set a monstrous she-serpent, Python, to plague Leto, and the young Apollo went after it in its cleft in the rocks of Parnassus and brought it down with his arrows. The Homeric Hymn says the name comes from a Greek word meaning to rot, because the serpent's body rotted where it fell. Apollo claimed the place as his own, and it became Delphi, the oracle the whole Greek world consulted, where envoys of kings and cities came asking whether to go to war, whom to marry and where to plant a colony. The Greeks called it the navel of the world.

At Delphi the god spoke through a priestess, the Pythia. She sat on a tripod, a three-legged bronze seat placed over a crack in the rock where holy vapours were believed to rise, and copies of the tripod were the proudest prizes at every great Greek sanctuary. Before she prophesied, the Pythia chewed the leaves of Apollo's sacred plant, the laurel. The nymph Daphne, fleeing from Apollo, had been turned into the first laurel tree, so the god wore her leaves ever after, broke his first branches in the Vale of Tempe, where he went to be purified after killing the serpent, and crowned his victors with laurel wreaths.

Over the temple door every pilgrim read two short commands: know yourself, and nothing to excess. Greek tradition credited both sayings to the Seven Sages, and the first became the motto of Greek philosophy.

The god's answers could cut both ways. Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia, sent gold to Delphi and asked how a war against Persia would go. The priestess replied that a great empire would fall if he marched across the river Halys. He crossed, Cyrus of Persia crushed his army and took his capital, and the great empire Croesus destroyed turned out to be Lydia, his own.

Even a god could be made to serve. Zeus once sentenced Apollo to a term as a hired hand in the house of King Admetus of Pherae, and the god of music spent it minding the king's cattle out in the fields. Some tellings blame the blood shed at Delphi; Apollodorus says it was punishment for killing the Cyclopes. Apollo grew so fond of his master that he later persuaded the Fates to spare Admetus on the day he was meant to die.

arachne-the-weaver-challenging-athena.context_blurb:
In Book 6 of Ovid's Metamorphoses, a young Lydian weaver named Arachne grows so proud of her skill that she boasts it matches Athena's, and she refuses to admit she owes anything to the goddess who invented weaving. Athena comes to her disguised as an old woman to warn her, then throws off the disguise, and the two sit down at their looms side by side.

Athena wove the gods in glory. At the centre of her tapestry she showed her own contest with Poseidon for the city of Athens: he struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and a salt spring gushed out, she struck it and an olive tree grew, and the people chose her gift. In the corners she wove warnings, mortals turned into mountains and birds for challenging the gods.

Arachne wove the gods in shame: twenty-one scenes of gods taking the shapes of animals and other things to trick and carry off mortal women. Zeus appears in more of them than any other god, in nine scenes, as a swan, an eagle, a shower of gold and more. The most famous panel showed Zeus as a great white bull on the shore of Sidon, kneeling so that the princess Europa could climb onto his back, then plunging into the sea and swimming her away to Crete. The continent of Europe carries her name.

Arachne's work was flawless. Athena, goddess of every craft, could not find a single fault in it, and that was more than she could bear: she tore the tapestry, with its pictures of the gods' crimes, to shreds with her bare hands. Then she snatched up the shuttle, the boxwood tool that carries the thread back and forth across the loom, and struck Arachne on the forehead with it, three times and then a fourth. The humiliation was too much for Arachne. She knotted a noose from her own thread and hanged herself.

Athena wet her with drops from a herb of Hecate and bade her live and go on hanging. The girl shrivelled: hair, nose and ears dropped away, her head dwindled almost to nothing, and her fingers turned into thin legs clinging to her sides. Arachne had become a spider, spinning her thread to this day. Her name is simply the ancient Greek word for spider, and the scientific class Arachnida takes its name from her story.

ares-reviled-the-war-god-the-gods-hate.context_blurb:
Ares is the Greek god of war, but not of war's planning, which belongs to wise Athena. He is the god of the battlefield's raw fury and slaughter, and Homer's Iliad hardly hides its contempt for him: Zeus himself tells him he is the most hateful of all the gods on Olympus.

Where Athena guards the craft and strategy of war, Ares, son of Zeus and Hera, loves the rage and the bloodshed for their own sake. He seldom rides into battle alone. Beside him go his two sons by Aphrodite, Deimos and Phobos, whose names mean Terror and Fear, and with them runs Enyo, the sacker of cities.

In Book 5 of the Iliad a mortal humbles him. The Greek hero Diomedes, with Athena herself driving his spear, stabs Ares in the belly, and the war god flees to Olympus to whimper to his father. Zeus gives him no comfort, only the verdict that he is the most hateful of the gods.

artemis-and-actaeon-torn-by-his-own-houn.context_blurb:
Artemis is the Greek goddess of the hunt, and in her stories she punishes any mortal who crosses her. The cruellest of those stories, told most fully by the Roman poet Ovid in his Metamorphoses, is the fate of Actaeon, a young hunter who saw what no man was allowed to see.

Artemis, Apollo's twin sister and a daughter of Zeus and Leto, was born on Delos on the same day as her brother. She is the maiden goddess of the hunt, roaming the mountains with her nymphs and hounds and carrying a silver bow; the deer is her animal, and the Romans called her Diana.

Actaeon was a prince of Thebes, trained in hunting by the centaur Chiron, and he loved nothing better than to run his great pack of hounds over Mount Cithaeron, the wild mountain between Thebes and Athens where so many Greek tragedies unfold. One day he blundered on Artemis bathing in a hidden mountain pool, and the goddess, to make sure he could never tell what he had seen, turned him into a stag.

He fled through the woods, and when he tried to cry out who he was, his voice came out as the bellow of a deer. In Ovid's telling it was his own pack that killed him: the hounds did not know their master in his new shape, so they ran him down and pulled him to pieces.

Ovid adds the grimmest touch of all. Actaeon's hunting friends came running up behind the pack, shouting Actaeon's own name and calling for their master to hurry and see the stag his dogs had caught, while the stag they were looking at was Actaeon himself, unable to answer.

athenas-birth-fully-armed-from-zeuss-hea.context_blurb:
Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and of war's craft, had the strangest birth on Olympus: she came out of her father's head. Hesiod's Theogony explains why it happened, and the Homeric Hymn to Athena describes how the whole world shook when she arrived.

Zeus had seized the throne of heaven by overthrowing Cronus, his own father. He married Metis, the goddess of wise counsel, but while she was pregnant Gaia and Ouranos warned him that her next child would be a son who would overthrow his father in his turn. So Zeus tricked Metis into shrinking small and gulped her down, unborn child and all. It ran in the family: Cronus had swallowed his own children, and Zeus escaped only because his mother Rhea gave Cronus a stone to swallow instead.

Some time later a splitting headache seized Zeus, like nothing the gods had ever felt, because the daughter inside him had grown to full size and her only way out was through his head.

The smith god Hephaestus split Zeus's skull with an axe, and out leapt Athena, not a baby but a grown goddess in helmet and breastplate, brandishing a spear, the weapon she carries in almost every statue ever made of her. Some said Metis, still alive inside Zeus, had forged that helmet and spear for her daughter. The Homeric Hymn says the world itself answered her war cry: Olympus shook, the sea churned dark, and Helios reined in the horses of his sun chariot in mid-sky, waiting until she took off her armour before he drove on.

demeter-and-persephone-the-pomegranate-s.context_blurb:
The Greeks explained winter with a story of a mother's grief. The fullest telling is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, an ancient poem that follows a goddess searching for her stolen child, a bargain in the underworld, and the founding of the most secret rites in Greece.

Demeter, an older sister of Zeus, was the Olympian who ruled grain and the harvest, the power that makes the fields grow. Her only child, fathered by Zeus, was a daughter named Persephone, also called Kore, the Maiden.

Persephone was out picking flowers in a meadow with her friends. Hades, lord of the dead and brother of Zeus, had asked Zeus for her, and Earth, at Zeus's will, grew a wonderful narcissus with a hundred blooms on a single root as a lure. As her hand closed on it, the earth gaped and Hades burst out in his golden chariot drawn by immortal horses, snatched her up and drove her down to be his queen.

No one would tell Demeter where her daughter had gone. For nine days she wandered the earth with flaming torches in her hands, touching neither nectar nor ambrosia. Only two had seen or heard the abduction: Helios the sun, who looks down on everything, and Hecate, the goddess of crossroads and torches, who heard the girl cry out. Hecate later became Persephone's attendant below.

In the shape of an old woman, the goddess took service at Eleusis as nurse to the infant prince Demophoon. To make him immortal she rubbed him with ambrosia in daylight and at night laid him in the hearth fire like a log, until his mother, Queen Metaneira, caught her at it and screamed.

Then Demeter turned her grief on the world. No seed sprouted, the oxen dragged the ploughs for nothing, and mortals began to starve. What finally forced Zeus to act was that with no harvest there were no offerings, and the altars of the gods stood empty of sacrifice. Zeus sent Hermes down to bring Persephone home, but before Hades let her go he slipped her a pomegranate seed, and whoever eats food in the underworld can never wholly leave it. The Hymn says one seed; Ovid made it seven, and later tellers six.

So Zeus made a compromise. In the Homeric Hymn, Persephone spends one third of every year below as Hades's queen and the other two thirds above with her mother, and while she is gone the fields lie bare; later poets such as Ovid made it half the year.

Demeter repaid the royal family of Eleusis by teaching them her secret rites, the Eleusinian Mysteries, celebrated for more than a thousand years by initiates sworn to lifelong silence, and the secret was never told. She also taught the prince Triptolemus to grow grain and gave him a chariot drawn by winged serpents, in which he crossed the sky to teach farming to the whole world.

deucalion-and-pyrrha-stones-thrown-over-.context_blurb:
Greek myth has its own great flood. Zeus, disgusted with the wickedness of the human race, sent a deluge to drown it, and only one good couple survived to begin the world again. The best-known telling is in Book 1 of the Roman poet Ovid's Metamorphoses, and the story stands beside Noah's as one of the West's great flood tales.

They were Deucalion, who ruled Phthia in Thessaly, and Pyrrha, his queen, the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora. Deucalion's father was the Titan Prometheus, whose name means forethought, the same Titan who stole fire from the gods for humankind; he saw the flood coming and warned his son to build a wooden chest.

Deucalion and Pyrrha shut themselves inside it as the waters rose, and they floated over a drowned world for nine days and nine nights. When the waters fell, the chest came to rest on Parnassus, the twin-peaked mountain above Delphi, holy to Apollo and to the Muses.

Alone in an empty world, they went to the oracle of Themis, a goddess of divine law, to ask how to bring back the human race. The answer was a frightening riddle: they must cast their great mother's bones over their shoulders. Pyrrha was horrified, thinking it meant digging up her mother Pandora's grave, but Deucalion worked out that the great mother was the Earth, and her bones were its stones.

The oracle had also told them how to make ready: they veiled their heads and loosened the girdles of their robes. Then they walked on, throwing stones behind them, and the stones Deucalion threw became men while those Pyrrha threw became women.

Deucalion and Pyrrha also bore a child in the usual way, a son named Hellen. His sons Aeolus and Dorus gave their names to the Aeolians and the Dorians, his son Xuthus fathered the Ionians and Achaeans, and the whole Greek people called themselves Hellenes after Hellen.

dionysus-twice-born-the-pirates-the-maen.context_blurb:
Dionysus, whom the Romans called Bacchus, was the Greek god of wild rites, ecstasy and madness, and the youngest of the Olympians. His festivals gave the world its first theatre. He was born twice, and his stories swing between joy and terror.

Above all he was the god of wine, the drink of crushed and fermented grapes, and of the grape harvest.

His mother was Semele, a mortal princess of Thebes, carrying a child by Zeus. Jealous Hera came to her disguised as her old nurse and whispered that her lover might be no god at all; let her make him prove it by showing himself to her as he truly was, in his full divine glory. Zeus had sworn on the Styx that Semele could have whatever she asked. He begged her to ask something else, but the oath bound him, and when he came to her as he truly was, the blaze of his lightning and divine glory burned her to death.

Zeus snatched the unborn child from her burning body and sewed him into his own thigh, and there Dionysus grew until he was ready to be born a second time: the twice-born god. He grew up and roamed the earth at the head of a frenzied company of women, the maenads, the raving ones, who wore spotted fawnskins and carried the thyrsus, a fennel wand wrapped in ivy and crowned with a pine cone.

In Euripides's tragedy the Bacchae, Dionysus came home to Thebes, his mother's city, and the young king Pentheus, his own cousin, would not honour him as a god and banned his rites. The god lured Pentheus up a pine tree on Mount Cithaeron to spy on the maenads. They spotted him, dragged him down and tore him apart, led by his own mother, Agave, who bore his head home on the point of her wand, sure in her frenzy that she held a mountain lion's head, until the madness lifted.

The Homeric Hymn to Dionysus tells how Tyrrhenian pirates once seized the young god on a seashore, taking him for a rich prince to sell as a slave. Out at sea, vines climbed the mast, wine ran over the deck, and the god turned into a roaring lion. The terrified pirates leapt overboard and, in mid-leap, became dolphins; only the helmsman, who had recognised the god and begged the crew to free him, was spared.

Dionysus took a mortal bride, Ariadne, a princess of Crete and Minos's daughter, who had given Theseus the thread that led him out of the Labyrinth. Theseus sailed off with her and then deserted her as she slept on Naxos, and there Dionysus found and married her, and later he set her bridal crown among the stars.

echo-and-narcissus-the-voice-and-the-poo.context_blurb:
Book 3 of the Roman poet Ovid's Metamorphoses tells one of the saddest love stories in Greek myth: a nymph who can only repeat what others say, and a beautiful young man who can love no one but himself. Both end as almost nothing, a voice and a flower.

Echo, a talkative mountain nymph of Boeotia, used to chatter at the goddess Hera to keep her from catching Zeus at his tricks, so Hera cursed her never to speak first, only to repeat the last words she heard. The English word echo is her name.

Narcissus, son of the river god Cephissus and the nymph Liriope, was a young hunter so beautiful that girls and boys alike fell in love with him, and so proud and cold that he sent them all away in tears. When he was born, Liriope asked the blind Theban seer Tiresias whether her son would live to old age, and Tiresias answered with a riddle: yes, if he never came to know himself.

Echo fell in love with him and followed him through the woods, unable to speak first. When he called out to ask whether anyone was there, she could only throw his own words back to him, and when at last she ran out to embrace him, he pushed her away, saying he would sooner die than let her touch him. She hid among the leaves and wasted away until only her voice was left.

One scorned lover begged heaven that Narcissus should one day love as he had loved and never win his love, and Nemesis, the goddess of retribution and punisher of pride, heard the prayer. Weary after a day's hunting, Narcissus stooped over a still, clear spring for a drink, and a lovely face looked up at him: his own reflection, though he did not know it.

He fell in love with it. Every time he bent to kiss the face or reached to hold it, his touch broke the surface, the water rippled, and the arms reaching back to him melted away, and he wept. He stayed at the pool, unable to eat or to leave, wasting away while Echo watched from the trees, and when he cried his last words to his reflection, she could only give them back, alas for alas and farewell for farewell.

When the nymphs came to burn his body on a pyre, the body had vanished; in its place, at the edge of the water, grew a flower with white petals around a heart of gold, the narcissus, which still bears his name.

hades-and-the-underworld-cerberus-styx-c.context_blurb:
In Greek myth Hades is both a god and his kingdom. When Zeus and his brothers divided the world by lot, Poseidon took the sea and Hades won the land of the dead, a shadowy realm under the earth. The Greeks pictured it in careful detail: a ferryman, a monstrous hound, rivers, judges and punishments without end.

A soul reached that realm by crossing a dark river, where the grim old ferryman Charon poled the dead across in his flat boat. He took no one who could not pay, so the Greeks buried their dead with a small bronze coin, an obol, under the tongue, and archaeologists have found such coins in real Greek graves. A soul without a coin had to wander the near shore for a hundred years.

At the gate stood Cerberus, a monstrous dog who welcomed every soul coming in but savaged any that tried to sneak back out. Artists and storytellers almost always give him three heads, though Hesiod gave him fifty and Pindar a hundred.

Hades owned a cap that made its wearer invisible. The one-eyed Cyclopes forged it for him, the same smiths who made Zeus's thunderbolt and Poseidon's trident, and others borrowed it: Perseus wore it on his raid against the gorgon Medusa, and in the Iliad Athena put it on to slip past Ares.

The land of the dead was laced with rivers, five in the classical count: Styx, river of hate and oaths; Acheron, river of woe; Cocytus, river of wailing; Phlegethon, river of fire; and Lethe, river of forgetting. The holiest was the Styx, which winds nine times around the underworld; the gods swore their most solemn oaths by its waters, and a god who broke one lay voiceless for a year and was shut out of Olympus for nine more.

Judges sorted the newly dead. Minos, once king of Crete, his brother Rhadamanthys, and Aeacus, once king of Aegina and grandfather of Achilles, sent each soul to punishment in Tartarus, to bliss in Elysium, or to the grey fields of asphodel.

Tartarus, the deepest pit, held the worst sinners. There Sisyphus, a cunning Corinthian king who had cheated Death twice, must roll a huge boulder up a hill for ever, only to watch it tumble down again just before the top.

The Greeks feared to speak the god's own name, so they often called him Plouton, "the Rich One," because all the wealth of metals and jewels lies underground in his realm; the Romans kept the name as Pluto.

hephaestus-thrown-from-olympus-the-thron.context_blurb:
Each of the Olympian gods of Greece has a craft, and Hephaestus's is the forge. He is the smith of the gods, who hammers out Zeus's thunderbolts, the armour of heroes such as Achilles and every marvel of metal the gods require. He is also the one Olympian who is lame, and his stories are full of falls, revenge and clever traps.

Hephaestus walks with a limp, the only Olympian not perfect in body, and he made braces of his own invention to support him.

The Iliad tells two stories of how he fell from heaven. In the first book, Hephaestus says that when he took his mother's side in a quarrel, Zeus caught him by the foot and hurled him out of heaven; he fell for a whole day and landed on Lemnos, whose people found him and honoured him ever after. In the eighteenth book his mother Hera tossed him away as a newborn for his ugliness, and he dropped into the sea, where the sea-goddesses Thetis and Eurynome caught him and kept him nine years in a hollow beneath the sea. That is why, years later, Thetis could ask him to forge new armour for her son Achilles.

Hephaestus had his revenge on Hera. He forged a beautiful golden throne and sent it to her as a gift, and when she sat down in it, invisible chains sprang out and held her fast, and no god but its maker could set her free.

The gods gave him the loveliest of wives, Aphrodite, but she gave her love to Ares, the god of war. In the Odyssey the bard Demodocus sings how Hephaestus forged a snare finer than a spider's web and dropped it over the pair in his own bed, catching Aphrodite and Ares together. He called the gods to come and look, and they roared with laughter at the trapped lovers. Poseidon bargained for their release; Ares slunk off to Thrace, and Aphrodite fled to Cyprus, to her shrine at Paphos.

His forge, in later tellings, lay deep under the volcano Etna in Sicily, where the one-eyed Cyclopes, the ancient smiths who had made Zeus's thunderbolts and Poseidon's trident, swung the hammers beside him.

Even his servants were his own work. Homer describes handmaidens of gold who help him in his house and, unlike any statue, can move and speak, with understanding in their hearts and strength of their own; they are the oldest robots in Western literature.

The Romans called him Vulcan, and the Romans placed his forge beneath Etna, so that the smoke rising from the mountain is the fire of Vulcan's work.

hera-the-peacocks-hundred-eyes.context_blurb:
Hera is the queen of the Greek gods, Zeus's sister and also his wife, the protector of marriage and of wives, whose son was Ares, god of war. Her stories are often stories of jealousy, aimed at the mortal women Zeus loved and the children he had by them, and one of them explains the eyes on a peacock's tail.

Her greatest temple, the Heraion, stood on the plain outside Argos in the Peloponnese, and the whole Argolid was her country, which is why Homer calls her "Argive Hera."

Zeus fell in love with Io, a young priestess who served in Hera's own temple, and to hide her from his wife he turned the girl into a white cow. The disguise fooled no one.

Hera begged the cow from Zeus as a present, and he could not refuse. She set over it a watchman who never slept all at once: Argus Panoptes, "the all-seeing," a giant covered in eyes, some always open while the others rested.

Zeus sent Hermes to free Io. Disguised as a shepherd, Hermes played on his pipes and told the long, drowsy tale of how the pipes were invented until every one of Argus's eyes closed, and then he cut off the giant's head. Hera mourned her loyal watchman. Ovid says she took his hundred eyes and set them into the plumes of the peacock, her sacred bird, which carries them still.

Her hatred fell hardest on Heracles, the son Zeus fathered on the mortal Alcmene. While the baby lay in his cradle she sent two deadly snakes to kill him, but the infant grabbed one in each fist and choked them both. His very name, Heracles, means "glory of Hera," because her lifelong persecution drove him to the labours that made him famous.

hermes-the-newborn-stealing-apollos-catt.context_blurb:
Hermes was the messenger of the Greek gods and the guide who leads souls down to the underworld. The Homeric Hymn to Hermes, an ancient poem in his honour, tells the comic story of his first day of life, when the newborn god invented an instrument, stole a herd and talked his way out of trouble.

His mother was Maia, a shy nymph whose home was a cave high on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, where Zeus visited her in secret; she was one of the Pleiades, the daughters of Atlas.

On the morning he was born, Hermes climbed out of his cradle and found a tortoise crawling past the cave. He killed it, scooped out its shell, stretched strings across it, and by afternoon he had invented the first lyre.

That same day he crossed the mountains into Pieria, where the sacred cattle of his elder half-brother Apollo grazed, and stole fifty of them. Any tracker could have followed their hoofprints home, so he drove the cattle backwards, and their tracks pointed away from the place they were really going. A baby's footprints beside the herd would still have given him away, so he wove himself a pair of huge sandals out of tamarisk and myrtle twigs. Then he slipped back into his cradle.

Apollo followed the strange trail to the cave and found a tiny baby in swaddling clothes who swore he was far too young to steal anything. Apollo hauled him up to Olympus to face Zeus. Zeus, watching his infant son deny everything with a straight face, burst out laughing at the cheek of it and told the brothers to settle it between themselves.

So Hermes took out his lyre and played. Apollo, the god of music, was so enchanted that he gave up his herd of cattle to keep the instrument, and from then on the lyre was Apollo's and the cattle belonged to Hermes.

marsyas-midas-and-the-asss-ears.context_blurb: In Greek myth, Athena invented the double-piped flute called the aulos but threw it away in disgust when she saw her own cheeks puffing out in a reflection on the water. A satyr named Marsyas picked it up and became so good on it he challenged Apollo himself to a music contest. The judges set the terms: whoever lost would be at the winner's absolute mercy. The outcome of that contest, and the related story of the Phrygian king Midas who judged a later music-match and got a strange reward for his ears, both come from Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 11.

pandora-and-the-jar-hope-alone-remaining.context_blurb: In Hesiod's Works and Days, Prometheus the wise Titan has stolen fire from heaven and given it to mortals. Zeus's revenge is to have the gods make the first mortal woman — Pandora — out of earth and water. He sends her down as a gift to Prometheus's younger brother. She comes carrying a jar (later mistranslated 'box') she is told never to open. The famous ending of the story turns on what is left inside the jar after everything else has flown out. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days.

poseidon-and-athena-the-olive-and-the-sp.context_blurb: In Greek myth, one Olympian is lord of the sea, of horses, and of earthquakes. His wife is the sea-nymph Amphitrite. In one famous contest he competes with Athena for the right to be the patron god of a new city in Attica. The two offer gifts to the local king and his council — he strikes the rock with his trident and she plants a tree — and the council then has to decide. The losing god is bitter about it for the rest of the city's history. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.

prometheus-fire-in-the-fennel-stalk-the-.context_blurb: In Hesiod's Theogony, Prometheus the Titan sides with Zeus against his own Titan brothers in the great war for heaven, and keeps his freedom after the Olympians win. He then plays a long double game as the friend of mortal men — tricking Zeus at a sacrifice at Mecone, and stealing fire from heaven and smuggling it to earth hidden in the hollow of a plant-stalk. Zeus's revenge is to have him chained to a crag in the Caucasus, where an eagle comes every day to eat his liver. Sources: Hesiod, Theogony and Works and Days; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound.

sisyphus-cheating-death-chaining-thanato.context_blurb: In Book 6 of Homer's Iliad, Homer gives Sisyphus a nickname that fits the whole story to come: he was, Homer says flat out, the craftiest of mortals. He twice cheats Death itself — once by chaining up the god of death in a cupboard so that nobody on earth can die until Ares has to come free him, and once by tricking Hades's queen into letting him go back up to the living on a technicality. His eternal punishment in the Odyssey and the famous essay of Albert Camus come down to one single endless task. Sources: Homer, Iliad 6; Odyssey 11; Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus.

tantalus-ixion-the-danaids-the-underworl.context_blurb: In Greek myth there is a special wing of the underworld reserved for mortals who committed outrages the gods could not forgive. Three of its most famous inmates each get their own eternal punishment: a king of Anatolia who served up his own son in a stew for the gods to see if they would notice; a king of Thessaly who tried to seduce Zeus's own wife while a guest at his table; and the fifty daughters of a king of Argos who were ordered to murder their husbands on their wedding night. Sources: Homer, Odyssey 11; Ovid, Metamorphoses; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca.

the-five-ages-of-man-gold-silver-bronze-.context_blurb: The Greek poet Hesiod wrote his Works and Days to his brother Perses, who had cheated him out of his share of their father's inheritance. Buried inside that poem is a myth of how the world grew worse across a series of ages, each race of mortals worse than the last. The ages are named for successively less noble metals (and one age named not for a metal but for a different kind of generation inserted between bronze and iron), and the final age is Hesiod's own. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days 109–201.

the-titanomachy-cronus-the-stone-and-the.context_blurb: Before Zeus and the Olympians ruled the world, the throne of heaven belonged to an older generation of gods — twelve of them, children of Gaia and Ouranos. Their king Cronus had learned he would be overthrown by his own son, as he had overthrown his own father, and so swallowed his children one by one as his wife Rhea bore them. For the sixth, Rhea substituted a stone wrapped in swaddling-clothes and hid the real baby away in a cave on Crete. The war that followed, when the hidden boy grew up and freed his siblings, ran ten years. Source: Hesiod, Theogony.

zeus-the-thunderbolt-the-eagle-the-disgu.context_blurb: Zeus rules the Olympian gods from the summit of Mount Olympus. His signature weapon is a single flash-and-crash object that no other god wields; his sacred bird is the one that soars highest; and his sacred tree stood at the oracle of Dodona. The old stories remember as many of his disguises as of his victories: he comes to one princess as a shower of gold, to another as a great white bull, to a third as a swan. The young Trojan prince Ganymede was carried up to be his cup-bearer. Sources: Hesiod, Theogony; Homeric Hymns; Ovid.

achilles-among-the-daughters-of-lycomede.context_blurb:
Thetis, a sea-nymph, married the mortal king Peleus, and their son Achilles grew into the greatest warrior of the Greeks. A prophecy haunted her: if he went to Troy, he would die young. So, in a legend told by the Roman poet Statius and the Greek writer Apollodorus, she hid the boy in the last place any recruiting party would search.

She sent Achilles to Skyros, the island of King Lycomedes, dressed as a girl to live among the king's own daughters, and nobody suspected the princesses had a warrior in their midst.

The boy needed a girl's name, and he went by Pyrrha, which means "red-haired" in Greek. The disguise lasted long enough for him to father a son with one of the princesses, Deidameia. That boy, Neoptolemus, was also called Pyrrhus, the male form of his father's secret name, a joke the Greeks never forgot.

Meanwhile the Greek fleet gathered at Aulis, and the seer Calchas warned the kings that Troy would never fall without Achilles. Finding a hero hidden in a palace full of princesses called for cunning, so the chieftains sent the craftiest man among them, Odysseus of Ithaca.

Odysseus came to the palace posing as a merchant and spread out fine cloth, jewellery and mirrors for the girls to admire. Among the pretty things he slipped a spear and a shield. The princesses reached for the finery, but one "daughter" ignored it and seized the weapons, and Odysseus had his man. Apollodorus tells it with an alarm instead: Odysseus had a war-trumpet blast sounded outside, and while the girls scattered, one of them turned toward battle like a soldier answering the call. Some vase painters showed this trumpet version.

The quiet island king had a darker story of his own. Years before, Theseus of Athens, the old hero who had killed the Minotaur, came to Skyros late in life looking for shelter, and Lycomedes took him up to a high cliff and pushed him off into the sea below.

achilles-drags-hector-round-the-walls-of.context_blurb:
Homer's Iliad, the great Greek poem of the Trojan War, has a champion on each side. For the Greeks it is Achilles, the deadliest fighter alive. For Troy it is Hector, a soldier defending a city, a wife and a baby son, and that is why his death below the walls is the darkest scene in the poem.

Hector was the eldest son of old King Priam and the shield of Troy, the prince who took the Trojans out to fight day after day and cut down Greek captain after captain. Homer lets us see him at home first. In Book 6 his wife Andromache brings their baby, Astyanax, to meet him, and the child screams in terror at the horsehair crest nodding on his father's bronze helmet. Hector laughs, lifts the helmet off his head, and only then takes his son in his arms.

The end comes in Book 22. Hector waits by the Scaean Gate while Priam and Queen Hecuba plead from the wall for him to come inside. Then Achilles comes at him in new armour forged by a god, and Hector's nerve breaks: he runs, and the two men race three full laps around the city walls, Achilles hunting him like a hawk after a dove.

Hector stops only when his brother appears beside him, promising to fight at his side. But it is a trick. The goddess Athena has put on his brother's shape to make Hector stand, and when he turns for a second spear, the space beside him is empty. The armour on Hector's back once belonged to Achilles himself, taken from the body of Achilles's friend Patroclus, and Achilles knows its single weakness: he drives his spear through Hector's throat, where the bronze leaves the neck bare. The wound leaves breath enough for last words. Hector begs for his body to be sent home, then foretells Achilles's own doom: Paris and Apollo, a Trojan prince and a god, will kill him at that same gate.

Achilles refuses the plea. He cuts through the tendons behind Hector's heels, threads leather straps through them and lashes the corpse behind his own chariot, then drags the prince through the dust while his parents and his wife watch from the walls. Nor does he stop. For twelve days, morning after morning, Achilles harnesses the body again and hauls it around the grave mound of Patroclus, until even the gods on Olympus are sickened.

Zeus finally orders the body returned, and the Iliad's final book ends in darkness and grace. Old King Priam crosses to the Greek camp by night with no weapon, guided by the god Hermes, kneels before his son's killer in Achilles's own tent and kisses the hands that killed his sons. Achilles weeps with him, the two eat together, and Hector goes home to be buried.

achilless-heel-the-arrow-the-styx-and-th.context_blurb:
Achilles, the deadliest warrior of the Trojan War, was half divine. His father was Peleus, a mortal king, and his mother was a goddess of the sea. She did everything she could to make her son proof against weapons, yet Homer's Iliad already hints at how, despite all her care, he would one day fall.

His mother was Thetis, one of the fifty Nereids, the sea-nymph daughters of the old sea-god Nereus. At her wedding to Peleus a golden apple marked "for the fairest" rolled among the guests, and the quarrel it started led in the end to the Trojan War.

In the Roman poet Statius's telling, Thetis took her baby to the River Styx in the underworld and lowered him into its black water, which made mortal skin impossible to wound. But she had to hold on to him somehow. Her fingers gripped his heel, so that one patch of skin stayed dry, and that is why any single weak spot in something strong is still called an Achilles heel.

Homer plants the ending early. Dying at Achilles's feet, the Trojan prince Hector warned him that he would fall at the Scaean Gate, the great western gate of Troy facing the Greek camp on the beach, the very place where Hector made his own last stand. Hector also named the killers: the Trojan prince Paris, and a god at his side. When the day came, Paris drew his bow and Apollo, the archer god and protector of Troy, steered the arrow home. Later tellers say it struck the one place the river never touched, the heel his mother had held.

aeneas-fleeing-troy-father-on-his-back-s.context_blurb:
Virgil's Aeneid, the great Latin epic of Rome, begins its hero's road in fire. Aeneas is a Trojan prince on the night the Greeks break into Troy, and Book 2 tells how he carried his family out of the burning city. The picture of a son bearing his father to safety became Rome's favourite emblem of duty to family and gods.

The Greeks have slipped into the city inside the wooden horse, and Aeneas is fighting in the burning streets when his mother appears to him. She is the goddess Aphrodite, whom Virgil, writing in Latin, calls Venus, and she tells him Troy is finished: his task now is to save his family and go. He races home, but his father, Anchises, will not budge. The old man was lamed by Zeus long ago for boasting that Aphrodite had loved him, and now he means to die with his city rather than flee it.

Then comes a sign. A gentle flame flickers over the hair of Ascanius, Aeneas's little boy, licking his curls without burning it, and the family takes it as a message from heaven. Roman tradition also calls the boy Iulus, a name that later linked him to the family of Julius Caesar.

Anchises agrees at last to leave, but he cannot walk and the child cannot keep pace in the smoke. So Aeneas, armed and armoured as he is, bends down and lifts Anchises up onto his own shoulders, and old Anchises clutches the household gods of Troy while Ascanius trots beside them, holding his father's hand. Around 1618 the young sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved that escape from one block of marble, three generations stacked into a single column, and the statue still stands in Rome's Galleria Borghese.

Aeneas's wife, Creusa, follows a few steps behind. Somewhere in the smoke and the stampeding crowds she drops behind, and when Aeneas reaches safety outside the walls she is gone. He draws his sword and plunges back alone into the flames, shouting her name. What meets him is her ghost. She speaks to him gently, telling him that a new kingdom and a new wife wait for him in a western land and asking him to care for their son, and three times he tries to hold her and three times she slips through his arms like air.

With the other refugees of Troy, Aeneas builds a fleet below Mount Ida and wanders the sea for years: to Delos, Crete and Sicily, then to Carthage, where Queen Dido gives him her heart. His voyage ends where the Tiber meets the sea in Latium, in central Italy, the river on which Romulus, his far-off descendant, will one day found Rome.

argus-the-old-dog-recognition-on-the-dun.context_blurb:
Homer's Odyssey is the Greek epic of a long homecoming. Its hero Odysseus, king of the rocky island of Ithaca, spends twenty years away from Penelope, his wife, and Telemachus, his son. When at last he reaches home, the first one to know him is not his family but an old dog.

The first ten of those years Odysseus spent fighting in the Trojan War, and the next ten trying to sail home across a sea full of monsters and angry gods. Meanwhile rude suitors had filled his palace, all of them hoping to marry Penelope, so when he landed on Ithaca the goddess Athena disguised him as a ragged old beggar, the kind of man nobody looks at twice.

His loyal swineherd Eumaeus, who had tended his master's pigs out in the hills all those years and never joined the suitors, walked the beggar up to the palace without guessing who he was.

Outside the palace gate lay Argus, the hunting dog Odysseus had raised before he left. No one cared for him now. Old and forgotten, he lay on a heap of dung, mule and cattle muck piled by the doors until servants could carry it off to manure the fields.

Everyone else was fooled. Eumaeus beside him did not know his master, nor did Penelope inside, but Argus knew him at once. Too weak to rise, the old dog dropped his ears and wagged his tail.

Odysseus passed by. And in that same moment, having seen his master once more after twenty years of waiting, Argus died.

the-cyclops-polyphemus-nobody-and-the-bu.context_blurb: In Book 9 of Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus sailing home from Troy and twelve of his crew land on an island of huge one-eyed shepherd giants, the Cyclopes, and walk into the cave of one of them hoping for a guest-gift. The owner comes home with his flock and rolls a huge stone across the mouth of the cave. The scheme Odysseus hatches to get out again involves a clever false name, an olive-wood stake sharpened to a point and heated red in the fire, and the fleecy undersides of a flock of sheep. Source: Homer, Odyssey Book 9.

circe-of-aeaea-pigs-moly-and-the-year-on.context_blurb:
Book 10 of Homer's Odyssey brings the hero Odysseus, still struggling home from the Trojan War, to the wooded island of Aeaea. Smoke curls up from a house of stone in a forest clearing, and the woman inside is both a goddess and a witch, a daughter of the sun god Helios.

Her name is Circe. She welcomes strangers in, feeds them, and turns them into beasts; tame wolves and lions, her earlier guests, already prowl her yard. She gave Odysseus's men cheese, barley meal, honey and wine. Then she struck the men one by one with her wand, and they became pigs, snouts, bristles and all, shut in her sty and fed on acorns.

Odysseus had sent only half his crew, under an officer named Eurylochus, who suspected a trap, waited at the door, and when he saw his comrades changed ran back to the ship with the news. In the sty the pigs wept, because inside the animal bodies their minds were still human: they knew who they were and remembered Odysseus, but they could only grunt.

Odysseus set out alone to rescue them, and on the forest path the god Hermes met him, the messenger of the gods and friend of travellers and tricksters. Hermes gave him a magic plant to guard against Circe's drugs, black at the root with a flower white as milk, which only gods can safely pull from the earth: the moly.

Hermes told him exactly what to do. When Circe struck him with her wand, he was to draw his sword and rush at her; she would let the wand fall and try to win him to her bed, and before he agreed he must make her swear the great oath of the gods that she would plot no further harm against him or his men. It went just as Hermes said. The wand struck, the moly held, and Odysseus came at her with his sword. Circe let the wand fall, stared at him, and greeted him as Odysseus, the man of many turns, because Hermes had warned her years before that he would come. Circe swore the oath, went out to the sty, and touched each pig with a fresh potion, and the men came back younger than before, taller and far better-looking.

Circe became their generous host, and they stayed on Aeaea a full year, feasting so well they nearly forgot Ithaca, until the men begged Odysseus to remember home. When he asked Circe the way back, she told him he could not go straight there: first he had to visit the dead and question the ghost of Tiresias, the blind seer of Thebes, in the underworld. That journey is the next book of the Odyssey.
