the-descent-to-hades-tiresias-odysseuss-.context_blurb: A witch had kept Odysseus and his crew as her guests on her island for a year, and when he finally asked to sail home to Ithaca she told him he could not go straight there — first he had to sail to the edge of the world and speak with the dead. Book 11 of the Odyssey, the famous Nekuia, follows him down. He pours a libation into a pit, draws his sword over it, and the shades of the dead crowd forward to drink — his old crewman Elpenor, the Theban seer Tiresias, his own mother Anticlea, and heroes dead at Troy. Source: Homer, Odyssey Book 11.

scylla-and-charybdis-six-heads-and-a-whi.context_blurb: In Homer's Odyssey, the witch Circe warns Odysseus about a sea-passage where two monsters wait on facing cliffs so that no ship can avoid both — one a six-headed cave-monster hanging over the strait and plucking crewmen off the deck; the other a whirlpool below that sucks the sea down and spits it back up three times a day. Ancient geographers later identified the strait with the narrow water between southern Italy and the island of Sicily. Source: Homer, Odyssey Book 12.

the-sirens-the-mast-and-the-wax.context_blurb: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus is sailing home from Troy when the witch Circe warns him about a stretch of sea where women sing so beautifully that any sailor who hears them steers his ship onto the rocks around their meadow. The crew gets past the island by one trick, and Odysseus himself hears the song by a different trick. Later tradition says the singers were half-bird, half-woman, and gave the three of them famous Greek names. Source: Homer, Odyssey Book 12.

the-cattle-of-the-sun-on-thrinacia-zeuss.context_blurb: Two prophets warn Odysseus that the animals grazing on the island of Thrinacia must never be touched. Seven great herds and seven great flocks live there — the deathless cattle of one of the gods — and never breed and never die. Trapped on the island by a month of contrary winds, Odysseus's crew finally break the taboo while he sleeps. The punishment follows the ship as soon as it leaves the harbor. Only one man will walk alive off the beach of the next island. Source: Homer, Odyssey Book 12.

nausicaa-and-the-ball-on-the-shore-of-ph.context_blurb: Long before Odysseus washes up on the beach where the princess Nausicaa will find him, he has been stuck for seven years on a far island with a sea-nymph who wants him to stay and be her husband. She even offers him immortality if he will forget his home. Freed at last, he is wrecked again on the shore of the Phaeacians and crawls under a heap of dead leaves to sleep. In the morning a king's daughter and her maids are washing laundry on the river and he wakes among them. Source: Homer, Odyssey Books 5–6.

penelopes-test-of-the-marriage-bed-roote.context_blurb: The suitors are dead in the hall of Ithaca; Odysseus has been bathed and dressed in fine clothes and Athena has made him beautiful again. But the woman who has waited for him longer than most people wait for anything comes down to the hall and will not so much as speak to him. She sits opposite him and watches, and finally lays one last test — a question only her husband could answer — about an object the two of them share that no one else in the house has ever seen made. Source: Homer, Odyssey Book 23.

the-stringing-of-the-great-bow-and-the-s.context_blurb: Odysseus has finally reached home in Ithaca after twenty years, but does not walk into his own hall as the king. He wants first to see who has been eating his stores. He is helped by his son Telemachus, by a loyal swineherd, and by a loyal cowherd. His wife Penelope — not knowing him — holds a contest among her suitors with a huge bow of the hero Iphitus. The contest ends in a hall-slaughter and a terrible hanging in the courtyard. Source: Homer, Odyssey Books 21–22.

the-wrath-of-achilles-and-the-death-of-p.context_blurb: In Homer's Iliad, Achilles quarrels with Agamemnon, the commander of the Greek army at Troy. Agamemnon forces him to give up a captive girl, and Achilles withdraws from the fighting and refuses to go out. The Trojans drive the Greeks all the way back to the ships. Patroclus, Achilles's closest friend, puts on Achilles's own armor and goes out in his place — and dies fighting Hector in that armor. Achilles's grief, his cry to his sea-nymph mother, and his black-ashed hair all follow. Source: Homer, Iliad 1, 16, 18.

the-shield-of-achilles-the-world-hephaes.context_blurb: Achilles's dearest companion Patroclus had gone into battle wearing Achilles's own armour and had been killed and stripped of it. Achilles now has nothing to fight in. His mother Thetis, the sea-nymph, climbs up to Olympus and asks the smith-god Hephaestus to forge him a new set in a single night. Book 18 of the Iliad takes six long paragraphs to describe only one piece of the armor — a round object on which the god hammers out two whole cities, a wedding, a lawsuit, farmers plowing a field, a lion attack, dancing youths, and the great river that rings the world. Source: Homer, Iliad 18.

priam-in-the-tent-of-achilles-i-have-kis.context_blurb: Book 24 of Homer's Iliad closes the whole epic with one of the most-praised scenes in Western literature. The aged king of Troy whose eldest son has been killed and whose body has been dragged behind an enemy chariot for days finally crosses the Greek lines alone at night, unarmed, guided by the god Hermes. He walks into the enemy camp, kneels at the hero's feet, and asks for his son's body. The two men eat together, agree to a truce, and go to bed in the same tent. The Iliad ends with a single line about the burial of the Trojan prince. Source: Homer, Iliad 24.

the-sack-of-troy-cassandra-at-the-altar-.context_blurb: After ten years of siege, the Greeks finally break into Troy through the trick of the wooden horse. The sack is told fullest in Virgil's Aeneid Book 2 and Euripides's Trojan Women. Priam is slaughtered at his own altar by Achilles's son Neoptolemus; the prophetess Cassandra is dragged out of Athena's temple; Hector's baby son Astyanax is thrown from the walls; and Queen Hecuba's granddaughter is sacrificed on Achilles's tomb. The Greeks burn the city to the ground and sail home — but the gods are already angry at them for how the sack was done. Sources: Virgil, Aeneid 2; Euripides, Trojan Women.

the-madness-of-ajax-slaughtering-sheep-f.context_blurb: After Achilles was killed at Troy, his god-forged armor was awarded by the Greek chieftains to the warrior who most deserved it. Two men were the contenders: the clever Odysseus, and the strongest fighter left in the whole Greek camp — the man who had carried Achilles's body off the battlefield. When the award went to the other man, the great fighter went mad in the night. Sophocles's play Ajax follows what happens through the next morning. Source: Sophocles, Ajax.

the-trojan-horse-odysseuss-stratagem-and.context_blurb: After ten years of siege the Greeks still could not break the walls of Troy, so one of their leaders proposed a trick to get inside without a battle: build an enormous hollow wooden horse, hide a picked band of warriors inside it, and sail the rest of the fleet out of sight behind the island of Tenedos. The whole scene — Laocoon with his spear, Sinon's tears, and the opening of the great gate from within at midnight — is told fullest in Book 2 of Virgil's Aeneid. Source: Virgil, Aeneid 2.

the-wedding-of-peleus-and-thetis-eriss-g.context_blurb: In Greek myth, a mortal king of the Myrmidons in Phthia married a sea-nymph in a wedding on Mount Pelion, and every Olympian god came to the feast — every god except one. The excluded goddess rolled a golden apple down the aisle inscribed with just two words. The quarrel that followed ran out of control, and set up the Judgment of Paris and ultimately the Trojan War itself. From that marriage was also born the greatest warrior of the war. Sources: Apollodorus, Epitome 3; Hyginus, Fabulae.

the-judgment-of-paris-power-wisdom-or-he.context_blurb: In the story that kicks off the Trojan War, a young prince of Troy named Paris is tending sheep on Mount Ida when three goddesses appear to him for judgment. They had been quarrelling over a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, and Zeus had passed the quarrel on to a mortal shepherd. Each goddess offers Paris a bribe. He chooses one, and the choice turns the long war on him and on his city. Sources: the Kypria (summarised in Proclus); Apollodorus, Epitome 3.

helen-and-paris-in-troy-the-muster-of-a-.context_blurb:
The Trojan War, the greatest story the Greeks told, began with a stolen wife. Homer's Iliad, later poets and the historian Herodotus all tell parts of it: an oath sworn by a crowd of suitors, a judge of goddesses, a king faking madness, a fleet beyond counting, and a woman whom some said never reached Troy at all.

Menelaus, king of Sparta, came home from a trip to Crete to find his wife Helen gone, and much of his treasure with her. She had sailed east across the Aegean with Paris, the son of King Priam of Troy, the same prince who as a shepherd on Mount Ida had judged a contest of beauty between Hera, Athena and Aphrodite and awarded the prize to Aphrodite, who had offered him the loveliest woman alive.

Years before, so many Greek princes had come to court Helen that King Tyndareus, her stepfather, was afraid the rejected men would turn to war. Odysseus of Ithaca had the answer: every suitor must swear to defend whoever won her. In return Odysseus asked Tyndareus to help him win the girl he had really come for, Penelope, daughter of Tyndareus's brother Icarius.

Now Menelaus called in that oath, and he turned first to his elder brother, Agamemnon of Mycenae, who took command of the whole Greek army.

Not every sworn suitor wanted to go. An oracle had warned Odysseus of Ithaca that if he sailed for Troy he would be gone for many years, so when the envoys came he played the madman, yoking an ox beside a donkey to his plough and sowing his furrows with salt. The Greek chief Palamedes saw through him. He set Odysseus's baby son, Telemachus, right before the ploughshare, and when Odysseus swerved to spare the child, the trick was over.

The fleet gathered at Aulis, a harbour in Boeotia facing the island of Euboea. There an angry goddess held back the winds, and Agamemnon paid a terrible price before the ships could sail.

Christopher Marlowe's famous line speaks of Helen's face launching a thousand ships, but that is a poet's round number. Homer's Catalogue of Ships, in the Iliad's second book, lists twenty-nine contingents and about 1,186 ships, with Agamemnon's hundred the largest.

Some Greeks told the story differently. The poet Stesichorus and the playwright Euripides said only a phantom Helen went to Troy, and the historian Herodotus wrote that the real Helen spent the war in Egypt, in the keeping of its king, where Menelaus found her afterwards.

In the third book of the Iliad, Helen stands on the walls of Troy beside old King Priam, who cannot tell one Greek leader from another. Looking down at the army on the plain, she points out the Greek chieftains to him one after another, Agamemnon, Odysseus and great Ajax, and tells him who each one is. The Greeks called the scene the Teichoscopia, the view from the walls.

iphigenia-at-aulis-the-winds-refused-the.context_blurb:
Before the Greeks could sail to Troy, they paid a terrible price. The story of Iphigenia, daughter of King Agamemnon, is told in two very different ways by two great Athenian playwrights: Aeschylus, who lets the knife fall, and Euripides, who lets a goddess snatch the girl away.

The huge Greek fleet gathered under Agamemnon at Aulis, a small harbour on the strait between Boeotia and the island of Euboea, and there it lay stuck, its sails hanging limp day after day. Agamemnon called in Calchas, the best seer in the Greek army, a reader of birds who knew what was, what will be and what had been.

Calchas gave his answer before the whole army: Artemis, the huntress goddess, was holding back the wind because Agamemnon had offended her, and in one telling he had killed a stag in her grove and boasted that he hunted better than she did. Her price was Agamemnon's own daughter.

Iphigenia was at home with her mother, Clytemnestra, far from the camp, so Agamemnon wrote home a lie: come to Aulis at once, for the girl was to marry Achilles, the most glorious young warrior in the camp. Mother and daughter set out happily. In Euripides's play, when Achilles learns that his name has been used as bait for a killing, he is furious, and he vows to fight the whole army with his own sword to protect her.

In the older and harsher telling, Aeschylus's tragedy Agamemnon, the sacrifice is carried out. They gag the girl to stop her cursing them, and the chieftains pay no heed when she cries out for her father. Long afterwards, when Agamemnon returns victorious from Troy, Clytemnestra, his wife, murders him in the bath to avenge their daughter.

In Euripides's gentler version, the girl changes. At first she begs for her life, but then she makes up her mind. Wearing a bride's veil, she goes to the sacrifice without fear and declares that she gives her own body to Greece so the fleet can sail and Troy can fall. As the knife comes down, Artemis takes pity and snatches her away, and in the girl's place a deer lies dying under the knife. The deer was the huntress goddess's own animal.

andromeda-on-the-rock-and-the-stone-king.context_blurb:
Perseus is one of the oldest heroes of Greek myth: a son of Zeus and the mortal princess Danae, raised by a fisherman on a small island, and the man who beheaded Medusa, the Gorgon whose gaze turned people to stone. Flying home with her head in a bag, he found a princess in deadly danger, and one rescue led to a wedding, a massacre and a sky full of stars.

Soaring above the Ethiopian shore on his flying sandals, Perseus saw a young woman chained to a sea-cliff while a monster swam in toward her. She was Andromeda, the daughter of Ethiopia's King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia, left there as an offering to the beast.

Her mother had brought this on her. Cassiopeia had boasted that her daughter was lovelier than the Nereids, the fifty sea-nymphs, and Poseidon, lord of the sea and master of those nymphs, was enraged by the insult. He sent a sea-monster called Cetus to ravage the coast, and an oracle declared that only one offering would stop it, so King Cepheus chained his own daughter to the rock.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses, as Cetus rose from the waves, Perseus dived on it from the air and drove the harpe, the curved sickle-sword Hermes had given him for beheading Medusa, deep into the monster's side. Cepheus gladly gave the rescuer his daughter's hand, but the wedding feast was broken up by an armed gang led by Phineus, Andromeda's earlier suitor, who claimed she was his by an older promise. Perseus pulled Medusa's head from its bag, and Phineus and his men turned to stone.

With his bride, Perseus sailed home to Serifos, the little island in the Cyclades where he had grown up and where his mother had taken sanctuary in a temple to escape the island's king.

Serifos was where his story began. Years before, Danae's father, King Acrisius of Argos, had sealed his daughter and her infant in a wooden chest and cast them adrift. The chest washed up on Serifos, and a fisherman named Dictys hauled it out of the waves in his net, opened it and raised the boy as his own. Dictys's brother was the king of the island, Polydectes, the very man who had sent Perseus after Medusa's head. Perseus strode into his hall in the middle of a feast, held up the head once more, and Polydectes and all his nobles turned to stone in their seats. Perseus made the good fisherman Dictys king in his place.

His work done, Perseus returned the gods' gifts. The nymphs got back their flying sandals and their cap that made the wearer invisible, and Hermes took back his sickle-sword. Athena, who had guided him from the start, received the polished shield and the Gorgon's head, and she set the head at the centre of her aegis, the goatskin she wears on her breast.

Last of all, the whole cast went up into the northern night sky: Perseus, Andromeda, Cepheus, even the monster Cetus. Cassiopeia sits there on her throne, and as the sky wheels round she hangs upside-down for half of every year, still paying for her boast.

atalanta-the-she-bear-the-boar-and-the-g.context_blurb:
Atalanta is the great huntress of Greek myth, a princess of Arcadia who could outshoot and outrun the men of Greece. Her story, told by Apollodorus and by the Roman poet Ovid, runs from a baby left to die on a mountain, through the most famous boar hunt in legend, to a deadly footrace and a pair of lions.

Her father, an Arcadian king, wanted a son, so when his queen gave birth to a girl, he ordered the infant abandoned on Mount Parthenion. A she-bear, the animal sacred to Artemis, found the child and nursed her, and later hunters took in the wild girl and raised her. Atalanta grew up serving Artemis and never missed her mark. When two centaurs, Rhoecus and Hylaeus, attacked her in the forest, she shot them both with her bow and arrows.

When Artemis loosed a monstrous boar on Calydon to punish its king, the heroes of Greece gathered to hunt it, Theseus, Peleus and Jason among them, and Atalanta was the one woman in their company. Her arrow was the first to wound the boar, so when Prince Meleager finished it off with his spear he gave her its hide as the prize. His uncles were furious that the trophy went to a woman, and the quarrel turned deadly.

Her father later recognised his daughter and welcomed her home, and he wanted her married. Atalanta agreed on one condition: any suitor had to race her on foot and win, and every man who lost would be executed. No one in Greece could run as fast, and young man after young man paid with his life. Melanion, who had seen those suitors die, knew he could never outrun her, so he begged the love goddess Aphrodite to help him.

Aphrodite gave him three golden apples, from the garden of the Hesperides in some tellings, and told him to toss one off the track whenever Atalanta drew level with him. She could not resist them. She stopped for each one, and by the third she had fallen too far behind to catch him.

Melanion won his bride, but he never thanked Aphrodite for her gift. Aphrodite took her revenge by filling the pair with sudden desire inside a holy shrine, a temple of Cybele in Ovid's telling, and for defiling the holy place the two became lions, yoked forever to pull Cybele's chariot.

bellerophon-pegasus-and-the-lead-tipped-.context_blurb:
Bellerophon is one of the great monster-slayers of Greek myth, the hero who rode the winged horse Pegasus. Homer tells part of his story in Book 6 of the Iliad, Pindar sings of the taming of the horse, and the tale climbs from exile and betrayal to a battle in the sky, and then to a long, hard fall.

Bellerophon was a prince of Corinth, grandson of Sisyphus, from the city that guards the narrow isthmus between two seas.

After an accidental killing, he fled to King Proetus of Tiryns for purification. Proetus's queen wanted him, and when he turned her away she accused him to her husband. Proetus would not kill a guest under his own roof, so he sent Bellerophon on to his father-in-law, King Iobates of Lycia, carrying a sealed letter that ordered its bearer's death, the only piece of writing in the whole Iliad. Iobates feasted his guest for nine days before he broke the seal. Then, unwilling to do the killing himself, he sent Bellerophon against the Chimera, a monster burning the crops and herds of Lycia, an errand he thought no man could survive.

The Chimera was one beast made of three: a lion's head at the front, a serpent for a tail, and the head of a goat rising from the middle of her back, with fire pouring from her mouths. From her comes the English word chimera, for any impossible hybrid. The seer Polyidus told Bellerophon that a fire-breathing beast could only be fought from above. On his advice Bellerophon slept a night in Athena's temple, where the goddess came to him as he dreamed and laid a golden bridle beside him; on waking he found it lying on the temple floor.

At Pirene, a spring in Corinth where a winged horse drank each morning, Bellerophon slipped the bridle on. This was Pegasus, the horse that sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her, and Athena's golden bridle was the one thing that could tame him. From the horse's back Bellerophon struck at the Chimera out of reach of her flames; later tellers say he drove a lead-tipped spear into her jaws, and her own fire melted the lead down her throat.

Iobates kept trying to get rid of him, sending him against the Solymi and then the Amazons, and Bellerophon beat them all. Pride undid him. He turned Pegasus upward to fly to the top of Olympus and sit among the gods, and Zeus loosed a gadfly to sting the horse; Pegasus bucked, and Bellerophon fell all the way to earth. Homer says he wandered alone after that, hated by the gods, eating his heart out.

Pegasus flew on without him to Olympus, and Zeus kept him there to carry his thunderbolts; later the horse was set among the stars as a constellation.

heracless-birth-three-nights-long-and-th.context_blurb:
Heracles was the strongest hero of Greek myth, and his troubles began before he was born. The Greek mythographer Apollodorus, the poet Pindar and the Roman poet Ovid tell how a god tricked his way into a Theban palace, how a goddess tried to stop the birth, and how the baby proved who his father was.

In Thebes lived Alcmene, a mortal princess married to the general Amphitryon. While Amphitryon was away at war, Zeus took on his exact appearance and lay with Alcmene as if he were her husband, and he made that one night last as long as three. Later that same night the real Amphitryon came home, and Alcmene conceived by both of them. She bore twin boys: Iphicles, son of Amphitryon, and Heracles, son of Zeus.

Hera, Zeus's wife, was furious, and she tried to stop the birth. Ovid says she sent the birth-goddess Eileithyia to sit outside Alcmene's room with her arms folded and her legs crossed, a spell that kept the baby from being born, and Alcmene laboured for days. Her quick-witted servant Galanthis ran out past the goddess and cried that Alcmene had already given birth. Eileithyia leapt up in surprise, the spell broke, and Heracles was born; the angry goddess turned Galanthis into a weasel.

Hera did not give up. When the twins were eight months old, she sent two serpents into the nursery to kill Heracles in his cradle. Little Iphicles shrieked and scrambled for safety. When the nurse came running, Pindar says, she found baby Heracles holding the snakes he had strangled, a dead serpent in each fist, and playing with them. That was the first proof that he was the son of Zeus.

His strength was a danger as well as a gift. As a boy in Thebes he took lyre lessons from Linus, the brother of Orpheus, and when Linus corrected him too harshly, Heracles lost his temper and struck his teacher dead with the lyre.

labor-1-the-nemean-lion-strangled-bare-h.context_blurb: A monstrous beast was ravaging the town of Nemea in the northern Peloponnese, eating farmers and their flocks. King Eurystheus of Mycenae sent Heracles to kill it as the very first of his twelve labors. The beast's hide was proof against any mortal weapon ever forged, so Heracles had to find a different way to kill it — and a different way to skin it afterwards. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-2-the-lernaean-hydra-and-iolaus-wi.context_blurb: For his second labor, King Eurystheus sent Heracles into a poisonous swamp in the Argolid to kill a monster that had been burning crops and eating cattle. Every time Heracles cut off one of the monster's heads two new heads grew back from the stump. His nephew Iolaus solved the problem with a burning firebrand from a nearby grove. Afterwards Heracles dipped his arrows in a specific thing he found inside the dead monster, which came back to kill him many years later through the shirt of Nessus. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-3-the-ceryneian-hind-of-artemis.context_blurb: For his third labor King Eurystheus sent Heracles after a deer that lived on Mount Ceryneia. Two things set this deer apart from any ordinary hind. Its horns were made of gold. And it belonged to the virgin goddess of the hunt, Artemis — which meant Heracles had to bring it back alive, without wounding it, without her anger falling on him. He chased it for a whole year. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-4-the-erymanthian-boar-and-the-sno.context_blurb: For his fourth labor King Eurystheus sent Heracles after a giant wild boar living on Mount Erymanthus. On the road up Heracles broke his journey at the cave of a wise centaur, who set roasted meat before him but hesitated to open a jar of wine said to belong to all the centaurs in common. The scent of the wine brought the whole mountain of centaurs down on the cave. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-5-the-augean-stables-and-the-two-r.context_blurb: For his fifth labor King Eurystheus sent Heracles into the land of Elis to serve one of the great cattle-kings of Greece — a king whose herds had never been cleaned in thirty years and whose cattle-yards were ankle-deep in filth. Heracles contracted beforehand to be paid a share of the cattle for the job. The way he mucked out the yards in a single day was itself the sort of answer only Heracles would give. The job's final twist is why he founded the Olympic Games at Olympia. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-6-the-stymphalian-birds-and-the-br.context_blurb: Heracles is set twelve labors by King Eurystheus, and most involve grappling with one huge beast. The sixth labor is different: he is sent to clear out a whole flock of man-eating creatures that have terrorised the countryside around Lake Stymphalia in Arcadia. He cannot climb into the marshy ground, cannot reach them with a sword, and cannot startle them off the lake. The goddess Athena hands him a bronze object that solves the problem. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-7-the-cretan-bull-that-minos-would.context_blurb: For his seventh labor King Eurystheus sent Heracles across the sea to bring back alive a magnificent white bull that was running wild through the fields and orchards. The bull had originally been sent by Poseidon as a sign to King Minos, who was supposed to sacrifice it back but kept it in his own herd instead and substituted an ordinary bull. The same bull was Pasiphae's. Heracles was told he could take the bull if he could capture it alone. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-8-the-man-eating-mares-of-diomedes.context_blurb: For his eighth labor King Eurystheus sent Heracles up to Thrace to bring back the four wild mares of King Diomedes, chained in bronze stalls because no rope would hold them. What made the mares so feared across Greece was what their master had been feeding them. The labor also costs the life of a young companion of Heracles's named Abderus, who gives the town of Abdera its name. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-9-the-girdle-of-hippolyta-the-amaz.context_blurb: The ninth of Heracles's twelve labors sent him far from Greece to the land of a tribe of warrior women beyond the Black Sea on the river Thermodon. King Eurystheus wanted a specific object the queen of the warrior women wore, a gift from the war-god Ares, as a prize for his own daughter Admete. The queen greeted Heracles well and would have handed it over freely — until the queen of the gods, in disguise, started a rumor through the camp. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-10-the-cattle-of-geryon-and-the-go.context_blurb: For his tenth labor Heracles was sent to the far western edge of the world, to an island called Erytheia, to drive home a herd of famous red-coated cattle belonging to a monster with three bodies joined at the waist. On the way out Heracles raised the two Pillars named for him on either side of the strait where the Mediterranean meets the Ocean, and borrowed from the sun-god Helios a magic golden cup to sail across the open sea in. The journey back drove him through Italy, where a fire-breathing giant named Cacus tried to steal part of the herd. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-11-the-apples-of-the-hesperides-an.context_blurb: For his eleventh labor Heracles was sent to steal a fruit no mortal was supposed to touch — a fruit that grew at the western edge of the world in the garden of the Hesperides, whose name means 'daughters of Evening.' A never-sleeping dragon coiled round the tree. On the way Heracles freed a certain long-tormented Titan who in gratitude told him how to accomplish the labor — a trick that turned on persuading another Titan to pick the fruit for him. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

labor-12-cerberus-dragged-up-from-hades.context_blurb: The cowardly king Eurystheus saved the very worst of Heracles's labors for last: descend into the land of the dead and bring back the great hound that guards its gates. Hades gave his permission on one condition — Heracles must subdue the dog using no weapons. Heracles was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries before he went down and brought up his cousin Theseus from the Chair of Forgetfulness on the way. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

the-shirt-of-nessus-heracless-last-day-o.context_blurb: Years after finishing the twelve labors, Heracles marries Deianira, a Calydonian princess and the sister of Meleager who had led the great boar-hunt. On a river-crossing, the centaur Nessus tries to carry her off; Heracles shoots him with an arrow still smeared in Hydra-venom from his second labor. The dying centaur tells Deianira to save some of his own blood as a love-charm against the day her husband might love another woman — and the lie kills Heracles on the pyre at the top of Mount Oeta. Source: Sophocles, Trachiniae; Apollodorus.

jason-the-one-sandal-and-the-argo-built-.context_blurb:
Jason is the Greek hero of the Golden Fleece, who sailed with the greatest heroes of his age in the first great ship, the Argo. Apollodorus and the poet Apollonius of Rhodes tell how a lost sandal sent him to the edge of the world, and of the wonders and monsters the Argonauts met on the way.

King Pelias of Iolcus had stolen his throne and feared to lose it, and an oracle from Delphi warned him to beware a man with one sandal.

Jason, the rightful heir, was coming home to claim that throne. At a flooded river he met an old woman and took her on his shoulders through the water. She was Hera in disguise, queen of the gods, who hated Pelias for neglecting her worship, and she never forgot Jason's kindness. In the current Jason lost a sandal, and he walked into Pelias's court wearing only one.

Pelias dared not kill him openly. Instead he sent him to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis, beyond the farthest shore of the Black Sea, where it hung in a grove of Ares watched by a sleepless dragon.

On the beach at Pagasae the shipwright Argus built the ship, with Athena herself guiding his hands; it was named the Argo after him, and its crew were the Argonauts. Athena set into its prow a timber from the sacred oak of Zeus at Dodona, the oldest oracle in Greece, so that the ship itself could speak and warn its crew.

The crew held heroes of every gift. Orpheus, the singer of Thrace, sat on the rowing bench with his lyre, and when the Sirens' song threatened to lure the crew to wreck, his music drowned them out and the Argo sailed safely past.

On the coast of Thrace they found Phineus, a blind old prophet starving because the Harpies, winged monsters, snatched and fouled his food whenever he sat down to eat. The Argonauts drove the Harpies off, and in thanks Phineus told them how to pass the Clashing Rocks. Those two cliffs, guarding the entrance to the Black Sea, slammed together to crush any ship. On Phineus's advice the heroes let a dove fly between them first; the cliffs closed on nothing but its tail feathers, and as they swung apart again the crew rowed through, losing only the tip of the stern. After that day the rocks never moved again.

At Colchis King Aeetes set Jason a deadly test: yoke two fire-breathing bulls with bronze hooves, plough a field, and sow it with dragon's teeth. Each tooth sprang up as an armed warrior. Jason survived only because Medea, the king's daughter, gave him a potion that made him proof against fire and steel.

She goes back with him to Iolcus, where her cauldron-trick plays a crucial role in Jason's revenge on his usurping uncle Pelias. Sources: Apollonius, Argonautica; Euripides, Medea.

meleager-atalanta-and-the-calydonian-boa.context_blurb: In Greek myth the three Fates stood at the newborn Meleager's hearth and prophesied that his life was tied to a single ordinary thing already in the room — a piece of wood burning right there in front of them. His mother Althaea snatched that log out of the fire and locked it in a chest. Years later, when a great boar sent by Artemis was ravaging Calydon, Meleager led the hunt — and the quarrel over the hide at the end of the hunt, and his mother's rage, both turned on that same log. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.

perseus-and-the-gods-gift-list-kibisis-m.context_blurb: A prophecy had warned King Acrisius of Argos that his own grandson would kill him. So he locked his daughter Danae inside a tower of bronze. Zeus still reached her, in a famous disguise, and the boy Perseus was born. Grandfather Acrisius sealed mother and baby in a wooden chest and cast it out to sea; a kindly fisherman on the island of Serifos drew them out of his nets and raised the boy. Later, when the local king coveted Danae, Perseus was sent off on an impossible errand — and the gods equipped him with the full tool-kit for it. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

perseus-at-the-gorgons-cave-medusa-pegas.context_blurb: In Greek myth three sisters live at the edge of the world — snakes writhe on their heads for hair, boar-tusks jut from their mouths, and any traveller who looks at their faces turns to stone. Perseus is sent to bring back one head. He finds the cave by first stealing a single eye and tooth shared among three enchantress-sisters nearby. From the neck of the beheaded sister two things leap out — a winged horse and a warrior with a golden sword. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.

theseus-on-the-road-to-athens-sinis-scir.context_blurb: The young Theseus grows up in the town of Troezen in his mother Aethra's household, not knowing his father. When he is old enough his mother leads him to a great boulder and tells him to lift it. Underneath are two tokens his absent father Aegeus, king of Athens, had left there years before. Theseus chooses the overland road around the Saronic Gulf — the hard way, through a string of famous roadside bandits he kills each by that bandit's own method. Source: Plutarch, Theseus 7–11.

theseus-ariadnes-thread-and-the-black-sa.context_blurb: The Minotaur lived inside a great maze at Knossos on Crete, so cunningly designed that anyone who went in could never find the way out again. King Minos of Crete had it built by his own household craftsman and demanded a yearly tribute of young men and women from Athens to feed to the beast. One year Theseus volunteered to go. He left Athens under black sails, with his father telling him to swap them for white sails on the return if he lived. Source: Plutarch, Theseus 15–22.

theseus-and-pirithous-stuck-to-the-chair.context_blurb: The two sworn friends Theseus and Pirithous thought themselves worthy of daughters of Zeus. First they set out to help Theseus win his chosen wife — a girl still a child, whom Theseus carried off and left with his mother Aethra in Attica. Then Pirithous proposed something bolder still: that they go together down into Hades and bring back the queen of the underworld. The two walked down through a cave at Cape Tainaron and were offered seats at Hades's table. Source: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.

andvaris-ring-the-cursed-gold-that-start.context_blurb:
The Volsung saga, the great Norse tale of the hero Sigurd and the dragon Fafnir, begins long before Sigurd is born, with three gods, a dead otter and a heap of gold. Every killing in the saga traces back to that gold, and above all to one ring that left its first owner's hand under a curse.

Odin, silent Honir and the trickster Loki were walking through the world of men when they came to a waterfall. On the bank sat a small brown otter eating a fish, and Loki killed it with one stone.

The gods skinned their catch and asked for a night's lodging at a nearby farm. The farmer, a wizard named Hreidmar, wept at the sight of the pelt, because the otter was his own son Otr, who took otter shape to fish the river. Hreidmar's two other sons, Fafnir and Regin, seized the gods and held them until their father was paid a blood-price: enough gold to cover the whole otter skin.

Since the stone was Loki's, the gods sent him to find the gold. He went to another waterfall, where the dwarf Andvari kept a great hoard in the pool beneath it. Andvari hid in the water in the shape of a fish, a pike in most tellings, but Loki caught him in a net borrowed from the sea goddess Ran and made him hand over all his treasure.

Andvari tried to keep back one small gold ring, but Loki saw it and took that too. Its name was Andvaranaut, which means "Andvari's gift". Losing it, Andvari laid a curse on it and on all the gold with it: the treasure would bring death to every man who owned it. The Poetic Edda poem Reginsmal keeps his curse, and centuries later Wagner and Tolkien both built cursed rings on its pattern.

Back at the farm, the gods stood the otter skin up and heaped the gold over it. Odin kept the ring hidden in his fist, but Hreidmar walked round the pile and spied a single whisker of the otter still poking through the gold, so he refused the payment until it was covered. To hide that last whisker Odin had to give up the ring, and so the curse passed to Hreidmar.

The curse soon struck. Fafnir stabbed his father Hreidmar to death in his sleep, drove his brother Regin away with nothing, and kept the whole hoard for himself. He hauled the treasure to Gnitaheid, a desolate heath, and as the years passed his greed for the gold changed him into a dragon, coiled on the hoard. Regin spent twenty years plotting revenge, and in the end he raised the boy Sigurd, who would kill the dragon with the sword Gram, take the cursed ring, and die of it in his turn.

angrbodas-children-fenrir-jormungandr-an.context_blurb:
In the Prose Edda, written in Iceland in the 1220s by Snorri Sturluson, the trickster god Loki has a secret family. With a giantess in Jotunheim, the giants' country, he fathers three monstrous children, and the gods fear them so much that Odin puts each one where it can do no harm. When the world ends, all three come back.

In Asgard Loki has a loyal wife, the goddess Sigyn, but in Jotunheim he keeps a lover, the giantess Angrboda, whose name in Old Norse means "she who brings grief". Her three children by Loki are a wolf called Fenrir, a serpent called Jormungandr, and a daughter named Hel.

Hel is terrible to look at. Snorri says one half of her is the colour of living flesh and the other half black as a corpse, so that life and death share one body. The gods brought the wolf up in Asgard itself, where Odin hoped they could keep him under control. But Fenrir grew so huge and savage that Tyr alone dared to walk up and feed him, and Tyr would later lose his hand when the gods tricked the wolf into chains.

Odin hurled the serpent into the ocean that rings the world of men, and there Jormungandr grew until he circled the whole earth and could bite his own tail. That is why he is called the Midgard Serpent, the World Serpent. Hel he cast down into Niflheim, the misty underworld, and made her ruler of the dead there, though not of all the dead. Warriors killed in battle go up to Valhalla. Hel takes in everyone who dies of illness or of old age.

Snorri describes her home like a grim joke. Her hall is Eljudnir, a name drawn from a word for being sprayed with damp; her dish is Hunger, her knife Famine, her bed Sick-Bed and her threshold Stumbling-Block. Even her servants are puns on slowness: the manservant Ganglati, the slow-mover, and the maid Ganglot, the slow-goer, because everything in Hel's hall creeps as slowly as death.

At Ragnarok, the last battle, all three children turn on the gods. Fenrir breaks loose and swallows Odin whole, and Odin's son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart. Jormungandr rises from the sea to meet Thor. Thor kills the serpent with Mjolnir, staggers nine steps away from the body, and falls dead of its venom. Nine, the number of the worlds on the world-tree and of Odin's nights hanging on it, runs all through Norse myth.

baldrs-death-mistletoe-hodr-and-the-gian.context_blurb:
Baldr is the best-loved of the Norse gods, and his death is the great tragedy of Norse myth, the first crack in the world on the road to Ragnarok. Snorri Sturluson tells it most fully in the Prose Edda, written in Iceland in the 1220s, and the Eddic poem Baldr's Dreams adds to it.

Baldr was the son of Odin and the goddess Frigg, so beautiful and kind that he seemed to glow, and every god in Asgard loved him. Then he began to have terrible dreams, and they were always about the same thing: his own death.

To save him, his mother Frigg went through all nine worlds and made everything swear never to harm him: fire and water, stones and earth, iron and all the metals, beasts and birds, trees, snakes and poisons, and even the sicknesses, so that no illness could take him either.

Loki could not bear it. He took the shape of an old woman, came to Frigg's fireside at Fensalir and got her talking, and Frigg let slip that one young plant, the mistletoe growing east of Valhalla, had seemed too young to need an oath. Loki cut the mistletoe, put it in the hand of Baldr's blind brother Hodr and guided his throw, and Baldr fell dead. The gods chose Hermod to ride down the dark roads to Hel and plead for Baldr's return, and Odin lent him his own eight-legged horse, Sleipnir.

Hel's price was tears: if the whole world wept for Baldr, he could go home. Everything wept but one, a giantess who gave her name as Thokk, an Old Norse word that means thanks, and Snorri says most people believed she was Loki in disguise. So Baldr stayed in Hel.

His body had already gone to the pyre aboard his ship Hringhorni, the greatest of all ships, so heavy that the gods could not shove it down the rollers; they sent for the giantess Hyrrokkin, who came on a wolf with live snakes for reins and launched it with one push that made sparks fly and the earth shake. His wife Nanna died of grief and burned beside him.

Yet the story does not end in darkness. Snorri says that after Ragnarok, when the earth comes up green again out of the sea, Baldr will return from Hel to rule it, and beside him will come Hodr, his blind brother, the two at peace at last.

beowulf-tears-off-grendels-arm.context_blurb:
Beowulf is the great Old English poem, written down in Anglo-Saxon England about a thousand years ago but set in the older heroic world of Scandinavia. Its hero is a young warrior of the Geats who sails to Denmark to save King Hrothgar's mead-hall, Heorot, from a monster that has haunted it for twelve years.

The monster was Grendel, a descendant of Cain, who hated the sound of harp-song in Heorot and came every night to devour Hrothgar's men. Beowulf and his fourteen Geat companions lay down in the hall to wait for him, and Beowulf shocked the watching Danes: he gave away his sword, took off his helmet and mail shirt, and lay down to meet Grendel with his bare hands and nothing else.

His reason was honour. Grendel fought without weapons, so Beowulf would take no advantage over him. At midnight Grendel came stalking out of the moors, and with one blow of his hand he tore the iron-banded door of Heorot clean off.

He seized the nearest sleeping Geat and ate him before anyone could rise; only when Beowulf is home again, reporting to King Hygelac, does the poem name that man: Hondscioh. Then Grendel reached for Beowulf, and Beowulf caught his arm and would not let go. They grappled on their feet in the blackness, and the fight was so violent that the mead-benches ripped loose from their iron pegs all around them.

At last Beowulf tore Grendel's arm off at the shoulder. The monster fled into the night, bleeding his life away, back over the moors to the cave he shared with his mother beneath a haunted mere, and there he died.

By daylight the hall was packed with Danes and Geats come to stare at the trophy: Beowulf had hoisted Grendel's whole shoulder, arm and clawed hand high up into the rafters of the hall, where everyone who came in could see it. The next night Grendel's mother came for revenge, and Beowulf had to follow her down into that same cave.

The poem itself nearly died. It survives in one single manuscript, and in 1731 a fire broke out at Ashburnham House in London, where the book was kept; the manuscript was rescued, but scorched, and every page still bears the burn at its edges. It is now in the British Library.

brynhild-in-the-ring-of-fire.context_blurb:
In the Norse Volsung saga, the young hero Sigurd has just slain Fafnir the dragon and Regin, the treacherous smith. Birds have told him of a road, and it leads him to the meeting on which the rest of his tragic story will turn.

The road climbed Hindarfjall, Hind Mountain, and from far off Sigurd could see its crown ringed by a blaze so high that no bird could fly through it. He rode straight at the flames on Grani, the horse Odin himself had chosen for him from a herd of stallions, a descendant of Odin's own eight-legged steed, and Grani leapt the fire without flinching.

Inside the ring stood a hall, and in it lay a figure in full armour, helmet on and sword at its side. Sigurd unlaced the helmet expecting a dead warrior's face and found a woman, asleep. Neither touch nor voice could wake her, so Sigurd took his sword Gram and slit her mail-coat open as easily as cloth. She opened her eyes, asked who had cut her byrnie and woken her from her long sleep, and named herself Brynhild, a Valkyrie.

Brynhild told Sigurd why she slept there. Odin had promised victory in a battle to an old king, Hjalmgunnar, but Brynhild defied him and gave the day to a young king, Agnar, so Odin punished her with an enchanted sleep on the mountain.

Centuries later Richard Wagner made this scene the climax of the third opera of his Ring cycle, staged in 1876, with the hero renamed Siegfried and the Valkyrie renamed Brunnhilde.

The Eddic poem of their meeting stops in mid-sentence, because in the Codex Regius, the one manuscript that holds it, an entire gathering of pages has been lost. Scholars call the gap the great lacuna, and what happens next has to be rebuilt from the prose Volsung saga.

brynhilds-revenge-guttorm-kills-sigurd-i.context_blurb:
In the Norse Volsung saga, the hero Sigurd married Gudrun, daughter of King Gjuki, while her brother Gunnar married Brynhild. Brynhild believed Gunnar had ridden through the ring of fire to win her; in fact Sigurd had done it, wearing Gunnar's face. The secret came out one morning at a river, and from there the saga runs to blood and fire.

The two queens were washing their hair in the river and fell to quarrelling over which of their husbands was the greater man. Brynhild bragged that no one but Gunnar had dared the fire. Gudrun laughed, told her the truth, and held up the proof: a ring, Andvaranaut, that Sigurd had taken from Brynhild's finger that night and given to his wife.

Brynhild went home, took to her bed, and for three days would not speak a word, and her silence frightened the whole household more than any shouting. When Gunnar came to ask what was wrong, she gave him a choice: Sigurd had betrayed them both, and she wanted Sigurd dead, or she would die herself.

Gunnar and his brother Hogni could not do it themselves. Years before, at Gjuki's hall, they and Sigurd had mingled their blood in the earth and sworn blood-brotherhood, and that oath forbade them to raise a hand against him.

So they turned to their youngest brother, Guttorm, who had sworn no oath to Sigurd. He was only a boy, with no stomach for killing the mightiest warrior alive, so his brothers cooked him a stew of wolf and serpent flesh with beer to make him savage. That night Guttorm crept into the bedroom where Sigurd slept beside Gudrun and drove a sword through his chest. Sigurd woke to the death-blow, snatched up his own sword, Gram, the blade that had killed Fafnir, and hurled it after the fleeing killer.

Gram caught Guttorm between the shoulders and cut him clean in two, so that one half fell forward out of the room and the other fell back inside it.

That evening Brynhild did not weep. She laughed once aloud, dressed in her finest clothes and drove a sword into her own breast. As she died she asked to be burned on Sigurd's own pyre, with Gram laid bare between their bodies as it had lain between them on the night he came to her in Gunnar's shape.

Wagner ended his Ring cycle with this story. Gotterdammerung, the Twilight of the Gods, the fourth and last of its operas, first staged in 1876, closes with the hero's murder and the queen's fire.

draupnir-odins-ring-that-drips-eight-mor.context_blurb:
Odin, chief of the Norse gods, wore a gold arm-ring of dwarf-work, one of the great named treasures of Norse myth. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda tells where it came from and what it did, and the ring turns up again at a funeral and a courtship.

Its name was Draupnir, the dripper, because new gold rings kept falling from it like drops of water from a wet blade. Snorri gives the exact schedule: every ninth night, eight new rings of equal weight dropped from it. Nine runs all through Norse myth, from the nine worlds to Odin's nine nights on the world-tree.

The dwarf brothers Sindri and Brokkr made it after Loki bet his own head on a contest of smithcraft. Loki lost and wriggled out on a technicality, saying the dwarves could take his head but not his neck, so Brokkr stitched Loki's lips together instead.

When Baldr, Odin's beloved son, lay dead on his funeral ship, Odin laid Draupnir on the pyre beside him, his last gift to his son.

The ring appears again in the Eddic poem Skirnismal. The god Freyr fell in love with Gerd, a giantess of Jotunheim, and dispatched Skirnir, his servant, to win her with eleven golden apples and Draupnir itself; she scorned the gold and yielded only to the threat of a curse.

fimbulwinter-three-winters-with-no-summe.context_blurb:
Norse myth tells how its world began, and it tells just as plainly how that world will end. The poem Voluspa, "The Seeress's Prophecy," and the Prose Edda of the Icelander Snorri Sturluson lay out the last days step by step: a killing winter, kin turning on kin, wolves in the sky, roosters crowing, a horn blast, and a final battle.

That end is called Ragnarok, the doom of the gods, when nearly every god of the Aesir falls in one last battle, the sky splits apart and the sea swallows the earth. Snorri says it begins with a warning: a monstrous winter called Fimbulvetr, the Great Winter, when snow drives in from every side. The name joins fimbul, "mighty," to vetr, "winter."

Frost bites hard and the sun gives no warmth. Three winters follow one another with no summer in between, and with no growing season there is no food. People turn on their own families. In the Voluspa's grim chain of names for that time, it is a wolf-age, an age of axes and swords and storm winds, when brothers kill brothers.

Then an old chase in the sky comes to its end. Since the world began, Snorri says, a wolf named Skoll, whose name means "treachery," has run behind the sun, while a second wolf hunts the moon. At the end of days the wolf catches the sun at last and swallows it, and the stars go out.

Roosters crow in three worlds at once: one in the land of the giants, a dark one down in Hel, and golden-combed Gullinkambi among the gods, waking Odin's chosen warriors in Valhalla. At that call Heimdallr, the watchman of the rainbow bridge Bifrost, lifts the Gjallarhorn and sounds the blast that calls every god to the last battle.

Yet not everything dies. Odin once went to test the wise giant Vafthrudnir, in the poem Vafthrudnismal, and asked him who would live through the Great Winter. The giant answers that a man and a woman, Lif and Lifthrasir, whose names mean "Life" and "Life-yearner," will hide in the wood called Hoddmimir's holt and walk out afterwards to people the new world.

freyja-cats-falcon-cloak-and-the-brising.context_blurb:
Freyja is the Norse goddess of love, beauty and gold, the most splendid of the goddesses in Asgard. She was not born among Odin's Aesir. She belonged to the Vanir, an older family of gods, and when the two tribes ended their war by swapping hostages, the Vanir sent Freyja, Freyr her brother, and their father Njord, the god of the sea and its riches.

Snorri says two great cats draw Freyja's chariot, a team no other god drives; Thor's chariot runs on goats. The poem Grimnismal gives her a share of the dead as well. Of the warriors who fall bravely, Odin takes only half; Freyja chooses the rest for her own home, Folkvangr, whose name means "People-Field."

Her greatest treasure is Brisingamen, the necklace of the Brisings, praised as the loveliest jewel in all the worlds. Four dwarves forged it deep under the earth, and the Icelandic tale called Sorla thattr names them: Alfrigg, Dvalin, Berling and Grerr. Each of the four set his own price before Freyja could have it.

She also owns a cloak of falcon feathers, the valshamr, which lets anyone who wears it fly. Loki borrowed it to fly into Jotunheim and rescue the goddess Idunn from the giant Thjazi, and again to find where the giant Thrym had hidden Thor's hammer.

Freyja married a god named Odr, who wandered off across the worlds and never came home. She searched for him under many names and wept for him, and her tears were tears of red gold, so the old skalds, the Viking poets, made "Freyja's tears" a kenning, a riddling name, for gold.

Loki once stole Brisingamen. In the Sorla thattr he became a fly and crept through the keyhole into her locked room, then became a flea and bit her until she turned in her sleep, and he unclasped the necklace from her neck. Snorri, quoting an older poem, tells how the necklace came home: Heimdall, watchman of the gods, tracked Loki down, and the two fought in the shape of seals at a sea rock called Singasteinn until Heimdall won Brisingamen back for Freyja.

Freyja bore Odr two daughters, Hnoss and Gersemi, and both names mean treasure, as if even her children were jewels to a grieving mother.

freyr-the-sword-he-traded-for-love.context_blurb:
Freyr is the Norse god of sun and rain and plentiful harvests, the giver of peace and plenty. Like his sister Freyja he came from the Vanir, the older tribe of gods, but he lived among the Aesir. His great tale is a love story with a hard price: to win a giantess, he gave away the sword that could have saved him at the end of the world.

When Freyr cut his first tooth as a baby, the gods gave him a whole world as a tooth-gift: Alfheim, "Elf-Home," the bright realm of the light elves.

One day Freyr climbed into Hlidskjalf, Odin's high seat, where only Odin and his wife Frigg were meant to sit, because from it a watcher could look into every world at once. Far away in Jotunheim he saw Gerdr, the daughter of the giant Gymir, lift her bare arm to open a door, and the arm shone so brightly that sea and sky lit up with its glow. Freyr came home lovesick, unable to eat, sleep or speak, and the worried gods sent his own servant Skirnir, whose name means "the Shining One," to find out what was wrong. Freyr told him, and sent Skirnir to win Gerdr for him. As his reward Skirnir took Freyr's sword, a blade that could fight on its own.

Skirnir rode into Jotunheim. First he tried treasure: golden apples, and then Draupnir, the dwarf-made ring of Odin that drips eight more rings like itself every ninth night. Gerdr turned both down, saying she had gold enough, and the threat of his sword did not move her either. So Skirnir cursed her: she would pine for ever, mocked by gods and men, and the only husband she would ever have would be a three-headed frost-giant she loathed.

The curse worked where gifts had failed. Gerdr agreed to meet Freyr after nine nights in Barri, a quiet grove far from the giants' halls, and there she became his bride.

But the price was still to be paid. At Ragnarok, Surt, lord of the fire-giants, will come from the blazing south with a sword that outshines the sun, and Freyr will meet him without a blade. Snorri says Freyr falls there for lack of the sword he gave away for love.

gleipnir-and-tyrs-hand-the-six-impossibl.context_blurb:
In Norse myth the trickster Loki fathered three monsters on the giantess Angrboda: Hel, who would rule the dead; a serpent that would grow long enough to circle the world; and Fenrir, a wolf. The gods feared the wolf most of all, and the story of how they chained him, told by Snorri Sturluson in the Prose Edda, cost one of them his hand.

The Aesir kept the wolf cub in Asgard, but he grew bigger and hungrier every day, and only Tyr, the god of war, had the courage to go near and hand him his meat.

The gods decided to bind him before he grew too strong. They forged a heavy iron fetter called Leyding and coaxed him to try it, as a test of strength, and Fenrir broke it with his first kick. Then they made a second, much stronger fetter, Dromi, and Fenrir strained and burst it so hard that its pieces flew far across the plain.

So Odin sent a messenger down to Svartalfheim, the dark world of the dwarves, to order a fetter no wolf could break. The dwarves sent back Gleipnir, a band as soft and slender as a silken ribbon, yet stronger than any chain. They made it from six things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. Snorri jokes that this is why cats walk silently and women have no beards: the dwarves used those things up.

The gods rowed Fenrir out to Lyngvi, an island in the black lake Amsvartnir, and dared him to test the ribbon. Fenrir smelled a trick. He would let them bind him only if one of the gods laid a hand in his jaws as a pledge of good faith, and only Tyr would do it. Once bound, the wolf found he could not break free, and he bit off Tyr's hand.

The gods made sure of him. They threaded the cord of Gleipnir through a great stone slab, Gjoll, drove it deep into the earth and pinned it down beneath a still bigger boulder. Then they thrust a sword into his mouth, its hilt against his lower jaw and its point in the roof of his mouth, to prop his jaws open. His slaver runs off the blade as a river until Ragnarok, when he will break loose and swallow Odin.

gram-in-the-barnstokk-the-sword-only-sig.context_blurb:
The Volsunga Saga is the Icelandic tale of the Volsungs, a family of heroes descended from Odin. It opens with a sword in a tree. A living oak named Barnstokk grew at the centre of King Volsung's hall, and its boughs reached up past the rafters.

On the night of a wedding feast, a tall old wanderer with one eye and a broad hood, Odin in disguise, strode into the hall and thrust a sword into the living trunk of Barnstokk, burying it up to the hilt. The bride was Volsung's own daughter Signy, Sigmund's sister, married that night against her will to King Siggeir; her later revenge on Siggeir makes her one of the saga's grimmest women.

The stranger told the hall that whoever pulled the sword out could keep it as a gift and would never hold a finer sword in his hand. Then he was gone. Every warrior there tugged at the hilt, and only Volsung's son Sigmund, one of the youngest men in the hall, drew it out. Its broken pieces would one day be forged again into Gram, the sword of Sigurd.

The tree's name carries its meaning. In Old Norse barn means child, as it still does in Swedish, Norwegian and Danish, and stokk means trunk, so Barnstokk is the "child-trunk," the family tree of the Volsung line standing in the heart of their hall.

grendels-mother-in-the-mere-the-giant-sw.context_blurb:
Beowulf is the great Old English poem about a hero from across the sea who comes to save the Danish king Hrothgar from a monster. Its hero has just torn the arm off the monster Grendel and hung it high in the mead hall Heorot. The celebration does not last: a second horror is coming, and Beowulf will have to follow it to the bottom of a haunted lake.

That night another monster raided the hall for revenge: Grendel's mother. The poem never gives her a name. She carried off Aeschere, the old warrior King Hrothgar trusted most, and she took back Grendel's arm from the rafters where the Danes had hung it.

Hrothgar told Beowulf where the monsters lived: a dark mere in the moors so cursed that a stag hunted by hounds would turn back on the bank and let the hounds take it rather than plunge into that water.

Beowulf was not a Dane. He was a Geat, a prince of the people who lived in what is now southern Sweden and nephew of their king Hygelac; he had crossed the sea because Hrothgar once did his father a kindness, and he would sail home to the Geats when the work was done.

Before the dive, a Dane named Unferth, the same warrior who had mocked Beowulf at the mead bench over a swimming match with his friend Breca, lent him a sword as a peace offering. The sword was Hrunting, an heirloom that had never once failed any warrior who carried it.

Beowulf put on his mail and helmet and leapt into the black water. The poem says he swam down for most of a day before he reached the bottom, a dive no man in armour could survive, which tells the listener this is no ordinary lake.

Grendel's mother seized him and dragged him into her hall, a dry, roofed chamber under the water, lit by an eerie fire. Beowulf swung Hrunting at her head, but the famous blade would not bite; it rang off her without cutting, and he threw it aside. Then he saw, hanging on the wall, an enormous sword made by giants in the days before the Flood, too heavy for any ordinary warrior. Beowulf seized it in both hands and struck off her head with a single blow.

Nearby lay Grendel's body, dead from the wound of the night before, and Beowulf cut off its head to carry home as a trophy. As he stood over the two corpses, the giant blade began to melt in the monsters' hot blood like an icicle in a thaw, until only the hilt was left in his hand.

He swam up to daylight with the hilt and the head. Grendel's head was so huge that four of his men had to haul it to the hall on a spear shaft. Beowulf laid the old hilt in Hrothgar's hands.

grimhilds-potion-and-the-ride-through-th.context_blurb:
The later chapters of the Volsunga Saga follow Sigurd, the young hero who killed the dragon Fafnir, to the court of King Gjuki on the Rhine. There a love story turns into a murder story, and almost every turn of it is the work of one woman with a cup.

She was Grimhild, Gjuki's queen, a sorceress far more dangerous than her husband, skilled in spells and in charmed drinks. Grimhild wanted the finest hero alive tied to her house, and she meant to do it through her only daughter, Gudrun. But Sigurd had already pledged himself to Brynhild, the valkyrie he had found asleep inside a ring of fire.

So at the welcome feast Grimhild handed Sigurd a cup of mead with a drug in it, a potion of forgetting. It was aimed precisely: it wiped Brynhild the valkyrie out of his memory, her ring of fire, his oath, everything about her.

With no memory of Brynhild, Sigurd married Gudrun, and at the feast he swore blood-brotherhood with her brothers Gunnar and Hogni, mixing their blood together, the strongest bond a Norseman knew outside his own kin.

Now Grimhild wanted Brynhild for her son Gunnar. Brynhild would marry only the man who rode through the flames around her hall. Gunnar's own horse shied from the fire, so he borrowed Grani, Sigurd's horse of Odin's breed, but under Gunnar Grani stood stock-still and would not take a single step.

So Grimhild's spell went to work: Sigurd and Gunnar exchanged faces, and Sigurd, looking like Gunnar, rode Grani through the fire and won Brynhild for his blood-brother. Before he left her, Sigurd took a ring from her hand, Andvaranaut, the cursed gold ring from Fafnir's hoard that he had once given her, and slipped another ring in its place; then he and Gunnar changed back.

Then the trap closed. When Brynhild learned how she had been tricked, she demanded Sigurd's death. Gunnar and Hogni were bound by their oath and could not strike him themselves, so Grimhild fed her youngest son, Guttorm, on the meat of wolves and snakes until he was mad enough to kill, and Guttorm stabbed Sigurd as he lay in bed.

gullinbursti-the-golden-boar-that-lights.context_blurb:
Freyr, the Norse god of sunshine and harvest, did not ride a horse. His mount was a boar of gold made by dwarf smiths, and so bright that it lit its own way through the darkest night. Snorri Sturluson tells its story in the Prose Edda.

A boar drew Freyr's chariot, one that dwarf smiths had forged from solid gold; in the Viking age boars were sacred to Freyr, and warriors wore boar crests on their helmets. Freyr was not one of Odin's Aesir. He came from the Vanir, the gods of plenty and the sea, who sent him to Asgard with his twin sister Freyja and their father Njord as hostages when the first war of the gods ended.

The boar was born of a bet. Loki had wagered two dwarf brothers, Sindri and Brokkr, that they could not match the treasures of other smiths. Sindri hammered at the forge while Brokkr kept the bellows going, and though Loki, in the shape of a fly, bit Brokkr's hand, the dwarf never stopped pumping, and the golden boar came out of the fire.

Its famous name is Gullinbursti, "Gold-Bristle," but Snorri gives it a second name too, Slidrugtanni, "cutting-tusk," in honour of its dangerous tusks.

Snorri says the boar could run through the air and over the sea faster than any horse. And no night was ever so dark that its glowing bristles did not light the road ahead.

gungnir-odins-spear-that-never-misses.context_blurb:
Odin, the one-eyed ruler of the Norse gods and lord of the slain warriors in Valhalla, carried a spear into every battle, and it will be in his hand when he rides out for the last time at Ragnarok. Viking-age carvings of Odin almost always show him holding it. Its name was Gungnir, and Snorri Sturluson, the poems of the Edda and the Icelandic sagas all tell what it could do.

Odin belonged to the Aesir, the warrior gods of Asgard, along with Thor and Baldr; Freyr and Freyja came from the other family of gods, the Vanir.

Like every great treasure of the gods, the spear had its own name: Gungnir, which may mean "the swaying one" or "the trembler." The Sons of Ivaldi forged it, the dwarf brothers who also spun golden hair for Sif, Thor's wife, after Loki cut off all her hair while she slept.

Snorri's most quoted line about it is that Gungnir never stopped in its thrust: once thrown, no shield or wall could halt it.

The spear began the first war of all. The Voluspa says that when the Aesir and the Vanir went to war, Odin opened it by flinging his spear over the army of the Vanir, a challenge that dedicated every one of them to him. Viking-age warriors copied the gesture. The Icelandic sagas tell of captains hurling a spear above the heads of the foe at the start of a fight, so that every warrior beyond the spear's flight belonged to Odin, a sacrifice promised to him before a single blow fell. Eyrbyggja saga and the tale of Styrbjorn both describe it: the enemy were given to Odin before the fighting began.

In the poem Sigrdrifumal, the valkyrie Sigrdrifa teaches the hero Sigurd where runes of power are carved, and one place she names is the point of Gungnir. Her list also includes the teeth of Sleipnir, the paws of a bear and the tongue of Bragi, the god of poetry.

Later retellings add one more belief: that an oath sworn on Gungnir's point was the most binding vow in the Norse world, used even by the gods, and that breaking it brought doom for life. That belief comes from later tellings rather than from the Eddas themselves.

Even Gungnir could not save its master. At Ragnarok Odin rides out at the head of his chosen warriors, and the wolf Fenrir swallows him whole; his son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart.

heimdallr-blows-the-gjallarhorn.context_blurb:
In Norse myth a shining god keeps watch where the world of humans meets the home of the gods. He has one task, to see danger coming, and one great moment, when he lifts his horn and calls every god to the last battle. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda and the old poems tell what he is and what happens when the horn sounds.

He is Heimdallr, the watchman of the Aesir, who stands guard where a rainbow bridge reaches up to Asgard so that no giant can cross unseen. The bridge is Bifrost, a burning arch of three colours running from Midgard to the walls of Asgard; the gods may ride over it, but a giant who tried it would be burned.

Snorri gives Heimdallr the keenest senses in all the worlds. Sleep matters to him less than to a bird, he sees a hundred leagues by night or day, and his ears are so sharp that he can hear the wool growing on a sheep's back and the grass growing on the earth.

When the horn sounds at Ragnarok, the gods gather in council, but Odin rides off alone one last time to the well under a root of the world-tree, to ask counsel of the severed head of the wise Mimir.

Heimdallr had walked among humans long before. In the poem Rigsthula he travels Midgard under the name Rig, spending three nights in each of three houses, and from those visits come the ancestors of the three ranks of Norse society: the thrall, the farmer and the jarl.

Bifrost itself does not survive the end. When the muster begins, the fire-giant Surtr rides up out of Muspelheim with a flaming sword, and the bridge breaks apart beneath him as he crosses.

heimdallr-gjallarhorn-and-grass-growing.context_blurb:
In Norse myth a rainbow bridge joins the land of men to the gods' home above, and one god stands guard at its upper end. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda calls him the white god and fills a whole chapter with his wonders: a strange birth, impossible senses, a horn hidden under the world-tree, and a last fight with his oldest enemy.

The bridge is Bifrost, the shimmering road from Midgard up to Asgard, and the watchman lets no giant across it. Its name may mean "shimmering way" or "trembling road," and Snorri says it glows with fire. He is Heimdallr, one of Odin's sons, whom Snorri calls the white god; he has teeth of gold, and so he is also called Gullintanni, "Gold-Tooth."

His birth was like no other god's. Snorri, quoting a lost poem, says Heimdallr was born of nine mothers, all of them sisters, out where the land ends at the sea.

His senses are beyond belief. Snorri says Heimdallr can hear the wool growing on a sheep's back and the grass sprouting from the earth, and every louder sound besides. Next Snorri praises his eyes: they reach a hundred leagues, as sharp in darkness as in daylight, and he needs less sleep than a bird. His hall stands at the top of Bifrost, at the point where travellers from Midgard reach the gods' country, and its name, Himinbjorg, means "Sky-Cliff." His horse is called Gulltoppr, "Golden-Top."

He keeps a great horn, Gjallarhorn, "the resounding horn," which he will blow just one time before the world ends; Snorri says it lies hidden under a root of Yggdrasil, next to the well where Mimir keeps his wisdom. When Ragnarok comes and the giants march on Asgard, Heimdallr will blow it, and its blast will be heard in all nine worlds. At that call the gods and all the chosen warriors of Valhalla will arm themselves and march out to the field to meet the end. No one bars the gates or kneels to swear new oaths. They go out to fight, knowing what is coming.

Heimdallr's own enemy is Loki, and at Ragnarok the two meet on the field and each kills the other. Their feud was old. In a story Snorri took from an older poem, the Husdrapa, Loki stole Brisingamen, the necklace of the goddess Freyja, and Heimdallr fought him for it in the shape of a seal out on a sea-rock, and won it back.

Heimdallr also walked among humans. In the poem Rigsthula he travels the earth under the name Rigr, staying with a couple in each of three homes, and from those visits are born the ancestors of the thralls, the farmers and the nobles.

heorot-the-hall-where-grendel-comes-at-n.context_blurb:
Beowulf is the greatest poem to survive in Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons, copied down in England about a thousand years ago. Its hero is a young warrior who crosses the sea to free a king's hall from a monster and dies, as an old king himself, fighting a dragon. The poem runs to 3,182 lines of alliterative verse and takes its name from that hero.

The story begins in the Danish court of Hrothgar, king of the Scyldings, who raised a mead hall grander than any other in the northern lands and showered his men with gold rings at his feasts. He set a great pair of stag's antlers on its gables and named it Heorot, "the hart."

For a time Heorot rang with feasting and song. Then, by night, a monster called Grendel crept from the fens, burst into the hall and carried off sleeping men to eat, and the Danes were powerless against him. The Christian poet gave the monster a family tree out of Genesis: Grendel was descended from Cain, the first murderer, whose crime against his brother Abel brought a curse on his line.

The Danes did not lack courage. The poet explains more than once that no blade could bite Grendel, for he had laid a spell on the edges of all weapons, and so for twelve years he raided the hall unbeaten.

Word of the Danish king's sorrow reached Hygelac, king of the Geats, a people of what is now southern Sweden, and Beowulf, a young Geat of Hygelac's court, resolved to sail south and face the monster. He chose the toughest fighters he could find, fourteen of them, and sailed with them to Denmark, fifteen men in all.

That evening Beowulf boasted before the court that since Grendel carried no sword, he would carry none either: he would meet the monster with his bare hands alone. Grendel came in the dark, tore the door open and devoured one of the sleeping Geats. Then he reached for Beowulf, who was only pretending to sleep, and felt a grip unlike any he had ever known. They wrestled until the hall shook, and when Grendel tried to tear free, Beowulf ripped the monster's arm out at the shoulder. Grendel fled to the fens to die, and the arm was hung up in Heorot as a trophy.

The poem survives in one manuscript only, known today as Cotton Vitellius A.xv. Scholars also call it the Nowell Codex. In 1731 fire swept through Ashburnham House in London, where it was kept, and singed its edges, but the book survived.

Heorot itself may have been real. Danish tradition, from the medieval chronicler Saxo Grammaticus onward, places the hall at Lejre, a village on Zealand, the large Danish island, and there archaeologists have dug up the foundations of huge long-halls from the Viking age and earlier.

hrungnir-the-whetstone-in-thors-forehead.context_blurb:
Thor, the Norse thunder god, fought many giants, but his hardest duel was against a giant made of stone. Snorri Sturluson tells the story in Skaldskaparmal, his handbook for poets: a horse race, a drunken boast, a clay monster with a coward's heart, and a piece of stone that stayed in Thor's head for ever.

The giant was Hrungnir, the strongest of his kind, whose heart, head and shield were all of stone. He was proudest of his horse, Gullfaxi, "Golden-Mane," and he raced it against Odin's eight-legged Sleipnir with each rider staking his own head on the result.

The race carried Hrungnir all the way into Asgard, and the gods offered him a drink. Drunk on Odin's mead, he boasted that he would kill every god, carry Valhalla off to Jotunheim, and take home the two loveliest goddesses, Freyja and Sif, Thor's own wife. That brought Thor home in a fury.

Because Hrungnir was Odin's guest, Thor could not simply kill him; instead he challenged the giant to a duel on giant ground. The terrified giants built Hrungnir a companion out of clay, nine leagues tall and three wide, and called him Mokkurkalfi. The only heart big enough for him was a mare's, and it was timid. When Thor came into view, the clay giant shook with terror and wet himself where he stood. Thor's servant Thialfi brought him down with ease.

Thialfi had already played a trick. He ran ahead and shouted to Hrungnir that Thor would attack from beneath the earth, so the giant laid his stone shield on the ground and stood on it, leaving himself open when Thor came at him through the sky. Thor won the duel, but he went home with a shard of Hrungnir's whetstone stuck fast in his forehead.

A wise-woman, the seeress Groa, came to sing charms over him, and as she chanted, the shard began to loosen. To reward her, Thor told her good news: he had rescued her long-lost husband Aurvandil, hauling him over the freezing river Elivagar in a basket on his back, and when one of Aurvandil's toes froze off, Thor had flung it into the heavens, where it shines as a star. Groa was so overjoyed that she forgot the rest of her charm, and the whetstone stayed in Thor's head.

huginn-and-muninn-thought-and-memory.context_blurb:
Odin, the one-eyed king of the Norse gods, rules from Asgard, yet no god can watch every corner of the world himself. So Odin keeps helpers who bring him news of everything, and their names tell what they carry. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda and the old poem Grimnismal describe them.

Every dawn Odin sends out two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, "Thought" and "Memory," to fly over all the earth, and they come back at breakfast to tell him what they have seen. Snorri says they set out from Odin's own shoulders, and that is how he knows so much of what happens in the world.

At his feet in Valhalla lie two wolves, Geri and Freki, whose names mean "Greedy" and "Ravenous." The poem Grimnismal says the wolves eat all the meat set before Odin, while he himself lives on wine alone. The pairs balance each other: birds for what Odin knows, wolves for what he feeds.

The ravens are older than the written myths. On helmet plates of the sixth to eighth centuries, dug up at Vendel and Torslunda in Sweden, a warrior with a spear rides with a bird on each side of him, centuries before Snorri Sturluson wrote the stories down.
