ignatius-loyola-the-cannonball-at-pamplo.context_blurb:
Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuits, one of the most famous religious orders of the Catholic Church. He began as a vain young soldier with his head full of knightly romances, and a single shot on a battlefield turned his life around. He told the story himself, near the end of his life, in an autobiography he dictated.

He was born Inigo in 1491 in the castle of Loyola in the hills of Gipuzkoa, the youngest of thirteen children, and he came of the Basques, the old people of Spain's mountainous north. He grew up as a page at court and then a soldier.

On 20 May 1521 he was one of the defenders of Pamplona's fortress when the French attacked, and he refused to surrender. A French cannonball tore between his legs and shattered his right leg. The French, admiring his courage, had him carried home to Loyola.

The leg healed badly, and a lump of bone jutted out below the knee. Ignatius, still proud of his courtier's looks, could not bear the thought of that deformity showing through the tight hose of a gentleman, so he had the leg broken and reset and the bone cut away, with nothing to dull the pain. It nearly killed him, and he limped for the rest of his life.

Through the long months in bed he begged for romances of knights and ladies, but the household had nothing of that kind; instead his brother's wife fetched him Ludolph of Saxony's Life of Christ and the Flower of the Saints, a collection of saints' lives. He noticed that daydreams of knightly love left him restless, while dreams of copying the saints left him at peace.

In March 1522 the changed man climbed to the Benedictine shrine of Montserrat in Catalonia. There he kept watch all night, like a knight before his knighting but in reverse, and left his sword and dagger hanging before the altar, the weapons of his old life laid down for good. He gave his fine clothes to a beggar and dressed in sackcloth.

Years later Ignatius was studying in Paris, an older man among young students, and he gathered friends there, Francis Xavier and Peter Faber among them. In 1534 he and six of them met in a little chapel on Montmartre and bound themselves by vow to poverty, to chastity and to obey the pope, and that vow is counted as the birth of the Jesuits. The pope approved the order in 1540, and Ignatius became its first leader.

joan-of-arc-domremy-the-voices-and-the-s.context_blurb:
Joan of Arc was a French farm girl who, during the Hundred Years' War between England and France, said that heavenly voices had sent her to save her country. At seventeen she led an army, and her story begins in a small village on the border of Lorraine.

At about thirteen, in her father's garden at Domremy, she began to hear voices. One said he was the archangel Michael, and the other two were the early martyrs Catherine of Alexandria and Margaret of Antioch. Year after year they urged her to go to the Dauphin Charles, drive out the English and see him crowned at Reims.

As a child she had danced with the other village children around a huge ancient beech just outside Domremy, which the villagers called the Fairy Tree, l'Arbre des Fees, and hung garlands on it on feast days. Her enemies would later try to make that harmless custom look like witchcraft.

In 1429 she walked to Vaucouleurs, the closest town held for the French king, and asked its captain, Robert de Baudricourt, for an escort to the Dauphin; he turned her down twice and gave way only on her third visit. For the eleven-day ride across country held by the English and the Burgundians, she had her hair cropped short and put on men's clothes, practical for the journey but a charge against her at her trial.

At Chinon, Charles tested her. He hid among his courtiers in plain clothes and put another man in royal robes on the throne, but Joan walked straight past the pretender and knelt before the real Dauphin.

She rode to relieve the siege of Orleans in white armour with a tall white banner, sprinkled with lilies, showing two angels holding the world, with the names Jhesus Maria across the top. She said she loved it forty times more than her sword. On 7 May 1429 she led the attack on Les Tourelles, the English fort guarding the bridge, and a crossbow bolt struck her between neck and shoulder, just above her breastplate. She pulled it out, went back to the fight that evening, and the fort fell; the next day the English abandoned the siege.

joan-of-arc-the-trial-the-flames-and-hol.context_blurb:
Joan of Arc, the peasant girl who led French armies and saw her king crowned at Reims, was captured within a year of her triumph. Her trial at Rouen and her death by fire were written down in detail, and twenty-five years later witnesses told the rest of the story at a second trial that overturned the first.

In May 1430, during the siege of Compiegne, she led a sortie against the enemy lines outside the walls. The drawbridge was raised behind her too soon, and the Burgundians, French lords allied with England, dragged her from her horse and took her prisoner. Held at the castle of Beaurevoir, she leapt from a tower window some sixty feet up, hoping to escape, and survived.

The Burgundians sold her to the English, who handed her over for trial at Rouen. The judge was Pierre Cauchon, bishop of Beauvais, a Frenchman loyal to England who hoped his verdict would make him archbishop of Rouen.

The judges set traps. Asked if she was sure she stood in God's grace, a question where yes would sound proud and no would confess sin, the unlettered nineteen-year-old answered that if she was not in grace, she prayed God would put her there, and if she was, that God would keep her so.

On 24 May 1431, at the cemetery of Saint-Ouen, she was shown the stake prepared for her, and she broke down and signed a paper giving up men's clothes and submitting to the Church. She could not write, so she signed it with a mark. Within days she was back in men's dress, and Cauchon declared her relapsed.

On 30 May she was carted to the Old Market square of Rouen, where a high stake had been built so the crowd could watch. The words set up above her named her crimes: heretic, relapsed, apostate, idolater.

Weeping, she asked for a cross. An English soldier tied two sticks together and handed them to her, and the Dominican friar Isambard de la Pierre fetched the tall processional cross from Saint-Sauveur, the church close by, and held it up before her eyes through the flames.

When the fire died, the executioner, Geoffroy Therage, had orders to collect everything that was left of her and throw it into the Seine, so that no one could keep a relic. He said afterwards that he feared he was damned for burning a saint. In 1456 a new trial overturned her sentence, and in 1920 the Catholic Church declared her a saint.

john-hus-at-constance-in-a-hundred-years.context_blurb:
Jan Hus was a Czech priest who demanded reform of the Church a century before Luther, attacking the sale of indulgences. Summoned to the Council of Constance in 1414 under a safe-conduct from the emperor, he found the promise of safe passage worthless: the council condemned him as a heretic, and he was burned on 6 July 1415. Later reformers honoured him as their forerunner.

Around 1400, Hus filled the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague with some three thousand townsfolk by preaching in plain Czech, the speech of the streets, while nearly every other preacher in Europe gave his sermons in Latin. The chapel had been founded in 1391 on the rule that all its preaching be done in Czech.

Before the burning, the churchmen at Constance stripped him of his priesthood: they clipped away his tonsure, pulled off his priestly vestments and crowned him with a tall paper cap covered in painted devils. Hus looked at it and said that Jesus had worn a far heavier and more painful crown of thorns for his sake.

john-of-the-cross-the-dark-night-of-the-.context_blurb:
John of the Cross was a tiny Spanish friar, barely five feet tall, who became one of the greatest poets of Spain. Together with a famous nun he founded a stricter branch of the Carmelite order, and his own brothers in religion imprisoned him for it, in a cell where he wrote his most famous poetry.

In 1567, at Medina del Campo, the young friar had made up his mind to leave the Carmelites for the stricter, silent Carthusians. Teresa of Avila, a fifty-two-year-old nun already reforming her convents across Spain, met him and talked him into staying to reform the friars with her instead.

Taking the name John of the Cross, he opened the first reformed house for men in November 1568, in a broken-down farmhouse at Duruelo, a tiny village in Castile, where the friars slept on straw.

His reform made enemies among the friars who kept the older rule. One December night in 1577 they seized him at Avila and carried him off to their monastery at Toledo, where they shut him in a windowless cell barely six feet wide. His diet was bread and water with a few bits of salted fish, and they flogged him before the community, and they held him there for nine months. In that cell he composed poems in his head, among them the Spiritual Canticle, and his Dark Night of the Soul grew out of the same ordeal.

One night in August 1578, after weeks of working the hinges of his door loose, he escaped. He tore his blankets into strips, knotted them into a rope with an old tunic at the end, and let himself down from a high window, dropping the last stretch onto a wall when the rope ran short.

julian-of-norwich-all-shall-be-well.context_blurb:
Julian of Norwich was an English holy woman of the late 1300s who lived walled up in a small cell as an anchoress, praying and giving advice through a window. She wrote down a set of visions she had during an illness, and her book holds the most famous line of comfort in English religious writing.

In May 1373, when she was about thirty, a mysterious sickness brought her close to death in Norwich, a large port city on England's east coast. A priest held a crucifix before her failing eyes, and the visions began.

Between about four and nine that morning she received sixteen visions, which she called shewings, of Christ's suffering on the cross and of other things. In one, she saw a tiny round thing lying in the palm of her hand, no bigger than a hazelnut, and understood that it was everything that is made, held in being only by God's love.

She recovered and lived for decades as an anchoress. Her own name is lost: we call her Julian after the parish church of St Julian in Norwich, against whose wall her cell was built. About twenty years after the visions she finished a longer version of her book, Revelations of Divine Love, the oldest surviving book written in English by a woman.

When she asked about sin and suffering, she says, Christ answered with a promise given three times in a row: "all shall be well," spoken twice, and then "all manner of thing," it ran, "shall be well."

Around 1413 a very different visionary came to her window: Margery Kempe, a loud, tearful pilgrim, who asked whether her fits of weeping really came from God. Julian told her they did, and Margery put the visit into her own book, the first autobiography in English.

More than five centuries later, as German bombs fell on England in 1942, the poet Eliot ended Little Gidding, the last of his Four Quartets, with Julian's promise.

teresa-of-avila-the-transverberation-and.context_blurb: In 1515 a merchant family in the walled Castilian city of Avila welcomed a daughter, Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada. She would grow up to reform the Carmelite order, first as a member and then as foundress of its stricter Discalced branch, and to become the first woman named a Doctor of the Catholic Church. Her autobiography describes an experience she called her 'second conversion' and a famous vision of an angel plunging a flaming dart into her heart — the Transverberation Bernini later carved in marble. She also wrote the great mystical treatise The Interior Castle, structured around seven mansions. Source: Teresa, Vida and El Castillo Interior.

thomas-aquinas-the-ox-of-sicily-and-all-.context_blurb: Thomas Aquinas was born about 1225 to a noble family of southern Italy. When as a young man he insisted on joining the brand-new Dominican order, his family literally kidnapped him and held him in their castle for a year to change his mind. Freed at last, Thomas went north to study under the greatest teacher in Europe, Albertus Magnus. Because Thomas was huge, heavy, and almost silent in class, the other students mocked him with an animal nickname. He went on to write the gigantic Summa Theologiae and became the central theologian of the Catholic Church. Source: Vita Thomae; Gui, Vita.

thomas-becket-at-canterbury-four-knights.context_blurb: Thomas Becket and King Henry II of England were so close in the 1150s that they hunted, drank, and rode together like brothers, with Becket serving as the king's Chancellor. In 1162 the king rewarded his old companion with the Archbishopric of Canterbury, sure the old friend would keep the clergy in line. He was wrong. Six years of conflict ended on the evening of 29 December 1170 in Canterbury Cathedral, where a party of four knights rushed in. An eyewitness monk later wrote down everything he saw. Source: contemporary eyewitness accounts.

thomas-more-the-kings-good-servant-but-g.context_blurb: Thomas More, born in London in 1478, was a lawyer, a scholar, and a close friend of the Dutch humanist Erasmus. In 1516 he published a little Latin book describing an imaginary island of perfect politics, with a title he had just coined from Greek roots meaning 'no place.' He later served Henry VIII as Lord Chancellor. When Henry broke with Rome, More resigned, refused the king's new Oath of Supremacy, and was tried and beheaded in 1535. His last words on the scaffold have gone around the world. Source: William Roper, Life of Sir Thomas More.

wilfrid-and-the-synod-of-whitby-the-dati.context_blurb: In 664 CE, two very different Christianities were growing side by side in Anglo-Saxon England: a Celtic tradition descended from Iona, and a Roman tradition brought in from Rome by Augustine of Canterbury two generations before. They disagreed on how to calculate Easter and on how a monk should tonsure his hair. Northumbria's royal household itself was split — King Oswiu kept the Celtic date, his queen Eanfled kept the Roman — which produced an awkward annual Easter clash in the same palace. The Synod of Whitby settled it, under the pro-Roman abbot Wilfrid. Source: Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica 3.25.

bedivere-and-the-returning-of-excalibur.context_blurb:
Le Morte d'Arthur, Sir Thomas Malory's great book, ends with the fall of Camelot. In the final battle Arthur fights his own son Mordred, nearly every knight on both sides dies, and Arthur himself is mortally wounded. Only two knights are left standing beside him, and one of them, Sir Bedivere, receives the king's final command: give Excalibur back to the water.

The other was Sir Lucan, badly hurt himself. When he bent to lift the king, the strain tore his wounds open and his heart burst, and he died at Arthur's feet, leaving Bedivere alone.

Bedivere carried Excalibur down to the lake, but the jewelled pommel and the golden hilt were so beautiful that he could not bear to throw them away. He hid the sword under a tree and went back to the king. Asked what he had seen, he said he had seen only waves and winds. Arthur knew at once it was a lie, because casting Excalibur into the water should have brought a marvel, and he sent him back.

A second time Bedivere gazed at the hilt, hid the sword again and returned with a second lie, the most famous line in the book: he had seen nothing but the waters wap and the waves turn wan, the water lapping and the waves growing pale.

This time Arthur turned on him in fury. He called Bedivere a traitor twice over and said that for the sake of a rich sword his knight would see him dead. He swore to kill Bedivere with his own hands if he lied a third time.

Shamed, Bedivere went down once more. He wound the girdle, the sword's own belt, around the hilt so it would fly clean, whirled the blade round his head and sent it spinning far out across the lake. Before it could sink, an arm rose out of the lake, clothed in white samite, a rich silk, just like the arm that had first given Arthur the sword, and caught it by the hilt.

The hand shook the sword three times and brandished it, then vanished with it beneath the water: three shakes to match Bedivere's three trips to the lake. Now at last Bedivere could tell the king the truth, and Arthur knew his sword had gone home.

camelot-and-the-round-table.context_blurb:
Camelot and the Round Table are the heart of the legends of King Arthur: a shining court where the best knights in the world sat as equals. The stories grew over centuries, from the Norman poet Wace through the French poet Chretien de Troyes to Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur in 1485, and every age added something.

Arthur's capital was Camelot, the city where his court sat and his knights feasted in the great hall, and every finished quest was reported back there. The Table was round for a practical reason. Wace, writing in French verse around 1155, says that at the feasts of Arthur's father, Uther Pendragon, the barons were forever quarrelling over who should sit in the highest place; a round table has no head and no foot, so Arthur made every seat equal.

Each year Arthur gathered the whole fellowship at Camelot for the feast of Pentecost, Whitsunday, and refused to eat until someone brought news of a marvel. In Malory, the Table itself came as a wedding gift. When Arthur married Guinevere, her father, King Leodegrance of Cameliard, sent it as her dowry; he had kept it since the days of Uther Pendragon.

Malory says the Table seated a hundred and fifty knights, each place marked in letters of gold with the name of the knight who deserved it. Leodegrance sent a hundred knights along with it, and Arthur filled the rest. One seat was always left empty: the Siege Perilous, the perilous seat, where any knight who was not perfectly worthy would die the moment he sat down. Only one knight ever sat there and lived. At Pentecost Galahad, the son of Lancelot, came to Camelot, the letters of his name appeared on the vacant seat, and he sat down in it; he would go on to achieve the Holy Grail.

The name Camelot is younger than the legend. It appears in none of the earliest Arthurian books: Chretien de Troyes coined it in the 1170s in The Knight of the Cart, his tale of Lancelot riding to save the captured queen. A real Round Table hangs in the great hall at Winchester, eighteen feet of oak weighing over a ton. It was made in the 1200s and left plain for centuries, until Henry VIII had it painted with Arthur and the names of his knights to impress the emperor Charles V on his visit in 1522.

The Tudor antiquary John Leland, travelling through Somerset in 1542, heard the local people call a hill near them the real Camelot: Cadbury Castle. Leslie Alcock's digs there between 1966 and 1970 showed that a powerful ruler had refortified the hill in Arthur's era, though nothing proves it was Arthur.

In the end the fellowship tore itself apart. Gawain's brother Agravaine, with Mordred, accused Lancelot of loving the queen, and when Lancelot rescued Guinevere from the stake he killed Gawain's brothers Gareth and Gaheris. From then on Sir Gawain led the knights who demanded vengeance on Lancelot, and their feud broke the Round Table.

excalibur-and-the-lady-of-the-lake.context_blurb:
Excalibur is the sword of King Arthur, the most famous blade in Western legend. In Le Morte d'Arthur, written by Sir Thomas Malory in the 1400s, it rises out of a lake in a hand clothed in white silk, and it goes back into the water when Arthur's reign ends. Its scabbard and its older names carry stories of their own.

The first sword Arthur owned, pulled from the stone, did not last. Riding out with Merlin, the young king met King Pellinore, a huge, proud knight who challenged him on the road, and Pellinore's blow shattered Arthur's blade. Merlin saved Arthur's life, and Pellinore later became his ally and a knight of the Round Table.

Merlin led Arthur to a wide lake and told him that in its midst stood a rock, and on that rock a dwelling as fair as any on earth, the home of the enchantress Malory calls Lady of the Lake. Then an arm clothed in white samite rose from the water, holding a sword above the surface. The Lady promised the sword to Arthur in return for a gift she would name later, and he rowed out in a barge and took the blade and its scabbard.

The French romance known as the Vulgate Merlin, and Malory after it, explain the name Excalibur in plain words: it cuts steel. Riding home, Merlin asked whether Arthur liked the sword or the scabbard better, and Arthur chose the sword. Merlin told him he had chosen badly, because the scabbard was worth ten of the swords. As long as Arthur wore it, he would never lose a drop of blood, however badly he was wounded.

Years later the Lady came to Arthur's court to claim her gift. Before Arthur could answer her, the knight Balin, newly freed from Arthur's prison, drew his sword and struck off her head in the hall, blaming her for his mother's death. Arthur banished Balin for the killing, and Balin rode toward his own doom, the Dolorous Stroke that wounded the Fisher King.

Merlin's warning came true. Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half-sister and one of his bitterest enemies, crept in while he slept, stole the scabbard and flung it into deep water, where it sank beyond all finding. Without it Arthur could bleed, and at his last battle, Camlann, he took his death wound. He ordered Excalibur thrown back into the lake. Twice Sir Bedivere came back without doing it, but on the third trip he threw the sword far out, and the arm in white samite rose, caught it and drew it under.

The sword's names are older than Malory. In his Historia Regum Britanniae, written around 1136, Geoffrey of Monmouth calls the blade Caliburnus and says it was forged in Avalon, the magical island. Older still is the Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, the earliest surviving Arthurian story, in which young Culhwch must finish some forty impossible tasks to win Olwen. There Arthur's sword is Caledfwlch, a name built from Welsh words for "hard" and "breach," often rendered as hard-cleaver.

galahad-the-perfect-knight-and-the-siege.context_blurb:
In the legends of King Arthur, the Holy Grail is the cup Jesus used at the Last Supper, hidden away in a castle of wonders. Many knights of the Round Table rode out to find it, and almost all of them failed. In Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, and in the French romance he followed, the Queste del Saint Graal, the one who succeeds is a young knight born to be perfect.

He was Galahad. At the feast of Pentecost an old hermit led him into Camelot in red armour, and he took his place in the Siege Perilous, a chair at the Round Table which had been death to every man who sat in it before, and he alone would find the Grail.

His birth came from a trick. Lancelot, Arthur's greatest knight, loved Queen Guinevere. Elaine of Corbenic, daughter of King Pelles, longed to bear Lancelot's son, and her nurse, the enchantress Dame Brusen, worked an enchantment so that for a single night Lancelot took her for the queen. Galahad was born of that night.

On the Pentecost when he came to court, a great stone came floating down the river to Camelot with a sword driven through it, and words cut into the stone promised the sword to the finest knight alive. Gawain tried and failed, but Galahad put his hand to it and drew it out easily. Arthur had drawn a sword from a stone to become king; Galahad drew this one as the knight of holiness.

The quest began, and most of the fellowship failed, Lancelot and Gawain among them. Only three knights saw the Grail uncovered: Galahad and his two companions, Percival and Bors. They came at last to Corbenic, the castle of the wounded Fisher King, whose wound would never heal, the very castle where Elaine had deceived Lancelot, and in its chapel the Grail was uncovered before them.

In the French Queste, no priest served them there. Christ himself stepped out of the Grail and gave the three knights communion with his own hand.

Then the Grail went overseas. Galahad, Percival and Bors carried it to Sarras, a city of wonders somewhere in the East, where Galahad was crowned king and reigned for a single year. He had asked to die in his moment of greatest joy. At Mass in Sarras he saw the Grail uncovered, and the wonder was so great that he died of joy where he knelt, and angels carried his soul up.

In that same instant, Malory says, a hand reached down from heaven above the altar and took the Grail and the holy spear away, and no one on earth has seen the Grail since. Percival became a hermit and soon died. Sir Bors alone rode back to Camelot to tell the whole tale, the last living witness of the Grail, and years later he stood beside Lancelot in the war that broke the Round Table.

gareth-beaumains-the-kitchen-boy-who-was.context_blurb:
The tale of Gareth in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur is the Round Table's great underdog story: a prince who hides his name, works a year in the kitchens, and wins his knighthood by deeds instead of birth. It fills Malory's seventh book, and years later it ends in tragedy.

At the feast of Pentecost a tall, handsome stranger came to Arthur's court at Camelot and would not tell his name. He asked the king for three gifts, and the first was simply his keep: food and lodging for a year. Sir Kay, the king's sharp-tongued steward, sneered at the young man's soft white hands, nicknamed him Beaumains, French for "Fair Hands," and sent him to scrub pots in the kitchen.

A year later a damsel named Lynette rode in, begging for a knight to save her sister from a terrible enemy who held her castle under siege. Beaumains claimed his second gift, the right to take her quest. Lynette was furious to be given a kitchen boy, and she rode behind him all the way, mocking him for smelling of grease. Her sister was Dame Lyonesse, shut up in Castle Perilous by the Red Knight, lord of the Red Launds.

On the road Beaumains beat four knights in turn, each known by the colour of his armour: a Black Knight, a Green, a Red, and last Sir Persaunt of Inde, the Blue Knight, and he sent every one of them to Arthur as a prisoner. Lynette's scorn slowly turned to admiration.

At Castle Perilous he found a grim warning. Around the Red Knight's pavilion hung nearly forty knights the giant had beaten, strung up by their necks from the trees, the shameful death of common criminals.

From morning till night Beaumains fought the giant, and at last he beat him. He spared his life on condition that he go to Camelot and yield to Arthur, and only then did the Red Knight give his true name: Sir Ironside. He had sworn to a lady to kill every knight of Arthur's he could reach, because her brother had been slain by Lancelot or Gawain. Beaumains had the hanged knights cut down and buried.

Then the secret came out. Beaumains was Gareth, the youngest son of King Lot of Orkney and brother to Gawain, Agravain and Gaheris, so the kitchen boy was Arthur's own nephew. He married Dame Lyonesse at the tale's end.

His death was cruel. Years later Lancelot killed Gareth by mistake while rescuing Queen Guinevere from the pyre, where Arthur had condemned her to burn for her love of Lancelot; Gareth had come unarmed, out of loyalty. Gawain had loved Gareth best of all his brothers, and he became Lancelot's mortal enemy, a feud that tore the Round Table apart.

gawain-and-the-green-knight-the-beheadin.context_blurb:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is an English poem written around 1375 by a poet whose name is lost. It tests a knight's honour in a winter's tale: a beheading game, a castle in the wilds, three days of temptation, and an axe waiting at the end of the year. Its hero is Gawain, King Arthur's nephew.

On New Year's Day, as Arthur's court feasted at Camelot, a giant rode into the hall, and everything about him was green: skin and beard, armour and horse. In one hand he held a sprig of holly as a sign of peace, and in the other a great axe.

He proposed a Christmas game. Any knight might strike him one blow with the axe now, if he swore to take a blow in return from the Green Knight a year and a day from then. The hall fell silent. Arthur himself began to rise to the challenge, but young Sir Gawain stepped forward and asked the king's leave to play the game in his place.

Gawain swung the axe, and the Green Knight's head flew off at one stroke. The body did not fall. It strode across the hall, picked up its own head by the hair, and climbed back into the saddle. Then the head opened its eyes and spoke, telling Gawain to seek him at the Green Chapel in a year's time to receive his blow.

A year later Gawain rode north through the winter. On Christmas Eve he came to a splendid castle in the wilds, and its master, a huge, ruddy huntsman named Bertilak, proposed a second game: each day Bertilak would hunt while Gawain rested, and each night they would trade whatever each had won.

While Bertilak hunted, his wife came to Gawain's room each day and tried to seduce him. Gawain courteously refused her, and each night he handed Bertilak the kisses she had given him. On the third day she pressed on him a girdle of green silk, swearing that no one wearing it could be killed, and Gawain, dreading the axe, kept the gift hidden from his host.

On New Year's Day he found the Green Chapel, no chapel at all but a grassy mound in a wild valley, and the Green Knight sharpening his axe. Gawain knelt and bared his neck. The first swing the Green Knight held back when Gawain flinched, and the second he checked though Gawain held still. The third came down at last, but it only nicked the side of his neck and drew a little blood. That small cut, the Green Knight explained, was the price of the hidden girdle.

The Green Knight then revealed that he was Bertilak himself. He named the one who had shaped the whole scheme: Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half-sister and a mistress of enchantment, who had sent him to Camelot to try the honour of Arthur's knights. She had watched it all at the castle, disguised as an old woman.

guinevere-the-queen-at-the-stake.context_blurb:
Guinevere is King Arthur's queen at Camelot, whose long secret love for Sir Lancelot at last broke the Round Table apart; her name comes from the Welsh Gwenhwyfar, often explained as "white phantom." Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur follows her to the bitter end: a trap, a fire, a rescue that kills the wrong men, and a convent.

Her father, King Leodegrance of Cameliard, gave Arthur a wedding gift that became the heart of his court: the Round Table itself, with a hundred knights to sit at it.

Her lover through most of the Arthurian tales is Sir Lancelot. Chretien de Troyes, a French poet writing about 1180, told how an enemy king kidnapped her and Lancelot climbed into a cart used for carrying criminals, giving up his honour as a knight to reach her.

In Malory's last books, Sir Agravaine and Sir Mordred, Arthur's son by his own half-sister, set a trap: with twelve armed knights they waited outside the queen's chamber to catch Lancelot inside. Lancelot armed himself as best he could and cut his way out past the ambush, and when it was over thirteen knights lay dead, Agravaine among them.

Guinevere, left behind, was seized. Arthur's own law left him no choice, and with grief he sentenced his wife to burn at the stake. At Carlisle they led Guinevere out to the pyre stripped to her smock, a plain linen undergarment, the shameful dress of the condemned.

As the fire was being lit, Lancelot and his kinsmen charged in, cut through the guards and carried the queen away. In the slaughter Lancelot killed Gareth and Gaheris, Gawain's brothers, who stood there unarmed because they loved Lancelot too well to fight him. Gawain had loved Lancelot above every other knight, and now he became his deadliest foe; the war between them tore the kingdom apart and opened the way for Mordred.

When it was all over, with Arthur dead after Camlann, Mordred slain and Lancelot far away, Guinevere took the veil at Amesbury and lived there in penance, rising to be abbess before she died. Lancelot came to the abbey at last, hoping to take her away with him. Guinevere met him one last time in the cloister, but only to send him off: she told him never to look on her face again and refused him even a parting kiss. Lancelot became a hermit and died soon after.

kay-the-seneschal-the-sharp-tongued-fost.context_blurb:
Sir Kay is King Arthur's foster-brother and the steward of his court. In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur he is a sharp-tongued, often rude knight, but in the oldest Welsh tales he is something much grander: a magical warrior at Arthur's right hand.

Merlin hid the infant Arthur, son of King Uther Pendragon, in the house of a country knight, and the knight's son was raised alongside him, the two boys believing they were real brothers. That son was Sir Kay. His father was Sir Ector, who raised Arthur in secret from babyhood.

On the day of a New Year tournament near London, young Arthur rode as Kay's squire. Kay found he had left his sword behind at their lodging and sent Arthur back for it. The lodging was locked, so Arthur pulled a sword from a stone in a churchyard and brought that instead. Kay knew what it meant and claimed for a moment that he had drawn it himself, but Sir Ector made him swear on a holy book how he had come by it, and Kay confessed the truth. Ector had Arthur set the sword back in the stone and draw it out again, and knelt to him.

Malory's Kay is famous for his scorn. When a young stranger came to court asking only for food and lodging for a year, Kay mocked his soft white hands, called him Beaumains, "Fair Hands," and sent him off to scour pots; the kitchen boy turned out to be Gareth of Orkney, Arthur's own nephew.

Culhwch and Olwen, a Welsh tale first set down in writing about 1100, remembers him as Cei, a hero with strange powers. Cei could hold his breath under water for nine days and nights, go nine days without sleep, and make himself as tall as the tallest tree. In that older Welsh layer, before Lancelot was ever imagined, Arthur's two closest companions were Cei and his friend Bedwyr, the knight later called Bedivere.

lancelot-of-the-lake-the-greatest-knight.context_blurb: After his father King Ban of Benwick dies of his wounds fleeing a burning castle, an infant is stolen from his mother's arms by a fairy — the Lady of the Lake — who carries him down into her enchanted underwater realm and raises him there. He grows up to be the greatest knight of Arthur's Round Table and the queen's secret lover. His love-affair with Guinevere and his madness in the forest for two years after Elaine of Corbenic tricks him both figure in Malory, as does the final scene where angels lift him to heaven at his death. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

merlin-the-mage-the-wizard-who-arranges-.context_blurb: At the young Arthur's court an old white-bearded man in a long robe advises the king on every disaster before it comes, arranges Arthur's own conception at Tintagel, sets up the sword-in-the-stone test to prove him rightful king, and in Geoffrey of Monmouth tells how a tower would not stand because two dragons were fighting beneath it. In Malory's telling he is sometimes called 'a devil's son.' He has one great weakness that he foresees and cannot avoid. Source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae; Malory.

merlins-end-the-enchantress-in-the-rock.context_blurb: In his old age the great wizard of Arthur's court falls in love with a beautiful young damsel of the Lady of the Lake's kin and follows her wherever she goes like a lovesick fool. He cannot leave her side. He teaches her every magical secret he knows, and when she has learned enough she uses the last of those secrets against him. In Malory she is Nimue (also spelled Nimueh or Niviane). The place where she buries him alive is the Breton forest of Broceliande. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 4.

mordred-and-the-battle-of-camlann.context_blurb: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the young King Arthur one night sleeps with a queen who is a guest at his court, not knowing that she is his own half-sister. She conceives a son by him that night. Years later that son rides as a knight of the Round Table, foments the quarrel over Guinevere and Lancelot that shatters the fellowship, seizes the throne while Arthur is away in France, and finally faces him on the battlefield of Camlann. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 21; Annales Cambriae.

morgan-le-fay-the-half-sister-who-steals.context_blurb: Arthur has three older half-sisters, all daughters of his mother Igraine by her first husband Duke Gorlois of Cornwall, born before Igraine ever married Uther Pendragon. The most dangerous of the three is a sorceress — married to King Uriens of Gore, mother of Yvain, and bitter enemy of her brother Arthur. She steals Excalibur's scabbard, which protects its wearer from bleeding, and tries to kill Arthur and Guinevere by various enchantments. At the end she is one of the queens who carry Arthur away to Avalon. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

perceval-and-the-fisher-king-the-questio.context_blurb: A country boy is raised alone in the wilds of Wales by his widowed mother. She keeps him deliberately ignorant of what knights are and what knighthood means — because her husband and her elder sons were all killed as knights, and she cannot bear to lose him the same way. This boy will grow up to be one of the Round Table's great knights and the first to glimpse the Grail. In Chretien de Troyes's unfinished Perceval le Gaulois the Grail procession passes before him and he fails to ask the question that would have healed the Fisher King. Source: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval.

the-barge-to-avalon-the-once-and-future-.context_blurb: King Arthur is dying after his last battle against Mordred at Camlann. He gives his most trusted surviving knight one last order: take Excalibur down to the water and throw it in. After the sword is returned to the Lady of the Lake, a black barge glides to the shore carrying three queens in black. They lay the wounded king on it with his head in a queen's lap, and sail him away. Later tradition says the barge carried him to Avalon — the Isle of Apples — and that his grave is in Glastonbury. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 21.

the-grail-as-the-cup-of-the-last-supper-.context_blurb: In the earliest Grail stories the holy cup is simply a mysterious vessel seen in a procession, and no one explains what it is. In the early thirteenth century one French poet first identified it with the cup used at Jesus's final meal with his disciples, in which a wealthy follower afterwards caught drops of blood at the crucifixion. In that version the same follower then travels west with it to the British Isles. In the German retelling by Wolfram von Eschenbach the Grail is instead something else entirely. Sources: early French and German Grail poems.

the-grail-procession-bleeding-lance-swor.context_blurb: The first thing to enter the supper hall in Chretien de Troyes's Perceval procession is a young man carrying a weapon that looks like an ordinary spear except for one uncanny detail — a single drop keeps falling from its tip without stopping. A silver platter and a sword follow it, and last of all comes a radiant covered dish of gold. Perceval watches it pass by without asking a single question, which is the one thing he was supposed to do. Source: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval le Gaulois.

the-round-table-fellowship-knights-quest.context_blurb: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, King Arthur has a great round wooden table set up at Camelot where his chosen knights sit as equals, none at the head. Every year on the high feast of Pentecost they ride in to Camelot together to renew their vows of knighthood. Their code — the Pentecostal Oath — binds them to always help a lady in need, never to murder, and above all to give mercy to any who asks mercy. The fellowship rises to a hundred and fifty and finally fractures over the queen's affair with Lancelot. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

the-sword-in-the-stone-whoso-pulleth-out.context_blurb: Uther Pendragon, King of Britain, has died leaving no acknowledged heir, and the barons are ready to fight each other for the crown. In Malory Book I, Merlin tells the Archbishop of Canterbury to summon every lord in the land to London by Christmas so that God can show a sign. In a churchyard they find a huge stone with a sword driven into it and an inscription in gold around the hilt. Only one person in all Britain can pull the sword from the stone — and it turns out not to be anyone the barons expected. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 1.

tristan-and-iseult-the-love-potion-and-t.context_blurb: In the old Cornish romance, a young knight of Lyonesse is sent by his uncle the King of Cornwall to sail to Ireland and bring back the Irish princess Iseult the Fair as a bride — not for himself, but for his uncle. On the voyage back he and the princess accidentally drink a love-potion her mother had prepared for the wedding night. The whole rest of their lives are shadowed by that drink. They are discovered, condemned, flee into a forest, and finally Tristan dies waiting for a sail of a particular colour. Sources: Beroul; Thomas of Britain; Gottfried von Strassburg.

uther-pendragon-and-igraine-conception-a.context_blurb: Long before Arthur is born, a king of Britain sits at a great banquet at his court and sees the beautiful wife of one of his own dukes. He falls violently in love with her on the spot. With Merlin's magic he enters her castle at Tintagel on the Cornish coast disguised as her husband and spends the night with her, while the real husband is killed on a raid elsewhere. The child conceived that night will become the greatest king in Britain's legendary history. Source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae; Malory.

wolframs-parzival-the-grail-as-a-stone-f.context_blurb: In the first quarter of the 1200s a Bavarian knight-poet sat down to retell, in Middle High German, an unfinished French Grail-poem by Chretien de Troyes. He turned it into an epic of about 25,000 rhymed lines that became the greatest German Arthurian romance. In his version the Holy Grail is not a cup at all; it is kept by a brotherhood of knights at the castle Munsalvaesche, and new names appear on it each year on a specific high feast of the Christian calendar. The hero's half-brother is black-and-white speckled. Source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival.

aengus-and-the-dream-the-swan-maiden-of-.context_blurb:
In old Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann are a race of gods, and their god of love and youth is Aengus, often called Aengus Og, "Young Aengus". His father is the Dagda, and his mother is Boann, goddess of the river Boyne. The Old Irish tale called The Dream of Aengus tells how he fell in love with a woman he had only seen in his sleep.

Aengus lives in Bru na Boinne, "the Dwelling of the Boyne", the vast stone mound roofed with grass beside the river that visitors now call Newgrange. Archaeologists date it to around 3200 BC, older than the Egyptian pyramids. One night, asleep in his mound, Aengus saw a girl lovelier than anyone he had ever known appear beside his bed; when he reached for her she was gone, and she returned every night for a year.

Love clung to Aengus even when he was awake. Four birds always circled his head, and the poets said they were his own kisses, turned into living birds. But the dream girl was out of reach, and he wasted away, unable to eat or speak. Boann searched Ireland for a year and found nothing, the Dagda searched for another, and at last they called on Bodb Derg, "Bodb the Red", king of the fairy mounds of Munster, who found her after a year's hunt of his own.

She was on Loch Bel Dracon, a lake in the west, among thrice fifty young women chained two by two with silver. She alone wore a single chain of gold around her neck, marking her as the fairest. Her name was Caer Ibormeith, "Yew-Berry", for the yew, Ireland's tree of forever, which lives for centuries in churchyards; she was the daughter of Ethal Anbuail, a lord in Connacht.

But Caer was more than a girl. Every other year, at Samhain, the first of November, she and her companions changed shape and lived a whole year as swans on the lake. Samhain is the threshold between summer and winter, when the wall between worlds grows thin. On Samhain morning Aengus came to the shore and called to her. She would leave the lake with him on one condition: he had to become a swan himself. He did, and joined her on the water. Then the two swans rose and flew home toward Bru na Boinne, singing as they went, and their song was so sweet that it put everyone in Ireland to sleep for three days and three nights.

How did Aengus come to own the Bru at all? By a trick of words. He asked for the mound, just for laa ocus aidche, "a day and a night", and the owner agreed. Then Aengus pointed out that Old Irish has no word for "a", so the phrase means just as well day and night, which is to say all of time, and the mound was his forever. In one telling he played the trick on his father, the Dagda; in Tochmarc Etaine, the Dagda coaches him to play it on Elcmar, the mound's earlier lord.

balor-of-the-evil-eye-and-the-eyelid-fou.context_blurb:
In Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann, the shining gods of Ireland, fought a long war against older and darker powers. Their most dreadful enemy was a king with one enormous eye that killed whatever it looked on. The old tale Cath Maige Tuired, which tells of the second great battle fought at Moytura, ends with his fall at the hands of his own grandson.

The Fomorians were monsters out of the sea who held Ireland before the Tuatha De arrived: misshapen giants, many with a single eye or a single leg, who crushed every people that tried to settle the island. Their king was Balor, whose one eye was so venomous that anything it looked upon fell dead, and men called him Balor of the Evil Eye.

He was not born that way. As a boy, Balor peeked over the rim of a great cauldron where his father's druids were brewing a spell, and the fumes rising off the brew got into his eye and left it deadly for ever. The poison made the lid grow so heavy that Balor could not raise it himself. In battle, four warriors hauled it open by a ring set in the lid, using ropes and hooks.

Once the lid was up, the gaze did not wound or blind or curse. It simply killed, and whole armies dropped dead where they stood in a single look.

Yet Balor had a fear of his own. A druid foretold that he would die not at the hands of an enemy king but by his own grandson. So he shut his daughter Ethlinn, his only child, inside a tower of crystal on Tory Island, off the coast of Donegal in Ireland's northwest, where ruins on the island are still called Balor's Fort.

The tower did not hold. Cian mac Cainte, a young warrior of the Tuatha De and son of the healer Dian Cecht, reached Ethlinn after Birog, a druidess, spirited him across the sea, and the son born to Ethlinn and Cian was Lugh.

Grandfather and grandson met at last on the battlefield of Moytura. As the four warriors began to heave up Balor's eyelid, Lugh, too far off to use a spear, whirled his sling and let fly a single stone, called in some tellings the Tathlum. The stone struck the half-open eye and drove it backward clean through Balor's skull, so that the deadly gaze fired the wrong way and killed the Fomorian army massed behind their own king. The Fomorians were broken for ever.

boann-and-the-river-boyne-the-well-of-se.context_blurb:
The River Boyne winds through County Meath in eastern Ireland, flowing by the ancient stone mound of Newgrange on its way to the sea. Old Irish myth says the river was once a goddess, and that it took her shape when she drowned. The medieval poems that tell how places got their names keep her story.

The river is Boann, a goddess of the god-race of Irish myth, the Tuatha De Danann. She died where the river rises, and her body became its water.

Its source was the Well of Segais, a hidden spring in the secret centre of Ireland and the source of all wisdom. Only Boann's husband, the god Nechtan, and three cup-bearers who served him might go near it. Nine hazel trees ringed the well, dropping their nuts of wisdom into the water, the very nuts that fatten the Salmon of Knowledge in Fionn's story.

Boann was proud and would not be forbidden. She went to the well and walked around it three times tuathal, against the sun, which in Irish tradition is the direction of ill omen and of challenge, as sunwise is the way of blessing. The water answered at once. It burst up from the well and chased her across the plain, tearing away an eye, an arm and a leg, and she drowned; the flood ran on to the sea and became the Boyne. Those three wounds are the classic Irish triple blemish, the kind of maiming that could cost a king his throne.

Boann also loved another god, the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De. To hide her pregnancy from her husband, the Dagda held the sun still for nine months, so their son was born in what seemed a single day: Aengus, the young god of love, who would own the great mound of Bru na Boinne beside his mother's river.

Boann's tale survives in the Dindshenchas, the lore of places, a whole body of medieval Irish prose and verse that explains how every important hill, lake, ford and river in Ireland got its name.

bres-the-beautiful-the-half-fomorian-tyr.context_blurb:
In the Irish tale Cath Maige Tuired, the Tuatha De Danann, the gods of old Ireland, lose their king. Nuada has his hand cut off in battle, and Irish law will not let a maimed man rule. The king they choose in his place is the most beautiful man of his generation, and his reign proves a disaster.

The Tuatha De crowned Bres, known as the Beautiful, in Nuada's place. His mother was the goddess Eriu, of the Tuatha De, but his father, Elatha, was a prince of the Fomorians, Ireland's oldest enemies, and the gods hoped a half-Fomorian king would buy them peace.

It bought them slavery instead. Bres let his Fomorian kin squeeze the gods with tribute until they toiled like serfs, and the Dagda himself, chief of the Tuatha De and owner of the cauldron of plenty, was put to digging ditches around forts like a common labourer.

Worse, Bres was mean, and an Irish king's first duty was to give food and drink freely to his guests, poets above all. When the poet Coirpre came to his hall, Bres lodged him in a small dark room and fed him three small dry cakes, with no meat, no butter and no ale. In the morning Coirpre stood on the hillside and spoke a poem against the king: Ireland's very first satire. From then on satire was so feared that Irish law protected satirists and set damages for their words.

Words had power in Ireland. The moment the satire was spoken, red boils broke out on Bres's face, and a blemished king could no more rule than a one-handed one. Bres was thrown down, the first Irish king brought low by a poem, and Nuada, now fitted with a hand of silver, took back his throne.

brigid-of-the-tuatha-poetry-healing-smit.context_blurb:
Long before the saint of Kildare, the Irish honoured a goddess named Brigid, one of the greatest of the Tuatha De Danann, the divine race of Irish myth. She was a daughter of the Dagda and a goddess of fire, and the saint who later bore her name took over, as many scholars think, her feast, her flame and much of her power.

Poets, healers and smiths all claimed her, and she bore a title for each craft: she was the poets' Brigid, the healers' Brigid and the smiths' Brigid. Her name is thought to mean the Exalted One. Her Christian namesake, Saint Brigid, founded her monastery in Leinster beside a great oak, at Cill Dara, the church of the oak, which English speakers call Kildare.

An old Irish word-book, Cormac's Glossary, calls Brigid the goddess poets adored and says she was really three sisters sharing one name, one sister for each craft. The war goddess called the Morrigan follows the same three-in-one pattern, with Macha and Badb as her sisters. Brigid's feast is Imbolc, 1 February, one of the four great quarter-days of the Irish year: the start of spring, when the ewes give milk again after the winter. The saint's feast falls on that very day.

Fire was hers above all. At Kildare a flame burned day and night and was never allowed to go out. Nineteen women tended it, each keeping it for one night in turn, and on the twentieth night, the story said, Brigid kept it herself. Gerald of Wales saw it in the late 12th century. On Imbolc Irish families still weave a Brigid's cross, a little four-armed charm of rushes cut that day, its centre woven into a square, and hang it over the door to guard the house for the year.

The saint's Old Irish Life, the Bethu Brigte, tells a startling story. At her consecration Bishop Mel read the rite for a bishop over her by mistake, and he refused to take it back, saying the honour came from God; so, in that telling, Brigid was made a bishop, an office no woman was meant to hold. Some scholars hear in it an echo of the goddess's old authority.

The Book of Invasions gives the goddess a household of sacred beasts: two named oxen, Torc Triath the king of boars and Cirb the king of wethers. All of them raised a cry across Ireland whenever plundering was done there.

lugh-at-tara-the-doorkeepers-list-of-art.context_blurb: In Irish myth, a young warrior in a gold king's diadem came to the gates of Tara during King Nuada's feast, leading a company of warriors and asking to be let in. The doorkeeper refused him unless he had a skill the court did not already have. The young stranger named art after art — carpenter, smith, warrior, harper, poet, physician, cup-bearer — and for each the doorkeeper named a Tuatha De master of that skill. Then he asked whether the court had a single man who was all of these at once. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

manannan-mac-lir-the-wave-sweeper-enbarr.context_blurb: In Irish myth Manannan mac Lir is the god of the sea, ruler of the Isle of Apples (Emain Ablach, the Irish cousin of Avalon), and keeper of a cluster of magical treasures. His horse Enbarr of the Flowing Mane runs on sea and land alike; his cloak of invisibility hides him from sight; his sword Fragarach, the Answerer, could cut through any armor and compel a bound man to speak only truth. The Feast of Goibniu held in his undersea halls keeps the Tuatha De from aging. Sources: Cormac's Glossary; Immram Brain.

midir-and-etain-a-fly-a-hundred-years-a-.context_blurb: The Tochmarc Etaine, 'The Wooing of Etain,' is one of the most intricate stories in all Irish myth. A Tuatha De god of a sidhe mound at Bri Leith falls in love with the most beautiful mortal woman ever born in Ireland and marries her. His first jealous Tuatha De wife turns the bride into an insect and blows her out of the house with a storm, driving the whole long cycle of transformations and rebirths that follows. Centuries later a High King of Ireland wins the bride back a second time — and the god comes for her again at a Tara board-game. Source: Tochmarc Etaine.

newgrange-aengus-tricks-the-dagda-out-of.context_blurb: On a bend of a river in County Meath, Irish farmers five thousand years ago raised a great round mound of white quartz and dark stone, with a passage running deep inside it. In Irish myth this mound was the palace of the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann. His youngest son Aengus tricks him out of it with a famous Old Irish wordplay on 'a day and a night.' Two other huge mounds — Knowth and Dowth — stand nearby. Source: Tochmarc Etaine; archaeology of the Boyne Valley.

nuada-silver-hand-the-king-who-lost-a-th.context_blurb: In Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland from four northern cities, and the first king to lead them onto the island carried a burning blade called the Sword of Light — once drawn from its sheath, no enemy could escape it. He lost his right arm at the shoulder at the First Battle of Moytura, which under Irish law disqualified him from kingship. The healer Dian Cecht and the wright Creidhne made him a working silver hand so he could reclaim his throne. His own son Miach made him a better one, and paid the price. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

nuadas-death-at-moytura-and-lughs-kingsh.context_blurb: As the Tuatha De Danann prepared for their great war against the Fomorians, the true king Nuada Silverhand did an unusual thing: he stepped off his own throne and put a younger champion in his place for the run-up to the battle. The young champion was Lugh of the Long Arm — a master of every art. Thirteen days later at the Second Battle of Moytura, Lugh brought down Balor of the Evil Eye with a single slingshot. The Morrigan then chanted the Fomorians off the field. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-children-of-lir-nine-hundred-years-a.context_blurb: In Irish myth a Tuatha De figure named Lir lost his first wife and married her sister Aoife to be a mother to his four small children. The new stepmother grew jealous of how much Lir loved the children and, on the edge of a lake, turned all four of them into swans with a druid's rod. Her curse kept them in that shape for nine hundred years, flying through three hundred-year sentences on three different stretches of water. Their long story is one of the Three Sorrows of Storytelling. Source: Oidheadh Chlainne Lir.

the-dagda-his-club-his-harp-his-cauldron.context_blurb: In Irish myth a huge, red-bearded, big-bellied god in a hooded cloak is the chief of the Tuatha De Danann. His people call him 'good' — not because he is kindly, but because he is skilled at every craft: war, magic, poetry, husbandry, cooking. He owns the Lorg Mor — a great club that killed with one end and brought back to life with the other — a cauldron that fed any gathering until all were satisfied, and a magical harp named Daur Da Bla. He lives in Bru na Boinne on the Boyne. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-fir-bolg-the-bag-men-and-the-five-pr.context_blurb: The Lebor Gabala Erenn, the Irish Book of Invasions, lists six waves of settlers who came to Ireland one after another. Right before the Tuatha De Danann arrived, one older people held the whole island. According to the Book of Invasions they were descendants of the earlier Nemedians who had been driven out of Ireland by the Fomorians and spent generations as earth-slaves in Greece before coming home. They divided Ireland into its traditional five provinces and ruled under their king Eochaid mac Eirc. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-fomorians-sea-monster-people-one-leg.context_blurb: Before any of the six waves of settlers arrived in Ireland, a dark race already lived on the rocky islands and coasts and made war on every incoming people — the primordial enemies of Partholon, Nemed, and finally the Tuatha De Danann. They are often described as misshapen — one eye, one arm, one leg — and cruel. Their shape in Irish myth echoes the giants (the Jotnar) of Norse myth who ring the gods' world in the same way. The second great battle at Moytura ends their rule. Sources: Lebor Gabala Erenn; Cath Maige Tuired.

the-four-treasures-lia-fail-spear-of-lug.context_blurb: When the Tuatha De Danann arrived in Ireland, the tales say they brought a sacred set of magical objects with them — one from each of the four northern cities of learning where their druid-teachers had trained them. The treasures are the Stone of Destiny (the Lia Fail) from Falias, the invincible Spear of Lugh from Gorias, the Sword of Nuada from Findias, and the Cauldron of the Dagda from Murias. In every medieval Irish source they are counted exactly the same way. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-milesians-and-amergins-poem-i-am-a-w.context_blurb: In the medieval Book of Invasions, six waves of settlers reach Ireland in turn — Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and one last people. This sixth and final wave sails in from Iberia and becomes the ancestors of the modern Irish Gaels. Their chief poet Amergin Gluingel ('White-Knee') speaks a famous nature-poem as he first sets his right foot on the Irish shore. The Milesians make a treaty with the defeated Tuatha De dividing Ireland between surface and underground. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-morrigan-at-the-ford-crow-prophecy-t.context_blurb: In old Irish myth a dark-winged bird was known to settle on shield-rims and spear-points as an army lined up for battle — and whichever side she chose was the side about to die. The Tuatha De Danann called this bird-shape one of their goddesses in the shape she liked best. She is a triple-goddess, sometimes paired with Macha and Badb, and she keeps a yearly tryst with the Dagda at the river Unius on the feast of Samhain. At the Second Battle of Moytura she chants the Fomorian king Indech off the field. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-sidhe-mounds-and-the-aos-si-where-th.context_blurb: After the Tuatha De Danann went underground into the hollow hills, later Irish tradition stopped calling them 'the Tuatha De' at all — they became a new folk under a new name, the beings that English-speakers now call 'the fairies' or 'the Good Folk.' Their mounds are called the sidhe. On the feast of Samhain the veil between worlds thins and they walk among mortals; the hawthorn tree is held sacred to them, and the lone 'fairy thorn' in a field is left standing. Source: Irish folklore; Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-six-invasions-of-ireland-from-cessai.context_blurb: A medieval Irish book compiled in the eleventh century, the Lebor Gabala Erenn — 'the Book of the Taking of Ireland' — gives the island an origin story in successive waves of settlers, one after another, each taking the land from the last. The first wave was led by Cessair before the Flood; another survivor named Fintan mac Bochra lived through the Flood as a salmon and spans the whole book. The last wave is the Gaels. The book is a monk's attempt to fit Ireland's pre-Christian history into the frame of Genesis. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-tuatha-de-danann-the-god-people-of-d.context_blurb: Irish myth tells of a supernatural people who arrived in Ireland long before the modern Irish, and who are the closest thing Irish tradition has to a family of gods. Their name literally means 'the people of the goddess Danu' (or Ana). They land in a dark cloud on the mountains of Connacht and burn their own ships on the beach so that there is no going back. Among their chief figures are the Dagda, Lugh, the Morrigan, Nuada, and Manannan mac Lir. After the Milesians arrive they go underground into the hollow hills. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

joseph-interprets-pharaohs-dreams-the-se.context_blurb:
Joseph, son of Jacob, was sold into slavery by his brothers and later thrown into an Egyptian prison on a false charge. In Genesis his rise begins with a pair of dreams that troubled Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and that no one at his court could explain.

In the first dream seven fat, sleek cows came up out of the Nile to graze in the reeds, and then seven thin, ugly cows came up after them and ate the fat ones. In the second, seven full ears of grain grew on one stalk, and seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, swallowed them up.

In the morning Pharaoh called for all the magicians and wise men in Egypt, but not one of them could explain the dreams. Then his cupbearer remembered a young Hebrew in prison who had read his own dream truly. Pharaoh sent for Joseph at once, and they rushed him out of the dungeon; before he went in, he shaved and changed his clothes, since a bearded prisoner was not fit for the Egyptian court.

Joseph told Pharaoh that the two dreams carried one warning: Egypt would have seven years of rich harvests, followed by seven years of hunger bad enough to wipe out all memory of the good times. He advised Pharaoh to set a wise man over Egypt and to gather a fifth of every harvest during the good years, storing the grain in the cities against the famine.

Pharaoh gave the job to Joseph himself. He gave him an Egyptian name, Zaphnath-paaneah, which Jewish interpreters read as "revealer of hidden things," and found him a wife, Asenath, whose father Poti-pherah served as priest at On, the city of the sun. Joseph was thirty years old.

dominic-and-the-black-and-white-habit.context_blurb:
Dominic de Guzman, born around 1170 in the Castilian village of Caleruega, founded the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans. He spent his life preaching in poverty, and his friars spread across the universities and cities of medieval Europe.

Before he was born, his mother, Jane of Aza, dreamed of a dog bounding from her womb with a blazing torch between its jaws, setting fire to the world. Later wits read the order's name as Domini canes, the hounds of God.

In 1203, riding through Languedoc in southern France with his bishop, Dominic met the Cathars, a sect the Church condemned as heretics, whose holy men tramped the countryside barefoot and penniless while Church officials rode past with loaded pack trains. He decided that only preachers just as poor could win the people back.

He gathered his first preachers at Toulouse, and Pope Honorius III approved the new Order of Preachers in 1216. Its friars wore a white tunic under a black mantle, the white said to stand for purity and the black for penance, which is why the English called them the Blackfriars.

Dominic did not keep his little band together. He scattered his brothers at once, sending them to preach and study at the leading universities of his day, Paris and Bologna, and as Jordan of Saxony records, he said that seed which is hoarded bears no fruit.

Dominic died in Bologna and was buried there in a marble tomb begun by Nicola Pisano. Almost three centuries later, in 1494, a nineteen-year-old Florentine sculptor fleeing trouble at home was hired to finish it, and he carved an angel bearing a candlestick and the saints Petronius and Proculus: the young Michelangelo.

bran-and-sceolang-fionns-hounds-who-were.context_blurb:
Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the Fianna, the warrior band of the old Irish Fenian tales, roamed Ireland on the hunt, a huge pack of hounds at his heels. Two of them were special, and the tale called The Birth of Bran tells why.

His two favourites were Bran and Sceolang, hounds that could outrun any deer and understood every word their master spoke. They were no ordinary dogs. Their mother was Fionn's aunt, the sister of his mother Muirne, so the two hounds were Fionn's own cousins. One variant makes her Fionn's sister instead, but cousins is how most tellings have it.

Their mother, Uirne, also called Tuiren, married Iollan of the Fianna and was carrying twins when a spell turned her into a hound. Iollan had once loved Uchtdealb, a woman of the Sidhe, the fairy folk who live in the hollow hills, and Uchtdealb came to punish her rival.

Uchtdealb came in the guise of a messenger from Fionn, coaxed Uirne away from home into the forest, and touched her shoulder with a hazel rod, the Irish wood of magic, and Uirne became a hound. When Fionn learned of it, he made Uchtdealb lift the spell, and Uirne was a woman again. Her pups could not change back, because the spell had shaped them from before their birth: they had been conceived under it and born as hounds, and they had never had any other body. Bran and Sceolang stayed hounds all their lives, and Fionn treated them as kin.

One Fenian tradition tells how Sceolang died. In the hunt remembered as the Chase of Thrush Glen, Sceolang and the pack pursued an enchanted deer, half black and half white, and that hunt was her last. Enchanted deer run all through Fionn's stories; his own wife Sadhbh had once worn a deer's shape.

cathbad-the-druid-and-the-prophecy-of-sh.context_blurb:
The old Irish hero tales of the Ulster Cycle centre on Emain Macha, the royal fort of King Conchobar mac Nessa in the north of Ireland. Its chief druid is a seer whose words drive the whole cycle: one prophecy makes a boy into Ireland's greatest hero, and another hangs over a newborn girl like a curse.

The druid was Cathbad, King Conchobar's chief adviser and, in one strand of the tradition, his father; at Emain Macha he taught a band of young pupils to read what each day would bring.

One morning Cathbad told his pupils that any warrior who first took up arms that day would win fame that would last as long as Ireland, but his life would be brief. It is Ireland's version of the choice of Achilles: glory or a long life, never both. Conchobar armed the boy Setanta that same morning. When Cathbad found out, he came to the king in anger, but the boy answered that he would rather have one brief life and undying fame than a long life that no one remembered. That boy grew up to be Cu Chulainn.

Cathbad stood at another cradle too. When Feidlimid's wife bore a daughter, Cathbad foretold that the child, Deirdre, would become the loveliest woman in Ireland and bring disaster on Ulster. The warriors drew their swords and demanded that the baby die, but Conchobar refused: he had her brought up hidden away, out of sight of every young man, meaning to marry her himself when she came of age. She saw Naoise, one of the sons of Uisliu, anyway, and ran away with him.

Cathbad's prophecy had named three things Deirdre would bring on Ulster: blood, ruin and exile. All three came. Conchobar lured the sons of Uisliu home under a promise of safe conduct and had them killed, and in the fighting that followed his royal hall at Emain Macha burned. Fergus mac Roich, Ulster's greatest warrior, had guaranteed their safety, and the treachery shamed him so deeply that he left Ulster for good, took service with Queen Medb of Connacht, and later marched at the head of her army against Ulster in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the Cattle Raid of Cooley.

cu-chulainn-kills-his-own-son-connla-at-.context_blurb:
The Ulster Cycle of Irish myth has many tragedies, and one of the bitterest is the tale called The Death of Aife's Only Son. It tells how the greatest hero of Ulster met a boy on a beach, fought him, and learned too late who he was.

As a young man Cu Chulainn, the Hound of Culann, crossed the sea to learn the arts of war from Scathach, a terrifying warrior-woman who kept her school on the Isle of Shadow. Scathach was at war with a rival warrior-queen, Aife, whose lands lay beside hers; Cu Chulainn beat Aife in single combat but spared her life, and in time she bore him a son.

Before he sailed home he left Aife a gold thumb-ring for the child: when the boy had grown big enough for it to fit his thumb, she was to send him to Ireland, and the ring would let father and son know each other. He also laid three geasa, unbreakable commands, on this unseen son: never turn back once he had set out, never refuse a challenge, and never tell anyone his name.

Years later the boy, Connla, landed on the strand of Ulster, refused to name himself and cut down every champion sent against him. When the news reached Cu Chulainn at Dun Dealgan, his wife Emer ran after him and begged him not to go, because she had guessed who the boy must be. He went anyway. Bound by his father's own geasa, the boy would not give his name, and Cu Chulainn killed him, and only then knew him by the ring.

Stories of a father killing an unknown son in single combat appear far beyond Ireland. Scholars point to the German Hildebrandslied, the lay of Hildebrand and his son Hadubrand, and to Ferdowsi's Persian Shahnameh, in which the champion Rustam kills his son Sohrab and recognises him only by the arm-clasp he had left with the boy's mother. The likeness is so close that some scholars propose a common Indo-European root.

diarmuid-and-grainne-the-elopement-and-t.context_blurb:
The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne is the great love story of the Fenian tales of Ireland. Fionn mac Cumhaill, the ageing leader of the war-band called the Fianna, is to marry a young princess, and she runs away with one of his best young warriors, starting a chase that lasts for years and ends on a mountain in Sligo.

The princess was Grainne, daughter of Cormac mac Airt, the High King at Tara, and she was promised to Fionn though he was by then older than her father. Among Fionn's young warriors was Diarmuid Ua Duibhne, who bore on his forehead a love-spot set there by a fairy woman: any woman who glimpsed it fell helplessly in love with him.

At the betrothal feast Grainne looked at white-haired Fionn and refused him in her heart. She passed round the drinking cups herself and drugged them so that everyone in the hall slept except Diarmuid. Diarmuid refused her out of loyalty to Fionn, so she laid on him a geis, an unbreakable magical command, to run away with her that very night.

Fionn and the Fianna hunted the lovers across Ireland for sixteen years, long enough for them to have five children on the run. Again and again they were saved by Diarmuid's foster-father, Aengus Og, the young god of love of the Tuatha De Danann and lord of the great mound on the Boyne, who hid them in mist and tricked their pursuers, and at last brought about a peace with Fionn.

Years after the peace, Fionn called a great boar hunt on Ben Bulben, the flat-topped limestone mountain with a sheer northern cliff that still looms over Sligo; the poet Yeats is buried in its shadow. The boar had once been a boy, Diarmuid's own half-brother, born to his mother by Roc; Diarmuid's father, Donn, killed the child in a jealous rage, and Roc, a druid, turned the body into a boar bound to be the death of Diarmuid.

The boar gored Diarmuid, though he dealt it a death blow as he fell. Fionn could still save him: since he had tasted the Salmon of Knowledge, well water that he brought could heal any wound, provided he carried it to the wounded man cupped in his two hands. Twice Fionn brought the water, and twice, remembering Grainne and the long humiliation of the chase, he let it run out between his fingers before it reached the wound. The third time he carried it all the way, but Diarmuid was already dead. Grainne cursed Fionn, and the Fianna were never the same.

An old king, a young bride, a young warrior bound by a spell of love, and a long pursuit through the wild: scholars see this tale as an ancestor of the medieval romance of Tristan and Iseult, though they still argue over which way the borrowing ran.

emer-and-the-wooing-cu-chulainns-wife-wh.context_blurb:
The Ulster Cycle is the old Irish treasury of tales about King Conchobar's warriors, and its greatest hero is Cu Chulainn. Most of his stories are battles, but one of the tales gathered around the Tain, Ireland's great cattle-raid epic, is a courtship. Its hero chooses Emer above every girl in Ireland, and her father tries to get him killed.

The tale is called Tochmarc Emire, Old Irish for "The Wooing of Emer." Cu Chulainn found her at her father's fort and spoke to her in riddles, and Emer answered him in riddles of her own, every bit as sharp as his. She was more than a match for him, and he wanted no one else.

Emer's father was Forgall Manach, Forgall the Wily, who kept a fort at Lusk, north of modern Dublin. He hated the match but dared not refuse the hero openly. Instead he came to Conchobar's court in disguise, praised the young man's skill, and told him that no warrior was finished until he had trained overseas with Scathach, the warrior-woman of the Isle of Shadow. Forgall's real hope was that the dangerous journey would kill Cu Chulainn and rid him of the suitor for good.

The trick failed. Cu Chulainn came home alive after a year with Scathach, fully trained, and stormed the fort at Lusk. He cut down two dozen of Forgall's men and carried off Emer and her father's treasure. Forgall himself, fleeing the hero, leapt from the rampart of his own fort and died of the fall, killed by his own walls rather than by any sword.

Years after the wedding, a later tale called Serglige Con Culainn, "The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn," tests the marriage. The hero fell in love with Fand, a fairy woman from under the waves and the wife of the sea god Manannan mac Lir. Emer came to their meeting with a band of women carrying sharp knives, ready to kill her rival. But when Emer saw how deeply Fand loved him, she offered to step aside and leave Cu Chulainn to the fairy. Moved by that generosity, Fand chose to give him up instead and go home to her own husband.

Manannan came for his wife. The sea god shook his cloak between Cu Chulainn and Fand, so that the two would never meet again in this world. Then the druids gave Cu Chulainn and Emer a drink of forgetting, and the marriage went on.

ferdiad-at-the-ford-four-days-killing-a-.context_blurb:
The Tain Bo Cuailnge, "The Cattle Raid of Cooley," is the great epic of ancient Ireland. Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley while a curse keeps every grown Ulster warrior in his sickbed. Only a teenage hero stands in her way, and the saddest fight of his life is against the friend he loved most.

That hero was Cu Chulainn, who held the river fords alone and killed Medb's champions one by one to slow her army. When Medb ran short of men willing to meet him, she turned to Ferdiad mac Damain, the one warrior in her host who had trained beside Cu Chulainn and knew all his feats. Ferdiad's skin was as hard as horn, and no ordinary weapon could pierce it.

The two were foster-brothers. Scathach, the warrior-woman of the Isle of Shadow, had trained them together, and they had learned their feats of arms side by side. So Ferdiad refused to fight his brother. Medb answered by sending her filid, the poets whose satire could raise blisters of shame on a man's face, to threaten him with verses that would ruin his name. Ferdiad decided he would rather fall to spears of valour than to spears of satire, and he went to the ford.

Their fight lasted four days, and the weapons grew heavier each day. On the first, from dawn to noon, they hurled light spears and darts at each other, and for all their skill neither man drew blood. By the third day they were hacking with great swords, and still neither could finish the other.

On the fourth day Ferdiad held his tall shield high against every throw. Cu Chulainn shouted to his charioteer Loeg for the Gae Bolg, the terrible feat Scathach had taught to him alone and to no other pupil, so Ferdiad had no defence against it. Loeg readied the barbed spear in the stream. Cu Chulainn did not throw it by hand: standing in the water, he cast it from the fork of his toes, up under the rim of the shield. It made a single wound going in and opened into thirty barbs inside.

Ferdiad died in the river, and the victory brought Cu Chulainn only grief. The ford took the dead man's name, Ath Fir Diad, the Ford of Ferdiad, and the town that grew beside it carries the name still: Ardee, in County Louth.
