fionn-mac-cumhaill-and-the-salmon-of-wis.context_blurb:
The Fenian Cycle is the body of Irish tales about the Fianna, a roving band of warriors and hunters who guarded the High King of Ireland. Its hero is Fionn mac Cumhaill, Finn MacCool in English, who grew up hidden in the wild, rose to lead the Fianna, and won all the world's wisdom from a salmon. His boyhood tale tells how a hunted orphan earned both his wisdom and his name.

The story begins in blood. Goll mac Morna, leader of a rival clan, had killed Fionn's father Cumhall in battle at Cnucha before the boy was born, and Goll took the captaincy of the Fianna for himself. He would have killed the baby heir too if he could have found him.

To keep the child safe, his mother sent him into the forest of Sliabh Bladhma, where the druidess Bodhmall and the warrior-woman Liath Luachra brought him up in hiding. In those years he went by the name Deimne, a word meaning sureness that also names a young deer. When he was old enough, Deimne went to the River Boyne to learn poetry from an old poet named Finnegas, who lived beside a pool on the river.

Finnegas was waiting for one fish. Nine hazel trees of wisdom grew over the Well of Segais at the Boyne's source, and their nuts dropped into the water; a salmon that ate them had swallowed all the knowledge in the world. Whoever first tasted that salmon would know everything. Finnegas fished for it for seven years before he finally landed it. He gave it to his pupil to cook, with a strict order: cook it, but do not eat a single bite. Then he walked away.

The boy turned the salmon on a spit over the fire, and a blister swelled up on its skin. He pressed it flat with his thumb, the hot juice burst and scalded him, and without thinking he stuck his burnt thumb in his mouth. In that instant all the salmon's wisdom, gathered in that one drop, passed into him.

When Finnegas came back, one look at the boy told him something had happened, and the boy confessed the burnt thumb. The old poet did not rage over his lost years. He said the prophecy had meant a boy named Fionn, "the fair one," so he gave the boy the whole fish and that new name, and Deimne was Fionn from then on. Ever after, Fionn had only to put his thumb to his mouth to know what he needed to know.

The same tale turns up in Norse myth. In the Volsunga saga, Sigurd kills the dragon Fafnir and roasts its heart for the smith Regin; he burns his finger on it, sucks the finger, and at once understands the speech of the birds, who warn him that Regin plans to murder him. In both stories a young man cooking a wonder for someone else gets its gift by accident.

fionn-sleeping-in-the-cave-the-once-and-.context_blurb:
Most heroes of Irish myth have a death-tale. Cu Chulainn died tied upright to a standing stone. But in one Irish folk tradition Fionn mac Cumhaill, chief of the Fianna, never dies at all: he sleeps in a cave beneath a hill with his warriors armed around him, waiting for the hour Ireland needs him most. The idea ties him to King Arthur and to some of the most famous art of the Romantic age.

The warriors of the Fianna lie in a ring on the cave floor, armour on and weapons beside them. At the centre of the ring hangs a hunting horn, the one thing that can wake them. The horn is the Dord Fiann, the horn of the Fianna. Sounded three times, it will wake Fionn and all his men, and the whole company will get up and go out to fight for Ireland.

Once, the story goes, a shepherd wandered into the cave by chance. He lifted the horn down and blew a single blast. All around him the sleepers stirred, rose up on their elbows and opened their eyes, and the terrified shepherd dropped the horn and fled from the cave. As the warriors sank back into sleep, they cried after him that he had left them worse off than he had found them. No one has blown the horn properly since.

The sleeping hero is one of the widest patterns in European legend, and the closest match is King Arthur at Avalon, the misty island of apples, where Malory says some men believe Arthur is not dead but will come again; the Latin verse said to be cut on his tomb names him a king once and a king to come, the once and future king.

Fionn's fame spread far beyond Ireland. In the 1760s a Scottish writer, James Macpherson, published poems he claimed were ancient Gaelic songs by Ossian, son of Fingal, the Scottish form of Fionn's name. They swept Europe: Napoleon carried them on campaign and Goethe quoted them in his novel Werther, though later scholars judged them largely a forgery built on real Fenian oral tales.

The name Fingal also clings to a sea cave on Staffa, an empty island off Scotland's west coast, where waves boom into a hall of six-sided basalt columns. Felix Mendelssohn visited it in 1829 and turned the roll of the swells into his Hebrides overture, often called Fingal's Cave.

But Cu Chulainn's famous horse the Grey of Macha will not let him. The horse turns his left side three times against the charioteer and refuses the harness; only when Cu Chulainn himself comes out does the horse consent — and even then weeps tears of blood onto his master's feet. The charioteer Loeg mac Riangabra, called the 'king of chariot-drivers,' is one of the most beloved of Cu Chulainn's companions and dies beside him at the end. Source: Aided Con Culainn.

oisin-in-tir-na-nog-niamh-of-the-golden-.context_blurb: In the Fenian tale, Fionn's poet-son is carried away over the sea by a woman of the Sidhe named Niamh of the Golden Hair to live on a distant island paradise where he will never grow old. He stays for what feels like three years. When he asks to go home to Ireland, Niamh lets him ride her horse Embarr of the Flowing Mane, warning that his feet must never touch Irish soil. Back in Ireland he finds three hundred years have passed; everyone he loved is dead. Then a strap breaks. The man who finds him is Saint Patrick. Source: Agallamh na Seanorach.

scathach-and-the-isle-of-shadow-cu-chula.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, the greatest teacher of arms in the world is not a druid or a king but a warrior-woman who runs a martial school on a stormy island off the coast of Alba. She takes the boy-hero Cu Chulainn as her pupil. On her island — identified in later tradition with the Isle of Skye — he learns the salmon-leap and twenty-six other feats of arms, meets his future wife Emer's challenger Ferdiad as a fellow pupil, and is given the Gae Bolg. Source: Tochmarc Emire.

setanta-and-the-hound-of-culann-the-boy-.context_blurb: The greatest hero of the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth is not born under the name he dies under. As a boy at Dun Dealgan (modern Dundalk) he is called Setanta — a nephew of King Conchobar mac Nessa, born to Conchobar's sister Deichtine. His father in the divine order is the god Lugh Lamhfhada. The way he gets his adult name is a famous scene: as a boy on his way to a feast at the smith Culann's house, with only a hurling-stick and ball in his hand, he meets the smith's great war-hound head-on. The boy's reward is the smith's new name. Source: Macgnimartha Con Culainn; Tain Bo Cuailnge.

the-cattle-raid-of-cooley-medb-ailill-an.context_blurb: The whole plot of the Irish epic the Tain Bo Cuailnge is set in motion by an argument in their royal bed at Cruachan — Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband King Ailill count up their possessions one evening and discover that Ailill owns a magnificent white-horned bull she has no equal for in her own herd. She determines to steal a rival bull from Ulster to match it. Medb sends ambassadors; her messengers, drunk, boast that they would take the bull by force if refused; the owner refuses; and the great Cattle Raid is on. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

the-champions-portion-at-bricrius-feast-.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle a sharp-tongued poet is so hated for his mischief that when he throws a great feast the warriors will only agree to come if he sits apart in a separate raised gallery, so his poison-verses cannot reach them across the hall. At that feast he stirs up a quarrel between three Ulster champions over who deserves the Champion's Portion of the roast — including a beheading-game with a huge rough herdsman carrying an axe that is the clearest ancestor of the Sir Gawain and the Green Knight story. Source: Fled Bricrenn.

the-curse-of-macha-why-the-ulstermen-lay.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle a supernatural woman comes to live secretly with a widowed farmer named Crunniuc. She blesses his household with prosperity and asks only that he never boast about her to strangers. At King Conchobar's assembly Crunniuc gets drunk and boasts anyway. The king, insulted, forces the woman — nine months pregnant — to race the king's chariot-horses. She wins the race and gives birth on the finish-line. Her dying curse lays the warriors of Ulster, from the ninth generation on, under the pangs of a woman in labour every time an enemy army comes near. That is why Cu Chulainn stands alone. Source: Noinden Ulad.

the-death-of-cu-chulainn-tied-standing-t.context_blurb: The Ulster Cycle names one hero above all — a young warrior of twenty-seven trained on the Isle of Shadow, master of the belly-spear, and the only Ulsterman who fights on when the rest of the province lies helpless under the Curse of Macha. He dies at the end of the cycle's death-tale, the Aided Con Culainn. In that last scene he lashes himself upright to a standing-stone at Clochafarmore in County Louth so that he will die on his feet, and a raven lands on his shoulder only when the hero-light has gone out of him. In 1911 the Oliver Sheppard statue of this death would stand in Dublin's General Post Office for the 1916 Easter Rising. Source: Aided Con Culainn.

the-fianna-entry-tests-and-the-outsize-w.context_blurb: In the Fenian Cycle of Irish myth a roving warrior-band lives in the wild forests of Ireland by season, sworn to defend the High King against foreign invaders in war and to hunt and feast in peace. Their leader is Fionn mac Cumhaill. The entry-tests to join the Fianna were legendary — a candidate had to defend himself with only a shield and a hazel stick against nine warriors throwing spears at him from a distance of nine furrows, to run through a forest without disturbing a plait of his hair, and to leap and stoop under branches at full speed. The poet Caoilte mac Ronain survives to the time of Saint Patrick. Source: Agallamh na Seanorach.

the-gae-bolg-the-belly-spear-cast-with-t.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, the hero Cu Chulainn carries one signature weapon that Queen Medb's warriors dread above every sword he owns — a spear given to him by his teacher on the Isle of Shadow, and the weapon he saves for the fights he is losing. It is cast from between the toes of the foot in the water and, once inside a body, opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb. The flesh has to be cut open around it to remove it. Its first mortal victim is his foster-brother Ferdiad; its last is Cu Chulainn himself, run through by his own weapon in the hands of the sons of Cailitin. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

the-geasa-of-cu-chulainn-taboos-that-sea.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle a druid may lay a magical prohibition on a hero at birth or on any warrior later in life — a single act the man must never do, on pain of ruin. Every hero has his own personalised set of these prohibitions, and cleverness in setting one against another is how enemies in the Irish stories finally bring the greatest heroes down. Cu Chulainn had a famous one: never to eat dog-flesh. The daughters of Cailitin force him to break it on the day of his death. The Greek word moira is a near-equivalent concept. Source: Book of Leinster.

the-giants-causeway-fionn-benandonner-an.context_blurb: On the north coast of County Antrim in Northern Ireland some 40,000 hexagonal stone columns march down out of the cliff and into the sea in a broad, flat pavement wide enough to walk on. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1986. In Irish folklore the pavement was built by Fionn mac Cumhaill as a bridge to walk over the sea and fight a Scottish giant named Benandonner. When he discovered the Scot was far bigger than he was, his wife disguised Fionn as her own baby in the cradle — and when Benandonner saw the size of the baby he decided the father must be unspeakable and ran home, tearing up the stones behind him. Source: Irish folklore.

the-morrigan-war-goddess-in-three-shapes.context_blurb: In the Tain Bo Cuailnge the Irish war-goddess the Morrigan comes to Cu Chulainn at the ford in her most beautiful young-woman shape, in the middle of the war he is holding off alone. She offers him two things together, one of them a gift no goddess offers lightly. He refuses her, and she promises in return to oppose him in the fights to come. Later she comes to him dying — in the shape of an old woman — milking a cow and offering him three drinks. Source: Tain Bo Regamna; Cath Maige Tuired.

the-ristrad-cu-chulainns-warp-spasm.context_blurb: The Tain Bo Cuailnge describes a physical transformation that comes over its young champion when he loses himself in combat: his body reshapes into something no longer human. One eye bulges out onto his cheek, the other sinks back into his skull, fiery flakes rise from his hair, and the hero-light burns above him. Later Irish literature holds this passage — the ristrad — as the signature battle-image of the whole tradition. The parallel to the Norse berserkergangr fury is clear. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge; Book of Leinster.

the-two-bulls-at-the-end-of-the-tain-don.context_blurb: The whole war of the Tain Bo Cuailnge is fought for one thing. Queen Medb of Connacht discovers that her husband Ailill owns a magnificent white-horned bull she has no equal for in her own herd — so she raises an army and marches on Ulster to steal a rival bull to match it. The dark brown Donn Cuailnge is the bull she wants. At the end of the epic the two bulls finally meet, fight a full day and a full night across Ireland, and the whole war ends in their duel. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

charlemagnes-revenge-hanging-ganelon-and.context_blurb:
The Song of Roland, the great French epic written down around 1100, tells how Charlemagne's rearguard was destroyed in the Pyrenees at the pass of Roncesvalles, because a Frankish lord named Ganelon betrayed it to the Saracens. Its last part is the old emperor's revenge.

Charlemagne turned his army back, but he came too late: on the mountainside lay Oliver, Archbishop Turpin, the twelve peers and their young captain, Roland, the emperor's own nephew.

In grief and fury Charlemagne chased the Saracen army deep into Spain and caught it at the Ebro, the great river of the northeast, where the Franks drove the pagans into the water and the current drowned them.

Back at Aachen, Ganelon was put on trial, and Frankish law let the case be settled by a duel, with God giving victory to the just side. Ganelon's kinsman Pinabel fought for him; Thierry, Roland's kinsman, fought for the emperor, and Thierry won. Ganelon was torn apart by horses, and Charlemagne's vengeance reached his whole clan: the thirty kinsmen who had stood surety for Pinabel were hanged that same day.

Even then the emperor got no rest. That night, as he lay in his palace at Aachen, the angel Gabriel came to him in a dream and ordered him to ride to war once more, to rescue King Vivien, whom pagans had shut up in the city of Imphe. The old emperor wept and tore at his white beard, but he rose to obey, and with that the poem ends.

durandal-the-unbreakable-sword-and-the-s.context_blurb:
The Song of Roland, the great French epic written down around 1100, tells of Roland, nephew of Charlemagne and one of his twelve peers, who died holding the pass of Roncesvalles. Roland's sword is almost a character in the poem, and its last scene is a struggle between a dying man and a blade that will not break.

The sword was Durandal, the sharpest blade in Charlemagne's army, and Roland loved it more than his own life. Its name comes from the Latin durare, meaning to endure, so Durandal is the sword that endures, the hard one that will not give way.

Durandal was a holy object as well as a weapon. Its hilt was hollow and held relics: a tooth of Saint Peter, the blood of Saint Basil, hair of Saint Denis and a scrap of the robe of the Virgin Mary. Charlemagne carried a famous sword of his own in the poem: Joyeuse, the joyful one, which shone like the sun and changed its colour thirty times a day.

At Roncesvalles the rearguard was broken, and Roland lay dying. He could not let Durandal fall into pagan hands, so with his last strength he struck the blade again and again on a great rock beside him to shatter it. The sword would not break. In the tradition it was the rock that split beneath the blade, while Durandal stayed whole, true to its name.

Unable to destroy it, Roland hid Durandal beneath his body and lay down with his face turned toward Spain, toward the enemy, so that when Charlemagne came back he would find his nephew fallen forward, still on the attack.

Medieval storytellers after the poem gave Durandal a far older history: it had first belonged to Hector of Troy and passed through many hands across the centuries before it came to Roland, tying the swords of French legend to the heroes of Troy.

el-cid-rodrigo-diaz-exile-of-alfonso-vi-.context_blurb:
Rodrigo Diaz, born around 1043 in Vivar near Burgos in Castile, was the most famous warrior of medieval Spain. The Cantar de Mio Cid, the oldest surviving Castilian epic, tells his story; it was written down around 1207 and mixes real history with legend.

He fought for Muslim emirs as well as Christian kings, and he grew so famous that friends and enemies gave him the same title of honour: El Cid, from an Arabic word meaning lord.

The poem opens with Rodrigo in tears, because King Alfonso VI of Leon and Castile, listening to the whispers of his enemies at court, has unjustly banished him from Castile. The real Rodrigo was exiled twice, in 1081 and 1089, and the poem folds the two into one.

An exile with men to feed must find pay where he can. For years the Banu Hud emirs of Zaragoza, in the Ebro valley, employed the real Cid against their Christian and Muslim enemies, a chapter the poem quietly leaves out. In the poem he carries two named swords: Colada, won from the Count of Barcelona, and Tizona, taken from King Bucar of Morocco.

His greatest prize was Valencia, the rich Muslim city on Spain's Mediterranean coast, which he took in 1094 after a long siege and ruled as his own until he died there in 1099.

The last part of the poem turns on a crime. The Infantes de Carrion, who had married the Cid's daughters Elvira and Sol, took them into the oak wood of Corpes, stripped them, beat them with belts and spurs and left them for dead. Their cousin Felez Munoz rescued them, and the Cid demanded justice from the king. The Infantes were defeated and disgraced, and the king arranged far better marriages for the daughters, to the princes of Navarre and Aragon, so that, the poem proudly says, the kings of Spain descend from the Cid.

A sword in the Museum of Burgos is honoured as Tizona, the blade won from King Bucar. Castile and Leon bought it in 2007 for 1.6 million euros so that it would stay in Spain, though scholars doubt it was ever his.

friar-tuck-the-fighting-friar-with-a-swo.context_blurb:
Friar Tuck is the fat, cheerful fighting friar of Robin Hood's band in Sherwood Forest, a churchman in a rough robe with a rope round his belly who would rather swing a blade than preach. He came late into the legend, and behind him may stand a real outlaw priest.

When Robin first met him beside a river, the friar did not flee or pray; he drew a sword, and he fights with a blade all through the old ballad of Robin and the Curtal Friar. Church law was said to forbid clergy to shed blood, which was part of the joke.

In that ballad Will Scadlock tells Robin about a sturdy friar no man could beat, and the friar turns out to live at Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire, a Cistercian house founded in 1132 that still stands as a great ruin. At the river Robin drew his sword and made the friar carry him over the stream on his back. The friar obeyed without a word, but he had his revenge in midstream, where he dumped Robin into the water.

The two fought with swords in the shallows until both were worn out. Robin blew his horn to call his Merry Men, and the friar whistled up his own pack of mastiffs, huge English guard dogs, which came charging out of the woods. Neither side could beat the other, and the friar ended up joining the band.

The ballad calls him a curtal friar. Curtal comes from an Old French word for short, and a short robe marked a mendicant, a friar who walked the roads living on alms, unlike a monk who stayed inside his monastery walls.

Tuck is missing from the oldest Robin Hood ballads altogether. His name first turns up in a fragment of a play written down around 1475, long after Robin's earliest poems.

There may have been a real Tuck. In 1417 King Henry V twice sent out writs against an outlaw going by the name "Frere Tuk," whose gang robbed and killed and set fire to foresters' lodges in Sussex and Surrey. A letter of 1429 named the man as Robert Stafford, chaplain of Lindfield, a village in Sussex. The ballad friar may have grown up around his memory.

guy-of-gisborne-the-horse-hide-disguise-.context_blurb:
Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne, number 118 in Francis Child's great collection of English ballads, is the darkest of the old Robin Hood songs. It has a monstrous bounty hunter, a duel in Sherwood, a gruesome trophy and a trick of disguise, and it ends with Robin's worst enemy shot through the heart.

The hunter came through Sherwood dressed in the whole hide of a horse, head, mane and tail still on, so that he looked like a monster. He was Sir Guy of Gisborne, and the Sheriff of Nottingham had hired him to bring in Robin for the price on his head.

The ballad begins with a quarrel: Robin and Little John fell out and went separate ways. Alone, Robin met the stranger in the horse-hide. They tried their skill at archery first, but the real fight came with swords, and it went on through two long hours of a summer day, blade hewing at blade.

Robin stumbled over a root, but he recovered and killed Guy with what the ballad calls an awkward stroke. Then he took Guy's head by the hair and stuck it on his bow's end. He drew an Irish knife and slashed the dead man's face until no woman alive could have told who he had been.

Meanwhile the Sheriff had caught Little John in the wood, and his men bound him fast to a tree, meaning to hang him there as soon as word came that Robin was dead.

Robin pulled off his own gown of Lincoln green and flung it over Guy's body, then put on the horse-hide himself, so that the dead man lay dressed as Robin and Robin walked out dressed as Guy. He raised Guy's horn to his lips and blew a loud blast, the signal the Sheriff was waiting for, and the Sheriff rode toward the sound, sure that his hunter had won.

Robin went up to Little John as if to finish him off, but cut his bonds with the Irish knife instead and put Guy's own bow in his hands. The Sheriff fled, and Little John loosed one broad arrow that split his heart in two, so the hunter's bow killed the man who had hired him.

little-john-john-little-of-the-quarterst.context_blurb: Robin Hood's second-in-command in the Merry Men is a giant of a man — the ballads say he stands seven feet tall and is the biggest fighter in the band. Everyone calls him 'Little John' as a joke, because his real birth-name goes the other way. He first meets Robin on a narrow footbridge over a brook, and the quarterstaff-fight they have there (which Robin loses) is one of the most beloved scenes in the whole cycle. His grave is said to be at Hathersage in Derbyshire. Source: A Gest of Robyn Hode; Child Ballads.

maid-marian-the-may-day-queen-who-wander.context_blurb: In the oldest Robin Hood ballads — A Gest of Robyn Hode, Robin Hood and the Monk, Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne — Maid Marian does not appear at all. She came into the Robin Hood cycle from a completely separate tradition of May Day games, in which a shepherdess named Marion was paired with a shepherd named Robin. The two folk-figures gradually fused. In some later versions she is identified with the noblewoman Matilda Fitzwalter. Source: Child Ballads; Pastourelle tradition.

robin-hood-of-sherwood-outlaw-of-the-gre.context_blurb: Robin Hood and his band of outlaws famously live hidden in the trees of one great English forest, in the county of Nottingham in the middle of the country. The ballads dress them in Lincoln green, arm them with the English longbow, and give them a code: rob from the rich, give to the poor, respect women, and defy the Sheriff. The oldest surviving ballads — divided into fyttes, the medieval word for 'cantos' — were written down in the fifteenth century, long after the figure himself. Walter Scott's Ivanhoe (1819) made Robin Hood famous all over again. Source: A Gest of Robyn Hode; Child Ballads.

robins-death-at-kirklees-bled-by-the-pri.context_blurb: Old and worn out from a life in the greenwood, Robin Hood falls ill with a fever and rides to a Yorkshire nunnery for the standard medieval remedy — bleeding. The nun who opens his vein is actually his own cousin, bribed by his enemies. She leaves the vein open too long and he weakens. The ballad ends with Robin, propped up at a window with his bow in his hands, shooting one last arrow and asking Little John to bury him wherever it falls. The spot is still shown to tourists at Kirklees Priory, though souvenir hunters have chipped away pieces over the generations. Source: Robin Hood's Death, Child Ballad 120.

roland-at-roncesvalles-the-rearguard-bet.context_blurb: Charlemagne's army is marching home from a long campaign in Spain and must cross the Pyrenees mountains through a narrow gorge that only a small unit can hold at a time. Charlemagne's own stepfather Ganelon has secretly promised the Saracen king that the French rearguard will be there alone. Charlemagne's nephew Roland and his twelve peers — including his dearest friend Oliver and the warrior-archbishop Turpin — hold the pass against hopeless numbers. The pass gives its name to the whole disaster. Source: La Chanson de Roland.

the-archery-contest-at-nottingham-robin-.context_blurb: In the earliest surviving Robin Hood poem, the Sheriff of Nottingham announces a great archery contest in the town square, hoping Robin Hood will not be able to resist trying to win it. The prize is a single valuable object every English yeoman covets. Walter Scott, writing more than three centuries later in a famous Scottish historical novel of 1819, famously embellished this contest: he set it in Leicestershire, had Robin shoot in disguise under a chosen alias, and added a cinematic ending that was polished further still by the Hollywood swashbuckler of the 1930s. Source: Child Ballads; Scott's novel.

the-cid-conquers-valencia-siege-feast-an.context_blurb: The Cantar de Mio Cid tells us that the Cid rings the city of Valencia and settles his warband in for a long, patient blockade. The poem states plainly how many months the warband penned the city in before it was starved into surrender. After the victory he sends to the monastery of San Pedro de Cardena where his wife Dona Jimena and daughters Elvira and Sol have been living, and brings them to Valencia to see the city from the tower. The daughters are then betrothed to the Infantes de Carrion. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid.

the-cid-dead-on-horseback-strapped-to-ba.context_blurb: The great warrior-hero of medieval Castile, Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar, is remembered across Spain by a shorter Arabic title given him by his Muslim opponents, meaning lord or master. He dies of illness while his newly-conquered Mediterranean port is besieged by a North African army of Berber reformers. In the legend his wife has his body strapped upright onto his famous warhorse and sent out at the head of his men to lead the final charge; the besiegers break and run believing they are facing him in life. Source: Cantar de Mio Cid; later chronicles.

the-sheriff-of-nottingham-the-unnamed-vi.context_blurb: In the ballads of Robin Hood, one royal officer sends his men into Sherwood again and again to catch Robin and hang the outlaws from the walls of his stone castle in Nottingham. His title comes from the Old English 'shire-reeve' — the king's representative in a county, in charge of collecting taxes by farming them out to local collectors. In the ballads he is never given a personal name; later tradition sometimes identifies him with the historical sheriff Philip Marc of King John's reign. Source: Child Ballads.

will-scarlet-much-the-millers-son-alan-a.context_blurb: In the Robin Hood ballads, Robin's outlaw band living in the forest with him has a famous nickname. Besides Robin's giant second-in-command, the band usually includes a hot-tempered swordsman in red, a stout miller's son good with the quarterstaff, and in later versions a wandering minstrel whom Robin rescues from a forced marriage. They all wear the band's uniform of the forest-green cloth woven in Lincoln. The core group grows out of English May Day folk-games as much as out of any historical outlaw tradition. Source: Child Ballads.
